en: Massaging his feet bestows some indescribable wisdom and prosperity;
by opening one's eyes to him, the darkness of foul odors is forever stilled;
and the water used as an offering for his feet, having washed away all evil, grants the highest beatitude.
May Hari, whose true nature is ineffable, dwell forever within our hearts— he who bears ascetic penances as if they were his own heroic exploits, and in whom there is no fear nor any limit.

He who, like a gift bestowed upon his enemies, brought about the conquest of his senses through knowledge; he who, like a sovereign over emperors, was the teacher even to yogins within the circle of the earth; that illustrious Laksmanasena alone was both a king and one liberated while yet living. (1)
He had a friend named Śrīvaṭudāsa, who was the crest-jewel among the great feudatories who followed the conduct of rival kings, and the sole vessel of incomparable affection.
Day after day removing the heat and the darkness while bestowing the moonlight of fame,
he is the manifest treasury of all arts, consisting of the nectar of imperishable truth.

From him was born the illustrious Śrīdharadāsa, a repository of supreme virtues, in whose house— being perpetually devoted to manly valor from his very childhood— the goddess Lakṣmī resided, and who was constantly celebrated in the assemblies of the learned for his mastery of the Vedas.
Devotion finds its rest in the moonlight of the toenails upon the lotus-feet of the Lord of Śrī.
This [work] of the poets consists of five verses for each of the sense-objects.

May connoisseurs long immerse themselves in these five streams here, filling the hollows of their ears and causing the joy of the *Śrīsūkta*— this nectar for the ears— to blossom forth, produced by that kinsman who acts without cause. 4.
The immortals [the authors], through five streams consisting of the erotic, the flattering, and the high and low [styles] under various pretexts, compose this *Saduktikarṇāmṛta* in due order. (5)
Thus, with these five streams, the *Saduktikarṇāmṛta* is composed;
[these are] the waves of the stream of the immortals.
Now, [the topics are] Dhātṛ, Ravi, the prostrations to Īśa, Mahādeva, Śiva, Hara, his sports,
questions and answers, his loud laughter, and the Gaṅgā on the highest part of his head.
The moon upon his crown, the garland of severed heads, the eye that destroyed the cities of the enemy,
the form of the fire-stone for the arrows of Śiva, and the commencement of the Tandava dance performed by Bhairava and Hara.
Then there is the dance that propitiates Hara, Gaurī, the Gaurī of the wedding,
the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) of the Mountain’s Daughter, Durgā, Kālī, and likewise Ardhanārīśa. ||3 3||
The amorous Pramathas, who bear the bee born from the arrow of the elephant-faced one;
then Hari and Hara with their consorts; and the celestial river’s praise for the daughter of Jahnu.
The Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, the Man-Lion, and the one born from the hand; the Erotic Man-Lion, Vāmana, Trivikrama, and the son of Bhṛgu.

This son of Daśaratha is now separated [from Sītā]; meanwhile, the childhood and boyhood of Kṛṣṇa— the wielder of the plow (Balarāma), the Conqueror (the Buddha), and Kalkin— along with his youthful sports, have become as if seen in a dream.
The question and answer, the sounding of the flute, the song, the arm, the supporting of the mountain,
the longing, the message from the cowherd women, Hari, and devotion to him.

Hari, who churned the ocean; the self-chosen husband of Lakṣmī arising from the churning of the sea; the embodiment of Śrī and Śṛṅgāra; born from the lotus-like lap of Kamalā; and whose praise is like the auspicious moon.
The digit of the moon, the lunar orb, the full moon, the radiant moon, its rays, the moonlight, and the state of the moon accompanied by its spot, darkness, and night-blooming water lilies. ||9||9||
Then there were clouds of mixed many forms that had reached the various regions, the wind,
the ocean at dawn on the southern shore, and the flower-bowed god of love.
Thus, this *Devapravāha*, characterized by the manifold heroism of Smara, has been composed by the skilled Śrīdharadāsa in ninety-five verses consisting of five parts.
Devapravāha:
1. Now, Brahmavīci was the sole direct friend of Śambhu; another was Dharmarāja, who was devoted to the Lord of the Gods.

"Whose life-breaths are they? Who has arrived first? And who indeed is to be addressed?"—knowing that these were the four world-protectors who had come for some purpose, may the Lotus-born One protect you, speaking simultaneously with his four faces in a voice raised at once.
O you who were cherished by Pālita, O destroyer of Kālanemi, [I am here] in anger for the purpose of striking you.
I believe that the Goddess Śrī, her mind bewildered by fear produced by the churning of her own abode, exerted herself to transform the lotus at the navel [of Viṣṇu] into a weapon;
may the words of the ancient sage, who was intent on protecting the Brahmins from such agitation, be gracious unto you. 2.
Of Bhaṭṭa Śrīnivāsa. (Sū.mu.
2.108) May He who is intent on awakening Viṣṇu for the sake of slaying the formidable Madhu and Kaiṭabha protect you!
The Creator’s four faces became simultaneously meaningful for him:
one face praised Śivā; another, distressed, begged for boons; a third threatened the two Daityas; and the other removed the confusion of Lakṣmī. 3.
That which was never before pierced by the rays of the moon, which cause a mass of frosty droplets to flow, [was pierced] by Vasantadeva.

May the luster of the teeth of the Creator’s first-born protect you—luster that, like the solar rays which are kin to the lakes of fresh lotuses, dispels the dense darkness clinging to the end of an aeon; and which, having issued from the moon-like face of the Creator during his initial act of creation, spreads rapidly in every direction. 4.
O Bījakasvāmin,
from that crushing defeat you suffered at the hands of the Kāpālika and others, your humiliation arose.

May he protect you for a long time— he who, when Guha repeatedly spoke out of childishness, "Let him be named Brahmā and so forth," saw that Gaurī was unable to stop the six-faced one's words with her two hands, and thus turned away fruitlessly from his four faces out of embarrassment.
5 (Su.Ra. 101, Sū.Mu. 2.105) 2. Sūryaḥ (The Sun)
To the one who is like a sapphire-stone upon the hood of the lordly serpent of the lofty mountain of sunrise, whose golden shoots are the trees of the sapphire sky,
and who is the caravan-leader for the multitude of yogis seeking to cross the ocean of saṃsāra.
Salutation to Savitṛ, who carries the full water-pot at his departure;
[this is] of Varāhamihira (Su. Ra. 1.50).

Salutations to you, the sleep that withers the clusters of lotuses, acting as a perfected elixir for the eye-sockets of the three worlds obstructed by the mass of darkness spreading in every direction.
To Divākara, whose hands are raised for the purpose of putting [enemies] to flight;
[this is the mantra] of Śrīkaṇṭha.
I worship the risen orb of the sun, which possesses the luster of a parrot’s beak, which is the friend of the forest of white lotuses, and which is like an earring upon the quarter of Indra.

May the twilight—the vermilion seal of the sky-tree, which has not fallen from its place, and which is the friend of the grove of night-lotuses—be victorious for the theft of darkness. (Su.ra. 149, Śā.pa. 86)
The Sun is the family umbrella of the Raghus, possessing the pale-red luster of the *kampilla* leaf, over the mass of Gaurī’s lord’s celestial tresses which are like clusters of *mandāra* flowers.
The moon is the elder brother of Hari, the churning mountain for the ocean of passion of the female cakora birds,
the life-giver of the lotus, and the crest-jewel of the king of mountains in the direction of Indra.
The Sun, the ordainer of the rites prescribed by the Vedas, the final oblation for the fire of sorrow of the night-lotus,
the elixir of Soma, and the seed of the universe— victory to him!
3. Obeisance to the Lord:
Even when the crown rises upward with speed, it remains bowed due to the surface of the earth sinking under the weight of his feet.

Salutations to you, the destroyer of the world’s afflictions and the slayer of Tripura; you who are praised by the assemblies of the foremost gods rejoicing in the unimpeded stability of the heavenly realm; you whom the Daughter of the Mountain did not abandon, even while she was bound by the incessantly throbbing right arm as she fled in terror.
Of Bāṇa: (Su.ra.
56) Salutations to the one who is beautiful with the moon as a chowrie kissing his lofty head;
To Śambhu, the foundational pillar for the construction of the city of the three worlds. (Su.Ra. 48)

This earth, surrounded on all sides by as many vast continents and sky-scraping mountains sealed by seven such oceans, appears like a horizontal dark spot upon the expansive jewel of his hood because it serves as his dwelling place.
Even that remainder went to the feet of Aṅgada; homage to that Śambhu!
(13.13) — by Ballaṇa (Su.ra. 38).
Salutations to that certain Being, who restrains speech, mind, and senses, whom this community of sages worships as the Lord consisting of light,
reflected in the multitude of mirrors of wisdom received from their gurus.
The darkness of ignorance, shattered by the rising moonlight of his own bliss, [belongs] to Hari. ||14||14|| Of Hari.
O bull-bannered one, beloved of the Giver of Wealth, whose half is the beloved,
skilled in the art of composition, born from the mind of the wise, destroyer of the cities,
moon-crested one, crest-jewel!
O Dhūrjaṭi, who causes terror to the serpents, salutations to you! [15] —
by Bhojadeva.
4. Mahādeva is his craft; the three worlds are his poetry; he who made the three Vedas for his Guru;
he who brought about the destruction of Tripura; and upon whose head the triple-pathed river (Gaṅgā) serves as a garland.
Victorious is that god whose weapon is the trident, who bears three blazing eyes as if to behold the three times, and who is the discernment of the three qualities (guṇas).
By Vasukalpadatta. (Su.ra.

30) May that unprecedented Sthāṇu protect you—he whose five branches bend downward, who possesses a shimmering circle of matted locks above, and who, though eternally leafless (*aparṇa*), dispels the threefold affliction of those who take refuge in him.

He whose matted locks on the head are arranged in the style of childhood and who receives the sprinkling of the waters of the celestial river, bears fruit— a hundredfold fulfillment of the desires— of those who possess devotion.
Do not desire Jahnu’s son as your object of passion, nor do you excessively honor even a bull; do not set your minds on wealth,
but take refuge here in that one art which has the fruit of immortality.

Thus may the Lord, the enemy of Smara, protect you—he who, though possessing a form that makes the bull his mount, is himself like one without wealth as he desires to bestow the instruction of the universe; he whose crest is adorned by the digit of the nectar-rayed moon.
May the poet-scholar Śrī Harṣa protect you—he who, under the guise of his prosperity, bears the earth; under the pretext of the river of the city of the gods, he carries water;
under the guise of the eye on his forehead, he bears fire; and under the pretext of the breath of the lord of serpents, he carries the wind.
May the moon-crested Lord grant you prosperity— he who perpetually expands the universe through the five elements, using the semblance of the vast cavity of his non-terrible (Aghora) face as the sky.
For Jayadeva, food is the same whether it be nectar or poison; his dwelling is the same whether in heaven or in a cremation ground;
and he makes no distinction between carrying water or fire.
Spending his time equally through both sovereignty and mendicancy,
the God who is curious about his own self— may that Hara sever the noose of saṃsāra for you from every side.
To Śiva, whom those learned in the Vedāntas call the One Supreme Person who stands pervading heaven and earth—of Vaidya Gadādhara. 5. Śiva.

May that Sthāṇu— who is sought by those desiring liberation through the control of their vital breaths and other faculties, as the word "Lord" (Īśvara) whose syllables are true to their meaning refers to no other object, and who is the inner witness—
be for your ultimate bliss, being easily attained through the yoga of steadfast devotion. 21.
By Kālidāsa.
(Vikramorvaśīya 1.1) [May Śiva protect you], who, under the guise of the shadow of his throat, makes the night of the kalpa appear as day, and whose crest-jewel is the Mandākinī.

May Śiva protect you— he who, under the pretext of raising his eyes upward, draws up the ocean of universal dissolution with his form; who, by the guise of sporting with his serpentine ornaments as if drinking from it, withdraws even the forty-nine winds at the conclusion of the kalpa.
In one place there is fire, in another a mountain; in one place it is strewn with human heads, and in another a river.
In one place there are coarse matted locks, elsewhere venomous serpents, and in another, fierce poison;
surrounded by such hosts of spirits and variegated with waves of funeral ash, this is the auspicious path for one who has abandoned worldly existence and departs so as never to return. (23)
Bilhaṇa’s creator himself, who by his speech restrains the voice for the sake of the world alone;
He extends enjoyments for the sake of the universe while his senses and mind are withdrawn from sense-objects;

he wields weapons to protect the worlds yet remains indifferent even to the preservation of his own body—may that Sadāśiva, the lord of yogis who is devoted to the welfare of others, be for your prosperity. (24)
When the Lord of Birds had flown far away and Murabhid (Viṣṇu) had cast his arms around Vaidya Gadādhara to seize him;

May Śiva protect the three worlds—he whose mind is established in the bliss of steady yoga, while the host of world-protectors bows down as the battle-array spreads and the wind is hushed; he whose serpent-garland remains motionless, whose crest-moon does not waver, and whose celestial river flows undisturbed. 25.
Of that very [person],
the erotic sentiment (harasṛṅgāra).
"O fair-browed one, hold your creeper-like arms thus;
take this stance, not too high, with your toes slightly bent; look at me for a moment as I dance Gaurī to the sound of my cloud-rumbling mouth-drum."
May the clapping rhythms of Śambhu, struck at the precise moments when the tempo is broken, bring you happiness.
(Su.ra. 60) — by Yogeśvara.
Her name was uttered by me somehow or other through delusion;
you surely know my intention. O Gaurī, be gracious for my sake; let forbearance be accepted, O compassionate one, and let your anger toward me be abandoned.
May the joined palms of love of the enemy of Smara (Śiva), who spoke thus at length, protect you.
Cakrapāṇi’s.
"O beautiful one, the moon, the child, having been nourished by streams of flowing nectar,
falls asleep; the lord of serpents has his celestial river obstructed by the creepers of his matted locks"—
thus did Śiva speak to Pārvatī, who was bashful during that playful dalliance of love.
May the crescent-moon crest-jewel [of Śiva], awakening his new bride, protect you!
[28] Of the *kakkola*.
The hearing of the Daughter of the Mountain was fixed on her charming speech;
her eyes fell upon the moon of her face; her tongue was submerged in the sweet nectar of her bimba-like lower lip; and her nose rested upon its own fragrance.
In the bliss of a long embrace, even the body of the Destroyer of Cities (Śiva) has dissolved—
by Umāpatidhara.
"O you who frequent the distant forest of wood! Abandon now these false flatteries; if I were to ever do so again, then the moon would fall to the earth!
Thus was the moon-crested Lord addressed by the Daughter of the Mountain, as he reached out to grasp the moon upon his crest.
May he, whose beloved is pleased by the falling at his lotus-feet—a gesture manifested through artifice—protect you.
(30) By the poet-scholar Śrī Harṣa. (Sū.mu. 2.8)
7. The Question and Answer of Śiva and Pārvatī:
"O Pārvatī, why are you so harsh? This is the innate nature of those born of the mountains. Why are you devoid of affection? Ashes are rough; they never disparage affection."
"Your anger toward me is fruitless; what fruit could there be in [directing it] at an immovable pillar? Thus was Śambhu rendered speechless by his beloved; may he bring you prosperity.
By Bhojadeva (Su.ra.
35): "O Gaurī, why are you angry with me? Am I not a cow? To whom should I be angry? 'With me'—by such inference [I understand]."
I know the truth even from your very name; yet,
these crooked words of the Mountain-born Goddess triumph in this way.

By Rudraṭa (Kāvyālaṅkāra 2.15, sū.mu. 99.6): "Who is this [woman] on my head? Why is there darkness here? O fair-browed one, why is there gloom when the moon of your face is present? And where is my beloved? "Right here, O lover! "But surely it is water! This much was asked by Umā.
"I shall not engage in a duel; remove her from my head this very instant"—may that enemy of Manmatha, who spoke thus while rendered speechless by your reply, protect you all.
Someone said:
"O Hara, O fair-limbed one, whose is this? Which one is situated upon your head? Is it matted hair, or does the swan resort to the matted hair? No, it is not the moon; the moon resorts to the water."
"O simple girl, this is ash; where is there water here? The ash is merely rippling.
May that Śṛṅgāra protect you, who thus conceals the triple-pathed river (the Gaṅgā).
Of someone:
"Blessed one, who is this who stands upon your head? What indeed is her name? Her very name is 'Śaśikalā' (Moon-crested); why have you forgotten even that which was so familiar to you?"

"I ask the woman; let Indu [the moon] say," said Vijayā, "if the moon is not authoritative, since the Goddess wishes to conceal it. May this deception of the Lord toward the celestial river protect you!
By Viśākhadatta. (Mudrārākṣasa 1.1, Sū.mu. 99.1) 8. Hara’s laughter, a bracelet on his hand, the lord of serpents with upraised hood, and an eye of blazing fire—

May the emergence of laughter from Paśupati protect you—a laughter manifested by the throbbing of his cheek at the thought that the bridegroom’s attire was so charming as to captivate the eyes of Gaurī: a throat curved like the deadly Kālakūṭa poison, and a garment of the hide of a lordly elephant. 36.
By Rudraṭa.
(Śṛṅgāratilaka 3.2a) Whose half-moon is made to blossom by the unrestrained luster of his teeth...

May the loud laughter of Śambhu as he dances— the laughter whose resonance is as deep as a mass of clouds and which dispels the obstruction of dense darkness with its moonlight— grant you prosperity. (37)
Of Saṅghamitra. (Su.Ra.
41) "Mother, tell me: what is this that Father has hidden in his hollowed palms?"

"Child, it gives sweet fruit; do not go, take it yourself"—when Guha was thus sent by his mother, may the outburst of laughter from Śambhu protect you, as he broke the meditative concentration of him whose mind was restrained, drawing away his joined palms at twilight. 38.
Of Yogeśvara. (Su.Ra.
59) The river of the world of the gods, pure with the essence of camphor, flows without obstacle.

May the waves of laughter of Śambhu protect you— laughter whose splendor fills the intervening space with the movement of arms rivaling great surges, which draw their life-force from the nectar-dripping moon swaying during his dancing movements, and which possess the flickering glances of playful serpents as their guardians. 39.
O Vācaspati, who is Bhṛṅgī? O Carcikā, who is Guha? There is no one for you; yet there is but one form for us two.
"Truly, Bhṛṅgiriṭi, truly; Moṭi would say the world is false!
Ask him nakedly whether your two of you are of one mind regarding marriage!"—may that outburst of laughter from Paśupati, as he dismissed those two along with their retinue, protect you. (40)
[The head of Hara],
from which the Gaṅgā flows, upon which a crescent moon rises, and from which rows of skulls fall away;

May the head of Dhūrjaṭi protect you— its mass of thick, tawny, and fierce matted locks loosened by exhaustion from the intensity of his violent dance, as he stumbles under the weight of that exertion, while a loud whirring sound expands from the gathering of fierce winds swirling within his chest.
Of Vīryamitra. (Su.Ra.
42) The worlds shine within the belly of Khaṇḍaparaśu, who dances at the twilight.
His head has the crescent moon licked by the flames of fire arising from the cavity of his forehead-eye;

it bears a falling hide, from which great serpents slither, while the waters of the celestial river flow down, and the mass of his matted locks whirls about with the flickering brilliance of leaping fragments of the moon. 42.
The throbbing face of the Lord of Yoga, which is unfamiliar with the rising of smoke and has never experienced the dominion of impurity.

May the head of the Lord of Beings— where the waters of tossing waves meet, where the skull is awakened by a touch that is free from blemish, where the beloved night is unknown, and where the serpent-garland is unaware of its harming of living beings— grant you a continuous succession of blessings, for it is exceedingly wonderful. (43)
Turbulent with the flow of the waters of the triple-pathed river (Ganges) issuing forth from the force of the dance of Vaidya Gadādhara.
Terror-inspiring with the lightning-flames from the eye on his forehead due to its rapid blinking,
and producing a roar by the friction of the wind rushing through the hollows of the rows of skulls—
may the cloud that is Śiva’s head, risen like the monsoon season, bring you prosperity. 44.
Of someone [there was] the interior taken possession of by the waters of the Ganges, with exceedingly spontaneous sprouts of jewels.

May the head of Dhūrjaṭi—the sole full pitcher for the pacification of obstacles for those setting out from here toward the city of liberation—grant you the attainment of the marvelous; its crown is like a shimmering sprout upon the circle of hoods of the lordly serpent Śreṇīśoṇa. 45.
The moon in the water;
10. The Gaṅgā on the head of Hara.
Deep in the hollow of his skull, thin within the joints of his matted locks, broad upon the contact with the crest-jewel of the serpent coiled around his head,
and soft at the corner of the crescent moon trembling in its swift course; The light of Śiva’s eye, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf, rests upon the forehead of the Lord of Creatures.
May the tumultuous roar of the Gaṅgā upon the head of Hara purify you for a long time.
(Su.ra. 53) — by Yogeśvara.
Victorious is that flood of Ganges water resting upon the lofty crown of Śambhu,
wherein the digit of the moon sinks and rises again like a minnow.
Of someone: (Su.ra.
45) That which wandered through the tawny mass of matted locks of Hara, which possessed the state of being like the buds of the rays of ten million moons.
May that water of the celestial river Ganges purify you— water which resounds with the majestic roar of its splashing against the rocky bowers of the Himalayan mountains.

To someone [it occurs]: “O Mother Bhāgīrathī, salutations to you, who are doubly profound upon the head of Hara, which is crowded by his half that is being divided by Gaurī. (Sāhityadarpaṇa-kārikā 1.77) ||49||
Of someone: (Su.ra. 78, Sū.mu.
1.24) Resembling pearls in human skulls and shells, and resembling jasmine in the creepers of matted hair;

May the droplets of the Ganges water protect you—droplets that appear like parched grain amidst the multitude of serpents upon the mass of Shiva’s coils, which resemble jewels; droplets tossed upward by the surging waves of the dancing whirlpools as they play upon the head of Hara. (50)
[The verse] of Naḍagāṅgoka (Śā.p. 106, Sū.mu. 2.53).
11. The moon on the head of Hara.
May that moon protect you— curved like the tip of a fresh,
broad vine, resting upon the fire-tawny head of the Enemy of Smara, and shining with the water of the Mandākinī flowing daily from his sprinkling.
Like a sprout released from a crystal-white skull— this is by Rājaśekhara (Su.ra. 46).

Triumphant is the shimmering play-moon of the Conqueror of Smara, who has placed his crown at Pārvatī’s feet; for, upon her slight offense, the beauty of her tears— marked by falling drops of collyrium— gradually faded away.
Filling the ears with their own moonlight-like rays from the jewels of their nails—
[this is] by Vāmana.
May the digit of the moon of Śambhu grant you auspiciousness— that digit whose reflection,
fallen into the triple-streamed Ganges, has assumed manifold curvatures through its waves,
and which the General Kātyāyanī gazes upon by the tilt of her banner-cloth.
The lord of the nāgas [offered] a garland of jasmine out of a desire for his own wife's awakening,
for the sake of the Lord of Umā.

Victorious is the Mandākinī, which flows from the trembling crest of the Lord of Girijā; it possesses the luster of unblemished white lotuses, touches the shimmering rows of foam, displays the graceful movements of flocks of swans, and bears the playful leaps of small fish.
The rays of the moon, kissing the mass of waves—
by Umāpatidhara.

May that Śiva and the Daughter of the Mountain protect you— he whom the mountain-born goddess, with a smiling face, addressed after she had fashioned a circle from a fragment of the moon’s digit and a bracelet broken in a lovers’ quarrel, saying, "Whoever shall see this..."
And that Kṛṣṇa, the moon of play, has his digits filled by the rays of his teeth.
(Vararuci) (Su.ra. 47, Sv 66, Śā.pa. 96)

The flame-like matted locks of Hari, spreading upwards, resemble the splendor of an anthill— the dwelling place of serpents that are like waves of the Ganges water— resulting from the ripening of the inner heat of his asceticism.
May the mass of Shambhu’s matted locks— tawny like the rays of the young sun, and cohabiting with the moon whose body is as tender as moist lotus stalks— protect you all.
Of the Lord of the Rakshasas: (Su.ra.
55) [The nectar] of the crescent moon licked by the wives of the fish and tortoises, which expands with the flames of poison issuing from the hissing hoods of Vasuki bound as a crest-ornament.

May the mass of matted locks of the Destroyer of Smara protect you— locks that were seized by the hair during his amorous play with Madana, and which were glared upon with anger by the Daughter of the Mountain as the celestial river flowed [from her eyes].
In Bhavabhūti’s work, there is at times the celestial river, at times a skull,
at times serpents, and at times the crescent moon.
Thus may the forest of matted locks belonging to the Lord of the Pramathas, endowed with these uneven ornaments, protect you.

May the forest of matted hair of the Lord of Bhavānī bear fruit for your welfare— [a forest] which, with the flames of his eyes leaping up like staffs, appears as if in full bloom through the rays of the moon, and which, with its serpent-creepers, seems as if it were covered in blossoms.
The row of withered skulls of the Creator bears the playful charm of massive, shimmering globules of foam from the overflowing stream of the celestial river that swirls around its edges.
The roots of Umāpati’s [tree] have their basins formed by the great serpent king coiled around them,
and they are watered by the surging floods of the celestial river as it flows down.
May the matted locks of Śambhu, which release flowers like moons and are golden wish-fulfilling creepers, bear fruit for the welfare of the worlds. 60.60
May the skull of Hara be for your peace; may the garland of skulls of the Lord of the worlds [bring] your welfare— [the garland] whose inscription...
In various places, the hosts recite word by word with not very well-known syllables:

"He will create the universe, he will speak, he will rule over the earth, he will be taught, he will tend the serpents, he will take delight among those possessed of passion, he will destroy the world, and he will enjoy the heavens. (61)
Of someone: (Su.ra.
54) From the hoods of serpents whose throats are distorted by the expansion of tight knots, and from which the fire of poison issues forth—

May the rows of skulls of Bhairava, strung together with elephant trunks, protect you— those skulls whose ghostly state has been dispelled by the essence of nectar melting from the moon scorched by his flames, which gape open and repeatedly gaze with tawny eyes out of thirst for blood.
By Bhavabhūti. (Su.ra.
39) Victorious is he who [releases] the moon squeezed by the knot of the serpent’s rope...
Upon the head of the Enemy of Tripura, there was immediately fashioned a garland of skulls from which the state of being a ghost had ceased through the flowing of nectar—
the very sound of the Veda of the Brahmās who have completed many kalpas.
Of someone: [The world] was scorched by the heat of the spreading mass of flames from the blazing mouth of the one who has an eye on his forehead. (Sāhityadarpaṇa-kārikā 1.84)

May the skulls of the moon-crested Lord— whose heads nod in the joy of inner dancing and which bear the weight of millions of fainting stars— bring you prosperity as they drip nectar from the crescent moon fixed upon them during the grand displays of his *tāṇḍava* dance while he utters your hymn of praise. May that Narasimha protect you— He upon whose head, during the performance of his Tandava dance, the serpent was distressed.

Some sustain themselves by the nectar of the moon from the crest [of Śiva] melted by the fire of his breath; some recite the *Ṛg* and *Sāman* hymns; some immerse themselves in the waters of the Gaṅgā;
some meditate upon their own Self; and some offer oblations into the fire of their eyes.

The world of the Lord was filled with jars dark as smoke, with mountains whose slopes were clearly splintered by thunderbolts,
with the waters of the ocean violently plundered by storms, with the sun obscured by flickering light, with rushing rivers overflowing in pride, and with worlds trembling in extreme terror.
May the rays of light rising from the eye of the Destroyer of Tripura nourish you.
[By] Someone.

That light which consists of twelve suns; that lamp for the nocturnal dalliance of the Daughter of the Snowy Mountain; that line of flames within the fire of youth which reduced the bones of Kandarpa to ashes;
and that meritorious fire of the Creator as he offered the oblation of the three worlds as fuel at the end of the aeon.

Stilled by bliss during their meditations, languid with grace in his presence,
bewildered for a moment and then struck with wonder, smiling at his own transformation,
yet cruelly squinting in revulsion when the Mind-born God drew his bow and was consumed— such were the glances of Gaurī.
May the glances of Śambhu protect you— glances tremulous with tears shed by his beloved as she wept.
(68) [By someone.]
In him, who was like a single speck of the tawny hue of a row of eyelashes compared to the entire mass of lightning-flashes,
the Sacrificer of Time offered the universe as an oblation within his slightly opened bud-like mouth;
the flame of that sacrifice resounded with a terrifying *jhāṅkāra* from the corners of his eyes, which were dripping with nectar falling from the moon upon his scorched crest.
May that third eye of the Enemy of Tripura, which was inflamed by the affliction of passion, protect you. (Bhavabhūti, *Mālatīmādhava* 1, after 5.2; *Śārṅgadharapaddhati* 99)
One eye was half-closed due to the application of yoga; the second was languid with the sentiment of love upon the slopes of Pārvatī’s breasts and hips;
while the other was inflamed by the fire of the wrath of Madana, who had drawn his bow far back.
May the three eyes of Śambhu, which possess distinct aesthetic sentiments during the moment of meditative absorption, protect you.
By Śrī Harṣadeva.

15. The commencement of the burning of Tripura: as the chariot, having lost its support, began to sink down to the very bottom of the earth due to the forceful placement of his feet upon the body of the all-enduring Earth, it fell unsteadily.
Now that the city of Maya has passed beyond the range of the Lord of Beings' vision, may your effort toward the swift discharge of the arrow from the earth lead to your welfare.
And [the temple] of Vaidya Gadādhara,
whose outer corners of the eyes are adorned with the coils of serpents retreating from the raised arm,
and whose vicinity to the shore is pervaded by the ocean surging forth in pursuit of his *pratyālīḍha* stance.

May the majesty of the Moon-crested Lord— the destroyer of the city of Māyā— be for our auspiciousness; his beauty consists of the crescent moon hanging from his matted locks, which are loosened by the fire blazing upon his forehead.

The moon in the water was flickering upon the silken fringes of their garments, still within the strands of their braided hair, dimly visible at the seams of their bodices, and like a blazing flame upon the slopes of their breasts.
Victorious is the Lord, whose eyes are moist with compassion, who, upon seeing the smoke-bannered fire [of Śiva] within the inner apartments of Tripura, lowered his bow from his hand.
Of the Peacock: (Su.ra.
61) When the Lord of Birds, exhausted by the sparks of the fire born from his eyes during sleep, had rushed forth in the hope of seizing the Ancient Puruṣa who had become speech;
Victorious is the limit of the aim of the Destroyer of Cities, whose bow was drawn by the string of the virtues of the preeminent serpent-king bowed in homage, as he discharged his weapon.
Of Murāri: (Ar.

7.114, Su.Ra. 31) He was gazed upon with love by the Goddess; with fear and agitation by the Asura women; with compassion by the sages, whose inner essence of reality was stilled; and with a smile by Viṣṇu, who asked, "What is this?"

May Dhūrjaṭi protect you— he who, when the city of Maya was being consumed by fire, was joyfully watched by the gods and by the proud Daitya heroes, who had restrained their agitation for their kinsmen as they drew back their weapons.
By Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa.
(Vs 1.3) 16. The arrow of Hara, though cast, caught upon her hand, and though struck away with force, still seized the hem of her garment—

May that fire of Śambhu’s arrow burn away your misfortunes— the fire which, like a lover who has recently committed an offense, was seized by the hair yet cast aside, was not looked upon with agitation when falling at her feet, and was brushed off even as he embraced the young women of Tripura whose lotus-eyes were filled with tears.
76. Of Amaru. (Amaru 2; Su.ra. 49) The beauty of vermilion upon her forehead, the ear-ornament made of liquid gold upon her ear-lobe—

May the fire born from the discharge of the arrow of the Destroyer of Tripura destroy your misfortunes— the fire that left the red dye of betel upon the faces of the wives of the demon lords, the smear of saffron upon their jar-like, swelling breasts, and the splendor of crimson silk upon the expanse of their hips.
Of Maṅgala. (Su.ra.
67) Having cast aside on all sides the curtain of dense smoke, with its expanding sparks...

May the Tandava dance of the Fire-god— the arrow of the Lord of the Universe— purify us; he who, having scattered handfuls of flowers under some pretext, placed his foot upon the mansions, whose great boundaries were enjoyed at will within Maya’s city, and who was smeared with fierce cosmetics as he pervaded the entire world.
Creating, through masses of clear smoke, the appearance of body-unguents washed away by the tears of the physician Gadādhara.

May the fire born from the discharge of Hara’s arrow destroy your darkness— this fire which, with its rays, displays upon the breasts of the women of Mayanagara the fresh beauty of a cluster of flowers withered by the summer heat, and upon their tresses the appearance of a fading musk-leaf. 79.
How indeed can the rainbow of the moon in the water or the beauty of Bhavānī’s lotus-bud fist [be compared to it]?
"Or how shall my left foot, adorned with jeweled anklets, assume the *pratyālīḍha* stance?"—
while the gods were thus engaged in deliberation,
may that Śiva (Dhūrjaṭi) protect us, who stood before them during the destruction of Maya’s city, when the fire of his arrow had scorched the Daityas.
80. 17. The eightfold form [of Śiva], the path of clouds, or the range of his mouth—[all these] possess fragrance.

May that enemy of Andhaka protect the world— he whose eight forms the gods repeatedly praise as "the one who carries," "the one who bears," "the friend," "the adversary," "the giver of lotuses," "the taker of lotuses," "the one who offers oblations," and "the one who receives oblations."
Of the illustrious Hanumān,
whose all-pervading power is equal to space, time, and the self, he shines forth therein.

May those forms of the enemy of Manmatha protect you— those forms whose rays become nectar for him, who was the source of their existence, who was his bile during the dawns, who bore the burden of his creation, and who carry the host that serves as his very life. 82.
[The mind’s action: (Kuval.
1056) He places a crest-jewel upon his head, adorns his forehead with a tilaka, and applies body-unguent to his frame.

May Śiva bring you prosperity—He who arranges his braided hair (dhammilla), displays the manifest beauty of his crest-jewel upon his head, delights the serpents, removes poison, and knows the seal of aesthetic flavor (rasa); He who, through those [serpents] which are like slender bodies bound in the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra), [attains] the joy of union. 83.
That [beauty] which the moon in the water consecrates in the place of her braided hair, and with which she, with palms joined in reverence during the twilights, [worships].

May that God, whose body is the universe and who wears the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, purify the world— he who, having drawn back his bow, meditates upon those [powers] which constitute his very self, and who, closing his eyes, brought them together with their own embodied forms into a state of flowing motion.
That which is the first creation of the Creator Sudhākara, which bears the oblation offered according to the ritual rules, and which is the priestess who offers it—

May the Lord protect you with those eight perceptible forms through which he ordains the two divisions of time, which abide pervading the universe as the qualities described in the Vedas, which they call the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) containing all seeds, and by which living beings possess their vital breaths.
By Kālidāsa. (Śākuntala 1.1) 18. Bhairava.
Wearing a mass of matted hair encircled by a skull-garland from which the head of Brahmā protrudes, fixed upon a cage of the Lord of the Dead fashioned from comets that serve as his staff,
and bearing around his neck a single-string necklace formed from the faces of the seven great sages.
May the Kāpālika at the end of the eon, whose equipment for his vows is easily obtained, protect you!
[The work] of someone.
May he be victorious—his body bound by garlands of red lotuses formed from the rows of severed heads of gods and asuras instantly destroyed; his silken garment drenched with thick drops of blood;
and his mouth wide open with the relish of devouring the three worlds in a single, unceasing gulp.
Ānanda belongs to Bhairava, who embraces the jar-like breasts of Kālarātri.
(87) — Umāpatidhara.
To him who bears upon his body the skull-bowl of Vaikuṇṭha held as an ornament on his hip, the skull of the Creator in his hand, the bones of the gods fashioned as ornaments for every limb,
and the white ashes of the entire world of moving and unmoving beings;
At the end of the kalpas, the wearer of the skull triumphs through his fierce vow of the skull.
Bhavabhūti.
When the entire world had been turned into a single ocean and rendered desolate, the Lord, accompanied by Kālī, was sporting there; with a loud, playful laugh released during his forceful play,
he suddenly beheld the reflection of his own body in the darkness pierced by the rays of his fangs and asked, "Who are you?"
"Who are you? Speak!"— saying this in anger, Bhairava granted them fearlessness and said,
"May he act for your benefit," [O devotees] of Vaidya Gadadhara.
At the end of the aeon, the Great Skeleton (Mahākankāla) lies asleep, his tusks piercing the three strides of Viṣṇu;
the flesh of the Primeval Boar is impaled upon the claws of the hand of Nṛsiṃha, who is joined to Śeṣa;
and both the Fish and the Tortoise have emerged from the world’s total state of being a single ocean.
But Mahābhairava, having become a fisherman, dragged out the great delusion of this master of the mind. (Sū.mu. 2.24)

19. At the commencement of the dance, Ambikā lowers the garland of lotus-faces hanging from her neck down to her knees; Nandin, for his part, appropriately tightens it with the lordly serpent of his matted locks, as if mistaking it for a crescent moon.

May that assembly protect you—wherein Kāla fastens his skin, Kālarātri brings a skull-bowl into her hand, and Śambhu descends to dance. Thus, during the descent of the dance, each member of the retinue is occupied with a distinct task.

2.29) "Nandin, take the lute that sounds as sweetly as a wagtail and prepare yourself;
Kuṣmāṇḍa, bring the vessel of ashes; Lambodara, come here!"

May the conversation of Śambhu protect you— conversations spoken in the theater courtyard to the Goddess, whose mind was captivated by the ornaments of his *tāṇḍava* dance, as he said, "O Goddess, gladden Skanda who has entered the interior of my palace.
O guardians of the quarters, move away; O clouds, leave the sky;
O earth, go to the netherworld; and O mountains, enter the surface of the ground—[all this] for the sake of the Lord of Yoga!
"O Brahmin, move far away from the dwelling place of our dancing god Śambhu;
this is a narrow space!"—may this exclamation of Nandin protect you.

"O Brahmin, rise up! O oceans, move far away! Maintain your steadiness!"—may these words of Nandin, uttered impetuously during the dance-performance of his eight-formed Lord, protect you.
Dvaipāyana’s [vision]: 20. The dance of Hari, wherein the worlds tremble, and the tortoises and serpents reel and bow as their bodies whirl about.

May the commencements of the Tandava dance of the Conqueror of Tripura dispel your calamities— dances during which the stars tremble, the pearls from the rows of necks of the moving lions are shattered, and the sky is filled with the rising, soaring, and circling celestial hosts of the gods.

by the effortless majesty of his arms, the Lord of Tortoises (Śeṣa) was overwhelmed by the weight of the earth bowing down [before him].

May the Tandava dance of the Moon-crested Lord destroy your misfortune—the dance that washes the sun, moon, and stars with the ocean waters tossed up by the wind of his outbursting breath; which terrifies the entire universe with the roar of mountain ranges falling through the force of his whirling arms; and which bestows sovereignty over the three worlds. (97)
Of Vācchoka’s [verses],
how many are flat (uttāna), how many are undulating (vellita), and how many have their middles bent by speed (rayād-ābhugna-madhya)?

May the three lines formed by the fire, the laughter, and the poison protect you— lines that appear when the Great Dancer, at the end of the aeons, suddenly begins his whirling dance, causing his arms to be cast down, raised up, and bent back in succession with the movements of the triple symphony.
May the mass of matted locks of Sāgaradhara, whirling from the force of the waters of the celestial river, protect you.

Hara is embarrassed by the playful, clamorous cries of the celestial damsels who are terrified at being swallowed as the circle of the sky sinks into the fierce waves born from the seven oceans, which surge upward due to the wind from the hissing of the hoods of the serpent-king agitated by that very speed. 99.
Of Brahmahari; (of Su.ra., verse 68, and of Karkarāja):
And of Bhīma, who is addicted to the grand display of the *tāṇḍava* dance at twilight, with its fierce whirling.
May the gale-winds from the regions where the circles of his staff-like arms dance protect you—
those winds whose sudden, impetuous surging caused the mountains in the battle arrays to fly up, so that Indra’s thunderbolt was looked upon once more [in vain]. 100.

O Śaṅkara, who art free from fear; you whose hand grasps the coils of the serpent; the bestower of enjoyment; the one who has crushed the hosts of the enemies of the gods;
the one worshipped by the Vṛndārakas (gods); you whose body is smeared with the ashes of the funeral pyre.
O you who are far beyond passion, O remover of misfortunes, be gracious!

O wielder of the Pināka bow, O Lord of Heaven,
O trident-bearer who pierces the great hearts of enemies,
O you whose vehicle is the bull, O you who are exultant in your majesty! Be present here.
O Savior who is without cause for the three worlds, be gracious!

O manifest Great Dancer, grant your grace and dance!
Of that very one.
O Bhava! O Śiva! You who are as fair as the ashes of a corpse; you whose body is entwined by Gaurī; you who wear a serpent as an upper garment;
O Smarahara! O Hara! O Bhīma! O Bhīmabhūta!
O Śaṅkara, who causes terror to the wicked, be gracious!
To him indeed...
O Lord of the Gods, who holds the bow of destruction; O fierce one, who are like a bee at the lotus-face of Caṇḍī;

O you whose garment is the sky, grant us the state of being free from all afflictions!
105 Of that very one.
22. Those sands which Gaurī causes the Lord to scatter over himself; those sands by which the Mandākinī adorns her crest;
and those sands which act as pollen upon the lap of the ketakī petals moistened by drops from the crescent moon.

May those particles of dust from the feet of the Mountain-born Goddess protect you— those which possess the magical power of playfully causing the blossoms of the *kaṅkelli* trees on the slopes of Kailāsa’s pleasure-grove to sprout.
The water of the Jahnavi, descending from the peak of Umāpati, washes away the lac-dye [from the feet] of those whose matted locks bear garlands of jasmine flowers.
May those toenails of the Goddess protect the universe— those nails whose rising, stainless rays eclipsed the moon when she fell at the feet of Śiva.
Of someone [Dakṣa] (Su.ra. 81):
She is the supporting staff for those drowning in the waters of the ocean of worldly existence, and the thunderbolt-edge that cleaves the mountain of the great asura Mahiṣa.
May she, the royal swan upon the lake of Śiva’s heart, grant you long-lasting auspiciousness.
By Bhagīrathadatta. (Su.ra.
86) I salute Gaurī’s breasts, which seem to smile as they have become pale from the intense embrace of Śiva, wondering, "To what state has the ascetic been reduced? (109)
The perfected mantra that accomplishes the desired fruit for Bhavabhūti.
O Goddess, consort of the enemy of Madana, whom both Bali and Brahmā worship; O daughter of the Lord of all mountains, I pay homage to you. 110.
Vāmadeva’s [work], 23. Gaurī at the Time of Marriage.

Having separated the medicinal dust from the serpent for the sake of the *gonāsa* snake, having bound herbs around the neck for the sake of the serpent, and wearing potent gems on her hand to counteract the poison residing there,
she recited the syllables of mantras taught by the aged women of her clan for the sake of her husband’s host of spirits.
May the Daughter of the Mountain protect you at the time of her marriage—both joyful and yet fearful. (Rājaśekhara; Viśvaguṇādarśabhāṇa 1.3, Surathotsava 102, Sūktimuktāvalī 2.36)
During the auspicious rites of her imminent wedding, Gaurī— busy with the worship of the gods—
beheld before her the painted image of her future husband,
Śiva; and after a long time, she somehow composed herself through a mixture of intoxication, smiles, anger, and shame.
"O beloved, may the handful of flowers offered at the word of an elderly woman protect you!
(112) — by Bhāsa. (Su.ra. 88, Śā.pa. 102, Sū.mu. 2.37)
"This is Brahmā; this is Viṣṇu; that is the Lord of the Thirty-three; and these are the Guardians of the World.

May Gaurī— who, though being consoled by the goddesses, had her hair standing on end with joy— be for your welfare.
(113) [By someone.]
Her vision clouded by smoke, her eyes refreshed again by the rays of the moon,

she gazes longingly at her chosen husband with downcast face; yet, out of shame before Brahmā, she looks once more with jealousy at Hari, who bears upon his foot-nails the Ganges reflected in their clear mirror-like surface.
May Gaurī— who, at the time of grasping his hand, stood with her hair standing on end from the touch— be for your welfare;
[this is by] Śrī Harṣadeva (Priyadarśikā 1.1).
Standing on the tips of her feet, made to bend low by the weight of her breasts,

she— modest in her desire to worship Śambhu— passed before the path of his three longing eyes; and as she placed [the flower] upon his head, she trembled with the breaking out of perspiration and horripilation.
May that handful of flowers, released by Girijā as it fell apart in mid-air, protect you!
(Ratnāvalī 1, Sū.mu. 2.38) — by the same author.
O Gaurī, O beloved, how is it that you have such perspiration? O Lord, O moon-faced one, why does this trembling arise from fear of the serpent-king due to the fire of your eyes? Be [calm].
"O Goddess, how is this horripilation? It is from the spray of the Lord's Ganges waters.
May Gaurī, who thus remained intent on concealing her emotion toward her husband, protect you for a long time.
By Lakṣmīdhara. (Su.ra. 75, Śā.pa. 104) O Śambhu, this is true: when Keśava was chosen by Lakṣmī during the churning of the ocean, you indeed ate crow-feces out of embarrassment and drank poison.
"O Pārvatī, it is true that we possess no good fortune; and the god Smara is our witness,"—may Gaurī, having thus called to mind [her husband] with a smiling face, protect you for a long time.

The breasts of Śrī Harṣadeva were covered with ashes by the vine-like silk garments hanging from his arms, while sandalwood paste was revealed upon them; and pearl necklaces were suspended from the serpents that served as his upper garments.
May the embrace of the daughter of the mountain king by the bearer of the Gaṅgā—though she was but a maiden—serve as a touchstone for the enduring essence of intense love; may it be for your welfare.
Upon the head of the moon in the water is the crooked river; the maker of night (the moon) is your ornament along with the venomous serpents; and a succession of piśācas is close at hand.
"You take [my wealth], yet you do not take my life; how is this so?"—may these words of the daughter of the mountain king, spoken in the anger of love, purify you.
The Lord Govinda does not take his hand, which delights in the serpent-bracelet, to adjust the knot of her lower garment;
nor does he extinguish with his own ashes the lamp consisting of the light from the eye in his forehead.

May that Pārvatī protect you— she who, though released from her deer-skin by Hara, still wears the skin of a black antelope out of fear, and who is overcome with shame due to her recent encounter with delusion.
25. One [image] of Durgā by Ācārya Gopīka, standing upon the head of Mahiṣa.
Furthermore, victorious is the pair of feet of the Mountain’s Daughter, which are reddened by the hue of rubies and bowed to by hosts of joyful gods. 121.
Like a lotus in the commentary on the auspiciousness of the three worlds, [this is] the moon in the water.
O Bhavānī, your goad throbs at the tip of your hand; O Goddess, even your hand-drum possesses that very fortune which is to be relinquished at the end of every calamity. 122
122. Hari’s back of the hand, with the fingers forming the *khaṭakāmukha* gesture due to the drawing of the bowstring.

May the sidelong glance of Ambikā protect you— a glance mingled with the mass of light from her shimmering nails, bearing the playful grace of bees wandering about out of longing for her ear-ornament of blossoming sprouts.
Of Amaru. (Amaru 1; Su.ra.
100) With the base of his arms bristling as the body of Mahiṣa was bent down by the pressure of his feet—

May the three lines of the Goddess protect you— lines that reveal wide, distinct, high, sparse, and clearly manifest white intervals between her limbs as she raises her trident and stretches her body, the edges of her bodice loosened as it gradually slips down. 124.
When Rudra’s host had fled, when the Sun was wavering, and when the wielder of the thunderbolt had his bolt shattered by Bāṇa—

When the moon had become apprehensive, when the wind had ceased, and when Kubera had abandoned his enmity, may Bhavānī—whose power is unimpeded even against Viṣṇu—protect you; she who, free from obstacles, slays the exceedingly wrathful Mahiṣa, whose impediments destroy manly valor, and who abounds in divine manifestations. 125.
125. Of that very [one], 26. Kālī.
The space remaining in his mouth was not easily found even in the sky; the quarters of the world were known to have no room left, being strewn with his thousands of swaying arms;
and the entire three worlds were not enough for him to fill with but five morsels.
May the fierce Bhairavī, the Night of Doom, who is suddenly and intensely wrathful, protect us for a long time—
[the work] of Bhāsoka. ||126||126||
O Kālī, the crescent moon is upon Your crest; the moon and sun are in Your two ears; the necklace of stars is around Your neck; the shimmering host of constellations is upon Your breasts;
the lightning is Your girdle; and the twilight is the belt fashioned for You—this is how You appear.
Your non-conformity with the world, which is not subject to the cessation of the cosmic age, is triumphant.
127 [Of someone].
Terrifying with its network of exposed bone-frames devoid of flesh, with a belly as deep as the underworld,
with eye-cavities as profound as the hollows of pits, with a forest of matted locks standing on end,
and occupied with pulling out fragments of the bones of Daityas caught between her teeth—
O fierce goddess, we bow to you, whose single-pointed nails are cruel and whose luster is unbroken.

I bow to you, whose eyes are like fires blazing within the stars, whose interior is filled with compassion for those wandering in the abyss, whose belly is as deep as the underworld from which the waters of the ocean were cast down by the wrathful Agastya,
and whose form consists of the essence of bones and a back where the fierce veins are concealed.
Carcikā, smeared with the blood of the Daitya women leaping up as they were struck by the tips of her fangs;
[this is] by Umāpatidhara.
Victorious is the clattering sound of your teeth as you crunch the bones of demons with a side-long glance,
a sound as terrifying as the roar of mountains splitting under the flames of the fire at the end of an aeon.
Victorious is Ardhanārīśa, that wondrous form blended with the Daughter of the Mountain, belonging to Śatānanda.
He is the cause of the loss of the playful grace of Tripura’s youth;
for upon his swelling chest, due to the height of one prominent breast, his serpent-necklace falls into a state of uneven positioning. 131.
Let the kisses upon the lower lip of the Aśleṣā star in the month of Māgha, along with their pleasant conversations and smiles, remain as they are.
"Far indeed is this mutual gazing upon each other's faces from becoming possible;
thus, for us two whose union in a single body has been rendered futile, what is this mockery of affection? May the smiling Ardhanārīśvara protect you! 132.
Of someone:
(Sv 68) O Moonlight, look! O Lord of Serpents, behold! O attendants, gaze upon this!

Victorious is the Lord who is half-woman with his beloved, his face bowed with a bashful smile upon hearing this speech of the celestial river— spoken with joy— describing the beauty of her feet, red with lac, against the chest of the Enemy of Kama, which is heavy with the weight of her breasts.
The lord of serpents, whose crest-moon meets with the beauty of the single breast of the Goddess Svacchandā, the sovereign of yoga.

May the Blessed Lord Ardhanārīśvara, who wears the sacred thread over the right shoulder, grant you happiness—he whose half is the light spreading from the calamity of burning the universe, while the other half has tears rising from compassion;
and whose two eyes, through their mutual impact, produce a *simasima* sound as they strike one another when remembered. (134)
Of Murāri: (Ar 7.38, sū.mu.
2.21) The braided hair and the matted locks, the pearl necklace and the serpent, and the gems—

May Ardhanārīśvara grant you prosperity— he who, with a single body, bears the bones of Brahmā, saffron, the powder of a human head, sacred ash, linen cloth, and the skin of an elephant, thereby demonstrating the oneness of all phenomena, as if he were a yogin. 135.
135. Of Śaṅkaradeva: 28. Ardhanārīśvara, whose nature is erotic (śṛṅgāra).
Half of his lip quivers from the power of recitation, while the other half trembles from intense anger;
one hand is placed upon his head to offer salutation, while the other is raised to cast it down;
one eye closes in meditation, while the other remains wide open and unblinking—thus he stands.
May that subtle form of his protect you, who, during the performance of the twilight rites, possesses desires and intentions equal [to those of all beings].
(136) [Of someone.]
With their girdles unfastened, their firm embraces unattained,
their kisses unobtained, and the beauty of each other's faces unseen,
they have experienced the pangs of separation while their bodies were already mingled with their beloveds.
May the body of the Enemy of Smara protect you, appearing like a companion to Sambhoga.
137. Chittipa.
May the Lord protect the worlds— he who, out of the essence of mature love, bears his beloved upon his body as if she were non-different from himself; yet, during their playful quarrel,

Or rather, he places his right hand solely upon the lotus-like left foot of Gadādhara.
138.138 [Gadādhara]
O Gaurī, while the God may indeed experience a joy born of incessant embraces as he holds your creeper-like body in union,
his gaze— though steady with love, sweet, tender, and charming— is not [as it should be].
"Having been seen," the inner organ of Tryambaka repeatedly faints;
[this is] Bhagīratha’s [verse]. (Su.ra. 82)
"O enemy of Madana, bestow upon another the favor of granting a portion of your own body;
I am not able to bear the celestial river on my head, nor can I perform prostrations at the twilight hour"—
having spoken thus, Umā, pierced by anger, began to tear apart her own body in order to separate herself.
May the arm of Śambhu protect you— the arm that, drawn by the forceful touch of her jar-like breasts, remains encircling them. (140) —
by Mayūra.
May that very Gaṇeśa alone, who emulates the conduct of Gaurī and the Lord of the Mountain, protect the worlds.
He shines with a face devoid of teeth in one part, like a man who has lost half his body and whose wife has been slain, leaving him with but a single tooth.
Of Vasukalpa: (Su.ra.
94) With bees flying up from his temples, trembling under the influence of fear, yet forming swarms above out of greed for the ichor, as they attempt to fall back down.
May Heramba, bearing an exceedingly beautiful splendor like that of a moving umbrella of peacock feathers,
accomplish the destruction of the world’s evils without obstacle.
Of that very [Lord]: (Su.Ra.
93) With his head adorned by the Ganges clinging to the surface of the sky reddened by the vermilion glow of twilight;
possessing a beautiful luster created by the garland of stars shimmering [upon it]; and having made the moon his ear-ornament.

May the leader of the Gaṇas bestow blessings upon you— he whose splendor consists of the grandeur of moving chowries in his pair of ears, appearing like masses of waterless clouds, and who is the ornament of natural grace.
The throat-sound of Daṅka, which produces terror in the elephants of the quarters with its roaring, deep, rumbling, and terrible resonance like a thundercloud.
May the pot-bellied one (Lambodara), engaged in his innate passion for dramatic play, shake his trunk and dispel all obstacles from your face.
May the dust from the lotus feet of Heramba, reddened by droplets of nectar from the mandāra flowers upon the crowns of the lords of the gods, remove all obstacles for me, a sinner. 145
145. Of Umāpatidhara; 30. Kārttikeya.
May Guha protect you— he who, having rolled for a long time on his father’s chest as he pleased, his body covered in ashes and dust,
suddenly leaps from the matted locks of Śiva into the fathomless waters of the Gaṅgā,
instantly uttering cries of "sīt" while his rows of teeth are struck by the freezing cold of the water.
May he protect you from misfortune, he who placed his hand upon an eye blazing with the crest of fire.
(146) [By Bāṇa] (Su.ra. 91, Sū.mu. 2.43)
Tearing open the cavernous mouths of Vāsuki with his flaming rays,
he counts the fangs mottled with venom from the corners of his mouth with his forefinger— touching those budding teeth in a wildly disordered sequence of one, three, nine, eight, seven, and six.
May the childhood charms of Vācaspati Śaktidhara bring you auspiciousness. (147) [By someone; Sūktimuktāvalī 95, Śārṅgadharapaddhati 105]

Having created a peacock sleeping with its head nestled within the fold of its wings before him, Śiva—his heart radiant with the clapping of his pair of hands as he laughed inwardly—asked the crying child, "O dear one, by whom was its head cut off? How did this happen? from his very childhood.
May the laughter of Kumāra, who was delighted by the sight of his head [being severed], protect you!
(Su.ra. 96) — by someone.
Out of curiosity for a flight of swans, he mistook her for a row of skulls adorning her;
out of a longing for lotus stalks, he shook her young crescent-moon forehead with his hand; and mistaking it for a red lotus, he opened wide the eye-socket upon her brow.
May the six-faced god, who occupies his father’s lap and is intent on playing with children, protect you!
(Balabhadra; Sūktimuktāvalī 92)
Having fashioned the beauty of his heavy mass of matted locks with the stalks of blue lotuses, and having placed the two curved ends of a lotus root against the region of the moon,
he then prepared a skin of white lotus fiber upon his mother’s lap using her variegated silken garment.
May Guha, acting like Rudra in play while being gazed upon by his two parents, protect the world. (150) —
[This is] Halāyudha’s.
31. If Bhṛṅgin is naked, what need has he for a bow? If he possesses weapons, what need has he for ashes? And if he has ashes, what need has he for a woman? If he has a woman, why does she hate Kāma?
Beholding this mutually contradictory behavior of his own master,
Bhṛṅgī maintains a body consisting of nothing but bones, rough and bound with dense veins.
"O Lord of Yoga (Su.ra. 103, Sv 2399), why have you come from home, my dear? Tell me, what is this new news there?
Has the God been conquered by the Goddess—[conquered] by means of the bull, the hand-drum, the ash, the lord of serpents, and the moon?"
While the Lord of the Barhis was thus speaking, may the sudden cry of Bhṛṅgirīṭi— born from the agitation caused by the loss of his master’s alms and ornaments— protect the world for a long time.
Of Tuṅgoka: (Su.ra.
98) This wife of mine is always hungry, and this son of mine has six mouths; even this Gaṇeśa himself, whose body is heavy with the burden of a belly so difficult to fill.
"Thus, how shall the Lord, the single bull, nourish his own family?"—
as if contemplating this, may Bhṛṅgī, whose body is but a withered skeleton, protect you for a long time.
"How could one who feeds on alms and wears a hide obtain wealth?"— thinking thus, Pārvatī herself formerly took away half the body of that blue-limbed Lord who was devoted to his ascetic vows.
If she were to forcibly seize even half of him while the Ganges remains upon his head, alas, O Lord, where would he be? Thinking thus, Bhṛṅgin, his heart distressed, withers away intensely.
He does not perform service for Bhavānanda, nor does he practice agriculture or trade; he has no paternal inheritance,
no wealth, no strength of kin, and no faction at all.

May the Lord protect you for a long time— he who, though he does not abandon his addiction to gambling and women, remains thin and emaciated as if thinking, "What fruit could there be for me from this? (155)
For someone [else],
there is a variety of groups;
the fat man will not go far, and this thin man is not capable of the journey.

May that mutual antagonism between Bhṛṅgin and Kūṣmāṇḍa— which was repeatedly contemplated at the outset by me alone, who thought, "Only I shall obtain the marriage feast there"— protect you during the wedding of Śiva and the Goddess. 156.
Of someone: How indeed does [the Lord] always protect the garland of human skulls immediately from the scrutiny [of others]? (Su.ra. 99)
Reflecting within himself on how the Lord [Śiva] protected Caṇḍī’s lion from the bull, her son’s peacock from the serpents, and so forth— the great skill of the Blessed One’s intellect—
Kūṣmāṇḍa daily nourishes the splendor of his belly, which is filled with steadfastness.
Of someone [it is said]: "The Goddess has given birth to a son; O Gaṇas, dance! Why do you stand still?"—thus she spoke with uplifted arms. (Su.ra. 97)

May the sound produced by the rattling skeletons in their cages— cages set in motion by each other, which exceeds the deep resonance of the beaten drums when Cāmuṇḍā joyfully embraces Bhṛṅgiriṭi without being asked— protect you. (158)
Of Yogeśvara: (Su.ra.
71, Sū.mu. 2.55) O Bhṛṅgin, release your horn; and you, O elephant-faced one, abandon the base of your tail!

"O Nandin, you are dull-witted; enough, O weakling Mahākāla, with this throat-grasping!"—having spoken thus, may the Bull, being led away while looking at the Three-eyed Lord whose neck was turned and whose dewlap was shaking as he watched with eyes full of embarrassment at the base of Pārvatī’s feet, bring you happiness. 159.
Of Abhinanda. (Su.ra.
77) Clad in the directions [as his garment], having a bull for his vehicle, wearing a human head and carrying a deer-skin;
