Thus, Kūṣmāṇḍaka, his belly nourished by excessive satisfaction, cried out "I am blessed! to the world. 160.
Of the Great Treasure (Mahānidhi), 33. Hari and Hara.
That which bears half-bound matted hair and half a crown, and which possesses both the splendor and the garland of the moon and the slow-moving Mars—
those two possessing the beauty of a blooming jasmine and a sapphire—
that [splendor] of Śrīkaṇṭha and Vaikuṇṭha is rendered formidable by their contact with the skull-topped staff and the discus.
I salute that singular form which bears the names of Nandin, Mahokṣa, and Tārkṣya as its ornaments;
[this is] by Rājaśekhara. (Su.Ra. 1639)

Upon the edge of his lotus-feet, he has a great serpent sleeping in playful repose within his bound locks of matted hair; he has released his own bull of prowess from the vicinity of his feet; he possesses a parasol made of the wings of the expanded bird of prey (Garuḍa); and he bears the splendor of a mace as his staff.
May the body of Hari-Hara, which is to be worshipped by Brahmā, purify the three worlds.
By Bhavānanda.
By him, whose mind-born passion was destroyed, the body of Bali’s conqueror was formerly turned into a woman;
he who bore the Gaṅgā; he who brought about the end of Andhaka;
he who is fond of peacock feathers; and of whom the immortals say that his head bears the moon and call him by the praiseworthy name "Hara."
May that Mādhava, who wears serpents as his necklace and bracelets, grant all things to you!
(163) [Bhāravi] (Sv 44, Sū.mu. 2.104, Sāh.D.

May the abiding together of the two gods who are enemies of the city of Tripura— the one whose body possesses a splendor as beautiful as the peaks of a mountain of snow and the other like a mountain of collyrium— be for your welfare; in that place,
the matted locks of the Lord of the Braids serve as a dwelling for serpents, whose hoods are agitated by the fear of Garuḍa.
And whose navel-lake has a lotus sleeping within it, encased in the luster of the crescent moon.
164. Of Tuṅgoka.
May that [Lord Śiva]—who is as radiant as a cluster of *jambū* fruits; who is beloved by the lord of serpents, the consumer of the assembly of hooded snakes;
whose head bears the Mandākinī flowing from his feet which possess the luster of the moon and the blooming lotus;
who is expert in both protection and destruction; and who perpetually kindles the arising of passion—may he ever protect us.
Even upon awakening, there is no contradiction in [perceiving] the single body of the Ocean and the Son of the Mountain (the Moon), which is the beloved of the Daughter of the Mountain (Lakṣmī).
165. Of the moon reflected in water.
May the body of Hari and Hara, joined with their beloveds,

which is half-and-half complete, which is the birthplace of the god of love who yearns for sensual enjoyment, and which is the destroyer of the sacrifice of Puruṣottama— may that body protect the worlds Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ.
If it has not already been snapped asunder by the forceful pulls of the playful, sidelong glances of Lakṣmī and Girijā, then it will surely remain sewn together by their mutual virtues.
May the body of the protector of Tripura’s enemy, blended with his matted locks and crown, and united with the two cities that destroy the vital breaths, protect you all.
[He] whose creeper-like arms were drawn back as they were shaken by the embrace of the necks of his own consorts— the daughters of the Mountain and the Ocean.
May that single body of the two enemies of Kāma and Kaṃsa— possessing the captivating beauty of crystal and emerald through their union in love— protect you.
There, on the neck of Bhavānī, which possesses a splendor equal to that of the Daughter of the Ocean, the dispute over the boundary between them never ceases.

May the incomparable union of the Lord of Yoga—the half of the God who wears a crown of a single *tamāla* leaf—with the half of the body of the Enemy of Cities, lead you to supreme bliss. (Śā. Pa. 110; Sū. Mu. 2.103)

In which [place] there arose a great fever of love, intense enough to shatter the playful jests of the Mountain’s Daughter and the Ocean’s Daughter as they failed to attain their union with one another.

With faces struck with wonder at the limit of Hari’s friendship shown by the Creator, and filled with bliss and contentment as the sages and gods together dispelled their delusions of duality through the joy of service;

May the Blessed Lord Hara, the teacher of all that moves and is stationary, who took half of Pārvatī’s body as his own necklace, protect you— he who was gazed upon by her with a frown of curved eyebrows drawn toward his feet.
The Ganges,
the splendor of Brahman, kindles the brilliance of the twice-born and destroys the onset of dullness in the intellect.

The water of your stream, O beloved of Kāśī, instantly quenches the growth of the powerful tree of evil deeds through its sprinkling; moreover, it leads even further upward those living beings whose forms are submerged, even beyond this world—what kind of process is this? 171.
The splendor of the daybreak for the arrival of the darkness of faults that are difficult to ward off amidst clamor.

May she— the digit of the moon that causes the white water-lily of liberation to bloom, the celestial river, and the victory banner of the city of the king of the gods (Indra) when shattered by the Kali age— be victorious! 172.
What is the use of the Lord of Planets wandering to sacred fords, if he is beheld for even a moment?
O Goddess, if your water has been drunk, then even nectar is in vain;
if you have been bathed in, the station of Viriñci is not far off;
and if you have been worshipped, liberation is in the palm of one's hand. 173
Just as the shore of Viriñci descends here before you, so indeed [is it].

O Goddess, with a body worn out by old age, I am like a sage desiring death; O Mother, the celestial women, submissive to my self-choice marriage, have likewise made even the sky such that its creeper-like arms are like tender sprouts. 174.
That alone is true austerity which has been performed, and that alone is the oblation offered, which is poured into the mouth of Jātavedas.

O Mother Jāhnavī, since nothing at all was given by me, nor was any devotion shown toward pilgrimages to sacred sites, and this person (pudgala) was filled with nothing more than [base desires] like a crow or a dog— by embracing you, may this internal fever of mine be stilled. 175.
175. Chapter 36: Praise of the Gaṅgā (Gaṅgāpraśaṃsā) of the Sentuti [Sūtra]

O Bhāgīrathī, daughter of Jahnu, wife of the ocean and mistress of Gaurī’s lord, who are the victory-banner and crest-garland of Dharma’s festival— I pray to you: [grant me grace] for one whose body rests upon a stone within your waters, swaying by your waves.
As I remember your name with my gaze fixed upon you, my life-breaths will depart.
(176) Lakṣmīdhara. (Su.ra. 1613; Sa.ka.ā. 4.183)
May I perform some service for my enemy as if he were a friend; may I feel no envy toward virtuous people, but rather possess a mind inclined toward compassion even for those of wretched nature;
and may I have a craving that destroys the stains of the Kali age, yet never diminishes in the worship of Kṛṣṇa.
O Goddess Mandākinī, you are the refuge for those who have faith; even the dull-witted find joy in you.
Of that very [river]...
Be gracious, O Śrīgaṅgā, you who are most beautiful as the crest-jewel upon the crown of Śiva;
may the tree of my worldly existence fall, uprooted by your surging waves,
so that I shall never again be born, even though I were the sovereign of the three worlds.
O Blessed One, may I become either a dog-cooker or a crow on your shore.
[Regarding] the sandalwood slipper.
When will there be joy for you, as you sit in a hut on the bank of the river— its slopes curved with spreading young *urvā* grass— and listen to the narrative threads told by Manu and others,
which bring about the restraint of the group of sense organs that cause blindness?
May I, being joyful, be free from the fear of abandoning [the path] toward the Blessed One, Bhava.
(179) By Gopīcandra.
With palms joined in reverence, I bow; grant me your grace,
O Goddess Gaṅgā, and become my unprecedented mother for me when I am in my final years and have reached my end.
Give water for the sake of binding the body,
[as] of Kevaṭṭapapīpa. ||180||180||
37. May the Fish incarnation of Hari purify the world— He whose mouth was slightly curved by His *oṃ*-sound, and whose middle part was full due to His affection for the non-dual Brahman.
Playing with the very waves of the ocean,
he shook his tail with vigor, as if saying "no, no" out of disdain.
He is the supporting ground for the restoration of the goddess Śrutī, daughter of Āvantyakṛṣṇa, who had been defiled by the wicked conduct of the Danujas.
Victorious is the body of Murāri in the form of a fish, which served as an island in the midst of the entire ocean that had become a single expanse of water.

Beholding his own form reflected in the mirror of the interior of the cosmic egg— which has been washed by the oceans tossed up by the force of its rotation— the Lord of Umā gazes with a pair of unblinking eyes.
May the two flanks of Śauri in his fish-form, tawny like fire, and his head, which has the appearance of the peaks of the golden mountain marked by the blazing sun and moon, protect you.

May that Lord Keśava, the playful fish who churned the expanse of the quarters by rubbing his sides against them and whose belly was as vast as the many oceans, protect the three worlds for Vasantadeva.
Within whose limbs, bounded by the vessel of the universe inlaid with the hair of his back and skin,
the world somehow grew old through the mere curiosity of his leaping.
May the Fish [Incarnation], who rendered the great ocean insignificant by the striking of his tail and whose delight in aquatic play was insatiable, grant you auspiciousness. (Su.ra. 135) [185]
Of someone:
38. The tortoise.
May the breath-winds of the Lord in his tortoise form protect you— winds that, due to the rubbing against the jagged peaks of Mount Mandara as it revolves behind him,
cause the waters to flow under the guise of tides by the force of their lingering momentum.
The coming and going of those who have gone forth remains unrestrained; even today, it does not rest within the ocean. (186) By Keśaṭācārya. (BhP 12.13.2; Su.Ra. 105, by Vākpatirāja; Sv 36)

While the Ocean of Milk was being churned, amidst a tumultuous roar unleashed by the sons of the gods and the Danavas, and while the three worlds were bewildered by the illusion of a sound as heavy as the violent bursting of the cosmic egg, he—
having attained immediate, passionless awakening— cast the long earth upward with the force of his speed.
Victorious is the King of Tortoises, whose neck and trunk are like a sturdy pillar, resembling a fierce supporting beam;
[this is] of Vasusena.
May the wondrous King of Tortoises protect you— he who, feeling sleepy from the itching of his back and tail caused by the friction of circling Mount Mandara, disregarded the agitation of the ocean;
for whom the earth, with its great mountain-pilings shaken by the effortless pressure of his shifting body, remained steadfast.
With its girdle of the moving ocean, whose jewels are the shimmering waves, the earth seems to dance.

May he purify you, appearing for a moment in the sky as if he were millions of clouds— clouds that, due to the excessive force of his striking his flanks, suddenly surge upward from their separation [from him] and then fall back again and again, drinking in and vomiting forth oceans with the speed of the sun.
The king of tortoises, by the slight movement of his body, caused the entire circle of the earth to tremble.
Of the Earth-Sustainer.
Salutations to Hari in the form of a tortoise, upon whose back the entire universe rests like a strand of moss, providing support for those seeking liberation.
In the case of Bhavānanda’s *Varāha*,
the scratching of his neck-itch was not performed upon mountains that were immediately crushed by his tusks.

Victorious is that Boar, whose desires were magnified by his sovereign power, who did not find satisfaction in plunging his limbs into the rivers where the water was scanty, entering only the hollows of their hooves; nor did he find delight in wallowing in the mud of the underworld, since he required only the tip of his snout for the lifting of the earth.
Of Varāhamihira. (Su.ra.
134) There exists [a lady] whose chest is marked with the seal of the leaf-design upon the breasts of Śrī.
The Lord, the master of the entire world, for whom the moon has risen from the lotus-face of his bride Madhu—

on the tip of his tusk, white as the new moon, which served as the body for his sport as a boar— the earth shone like a single musta-grass root uprooted from the bed of the pond that was the ocean of dissolution. (192)
Of the naked one: (Su.ra.
104) This very Candrakalā is worshipped with the lotus-eyes of the Nāgavantiyas.

May the tusk of Madhuripu protect you for a long time—that tusk which was gazed upon with joy by the world-elephants (diṅnāga) as capable of removing his burden; which was touched by the elephants of the quarters with their long trunks extended straight; and which, having pierced the earth, emerged with the hope that it was a lotus stalk.
The hair on the tips of Keśava’s nose was moistened by the spray from the ocean waters splashing up at the sound of his terrible snorting.

May that primordial Boar grant the destruction of your misfortunes— he who was gazed upon steadily by the gods as a mass of stars was pierced by the tips of his bristles, and through whose connection with the reflection of the nether world entering and receding as it was drawn in and cast out by his breath, the splendor of day and night became manifest. 194.
By whom [Narasiṃha], because of the notion that it was a lotus leaf turned face-downward, the tortoise was gazed upon for a long time;

May that Hari, the boar who sports in the puddle of the single ocean, purify you— he by whom the lord of serpents was sniffed with the mistaken notion that he was a charming lotus-stalk vine, and who lifted up the orb of the earth like a lotus root, finding delight only in the single pool of the universal ocean.
Of someone:
40. Narasiṃha (The Man-Lion)
With teeth that acted as a half-moon covering, with an inner mouth resembling the twilight,
with eyes like the rising sun, with creeper-like eyebrows forming the arc of a rainbow,
and with lightning-like flashes emerging from the form of his throat-skin which was deep with internal resonance;
May Nṛsiṃha, who has filled the sky with his wide-spreading mane, protect the world.
196. Of Murāri.

The sound produced by the friction of the saw-like claws of the quivering talons;

the night— feeling as if it were day— was filled with trembling fear among the flocks of owls, while the groves of lotuses somehow managed to remain asleep despite their blossoming.
Of Yogeśvara. (Su.ra. 923) 85. Bahurūpakacandra.

Now, alone in the ocean of the sky, there is that god who is the sacrificial feast of nectar for the city of Indra, the wish-fulfilling jewel for awakening the night-lilies, and the magical spell for dispelling the pride of the deer-eyed women; he stands before us, the vanquisher of all darkness.
Behold, the moon, the merchant of the five-arrowed god, raises its vessel for the voyage. 423.
423 Of Hari.
Victorious is this vessel of nectar, the watering trench for the tree of the bodiless god;
the skull-bowl of the day of death for the Kapalika of Time;
and the whetstone for the arrows of the one whose banner bears the sea-monster.
Śvetabhānu is the mirror for the ladies of Amarapura,
[the enemy] of Tripura.

It is the play-camphor lamp for the deer-eyed women of the gods; it is the sovereign umbrella raised high over the empire of Love for passionate women; it is the waving fly-whisk that dispels their fatigue;
and it is the charming pillow for the cheeks of Madana’s bride, marked with the seal of musk-paste.
The moon shines as an island in the ocean of the sky, a playful swan for the celestial city.
86. Sunset.
Just as this glorious moon, the producer of nectar, causes the mind to suspect it is a golden lotus upon the ocean at the edge of the western mountain,
so too does this [person] cause a thirst for the liquid nectar of the flow of their loveliness.
Even a spot [on the moon] assumes the beauty of a row of falling bees. (Su.ra. 940) — by someone.
With its footprints concealed and sinking down, bearing a streak of dark mud-like stains,
it clings to the western shore of the ocean of the sky.
The king of tortoises is like one who is out of joint and lying on his back; this is from Śatānanda’s *Sudarśanārahasya* (9.78).

The stars, their light stolen away, possess only the luster of specks of frost; moreover, the rays of the sun gather at the base of the eastern mountain, while the expanse of its shadow, now slackened, rests upon the shore of the western ocean.
The moon possesses a clear luster like the beauty of a fully ripened lavalī fruit;
[this is] of Śarva. (Su.ra. 9.73)
The moon, indistinguishable from a lotus, rolls in the western ocean;
on the mountain of sunrise, it is but a palmful of heat that has grown; for a moment, this unrestrained light plunges into the very stage of the sky.
The darkness is as dark as the *mālatī* vines on the banks of the daughter of Mount Kalinda.
(Sū.mu. 82.20) — by Sihaṇa.
The moon, the maker of night, had fallen from its own station like a king from his realm;
the stars were scattered like his subjects who had fled their homes; and the lily ponds, shorn of their beauty, were closed like his harem women deprived of their splendor.
It was utterly destroyed by masses of darkness, like by the wicked attendants of that very Lakṣmīdhara.
||430|| Lakṣmīdhara’s.

87. The moon is the lofty ornament of the Lord of Beings’ attire, the life-sustainer of the assemblies of the gods, the crest-jewel of the nights, the family enemy of unchaste women, and the primordial mountain of the streams of nectar.

Victorious is this moon— the source of distress for the lotuses, the banner of the fish-bannered god of love in his arts of passion, the sole kinsman of the oceans, and the very root of joy for the clusters of night-lilies.
The moonlight of Śaraṇa is the abode of the playful charms of lovely young women; it is a lake of nectar-waves,
a mass of butter from the ocean of milk, and a cooling stone for the waters that alleviate the earth’s distress.
The moon— the forehead mark of the night, the unique abode for the vow of love of the deer-eyed women, and a shower of camphor for the daylight that is the beggar-bird cakora— is now on its way.
When the moon, the inner controller of wanton women, acts as an enemy by serving as a sandalwood paste-mark upon the eastern cheeks of their beloveds; (Su.ra. 955)
The moon repeatedly scatters its web of moonlight, while the cakora birds, uttering sweet flatteries for their beloved mates, drink from the channels carved from moonstones.
Having transcended the quarters and time by Hari’s glories, as if like the sky, where indeed has it gone;
and where indeed has even the seal of the fresh lotus bud quickly vanished?
Where is that fortitude of the ocean known [to exist], when even this entire world is thrown into turmoil by the moon as it rests upon the slopes of the mountain of sunrise?
Of Aparājitarakṣita:
(Suvarṇarāṣṭra, 925) Dwelling at the foot of Mount Hari, surrounded by bears, generating coolness through the flow of breezes, and delighting the night-lotuses—
Slaying the darkness of the night-stalkers, this lord of stars, marked with a broad blue spot, shines forth; how wonderful that he is now without his bodiless foe!
O fragrant one!
88. The wind, plunging into the waters, rolling in the pollen of flowers, and shaking the trees—

The intoxicated wind of King Smara wanders at will, striking travelers in their hearts with its rows of mad cuckoos’ cries and its unrestrained clamor, and causing the garments of the city women to fall away. (436)
For someone,
the greatness of his mass of matted hair was fashioned by garlands of *alīna* flowers.
In the expanse of the flowering forests, the breeze— its surface covered with the dust of blossoms as if with ashes— moves slowly, slow like a wandering mendicant intent on gathering flowers. (437)
Of Vīryamitra: (Su.Ra.
1134) A blossoming lotus that provides relief from the sweat born of the battle of amorous passion.
This breeze, raining down the touch of the Vraja’s fragrance, blows gently;
it is cool with its fresh embraces of the sap dripping from the new mango sprouts snapped by the beaks of cuckoos, and it belongs to the gazelle-eyed women.
Of a certain [person],
there was a row of lotuses gathered in the ponds of the pleasure grove.
These winds, which seize the manifest nectar [of the flowers],
wipe away from the cheeks of passionate women— now possessed of fresh intoxication— the sweat born of the exhaustion of the battle of love. 439.
These [verses] of Gadādharanātha concern the mature amorous sports of the wives of the village chiefs.

In every lake, the fragrant breezes blow at will, carrying with them the excellence of the scent of *gundra* grass as it breaks under the pressure of the boars' tusks— breezes that are the adversaries of the abundance of sweat surrounding the breasts of women suffering from love's fever.
Of someone.
(Su.ra. 1141) 89. Dakṣiṇavātaḥ (The Southern Wind).
Kissing her face, rolling over the slope of her breasts, tossing her locks of hair,
casting aside the hem of her garment, inflaming the play of the mind-born god,
agitating her limbs, unsettling her heart, and utterly uprooting her pride.
The Malaya breeze embraces every limb of women like a lover;
by Vinayadeva (Su.ra. 1133).
These friends of the God of Love, who dwell in the caves of Mount Malaya, are the masters in bestowing the playful dance upon the clusters of branches of those trees;
they resound with the humming of bees intoxicated by mango blossoms and filled with affectionate *huṃ* cries.
Alas, what misery! The winds, which slay the lives of young women on the road, are blowing forth.
(442) [Of Śrīpati]
Moving slowly due to the fatigue of rubbing against the dense, full breasts of Andhra women, they set in motion the beautiful necklaces and heavy braided tresses of Dravidian brides,
and they inhaled the lotus-forest of the faces of Sinhalese women and the cheeks of Kerala women.
The southern winds, fragrant with the scent of the Malaya mountains, blow gently as if kissing [the earth]. (Su.ra. 1126) — by someone.

Those who provide a swinging play for the fawn-eyed women, who instantly cut away the essence of their mental anguish, and who are the preeminent masters in the initiation of love throughout the three worlds—
they cause the king of melodies, the fifth note (*pañcama*), to roll upon the throats of cuckoos.

The southern winds blow at their own will, serving as great witnesses to the victory of Love. (Rājaśekhara; Viśvaguṇādarśabhāṇa 1.27, Śārṅgadharapaddhati 3816, Sūktimuktāvalī 59.29, Subhāṣitaratnabhāṇḍāgāra 1145)
Gently, very gently, they touch the broad cheeks of the Dravidian women;
curling as they move, they toss the Bakula, Lavalī, and Nāgapuṃnāga vines upon the curls of the Karṇāṭaka women.
The winds blow from the direction beloved by Lopāmudrā’s husband.
(445) [Attributed to someone.]
90. The river breeze,
gently swaying the waves along the banks and causing the blossoming young *karuṇa* and jasmine flowers to dance with joy, [blows].
For here, in the fresh spring, the breezes blow— steadfast in dispelling the exhaustion from the battle of love for women.
Shaking the campaka trees on the grounds surrounding the Kāverī, a certain breeze gently scattered the nectar of the clusters of kunda flowers.
The curling locks of hair on the foreheads of the women of Lāṭa, their arrangement loosened by the rain of affection from their beloveds, dance as they fall straight down to the very roots.
Of Acala: (Su.ra.
1129) O friend, this breeze—cool with droplets from the cascades of the Revā river, gentle through contact with blossoming cloves, and beloved by the fawn-eyed women—is as dear to me as a lover.
It kisses the face, produces trembling, tears open the garment, spreads sighs, causes horripilation, and pulls at the ends of the hair.
For someone,
it carries the fragrance akin to the milk of a fresh sprout from a creeper resting on the slopes of the Malaya mountain.
This breeze from the water’s edge, slightly trembling, is intimately acquainted in secret with the women of the Pāṇḍya land.
Rolling upon the stage of the embrace of the rising waves of the Kāverī, the elephants of Umāpati Dhara—
frightened by the powerful roar of the lions that are cuckoos— have fled to distant lands.

O fierce one, these winds blow in Caitra, fragrant with the hallīsaka dance of swaying creepers and the kaṅkelli and mallī flowers that serve as the play-palms for young women, O daughter of Mitrāvaruṇa. (450)
Of the Rākṣasa: (Śā. Pa. 3810) 91. On the shore of the ocean, the sea breeze blows through the young betel vines.
The breeze is skilled in the art of movement, moist with thick mist,
and pleasant with the astringent fragrance of wild betel nuts crushed by the teeth of celestial women. 451.
Showering a downpour of spray from the shores of the salt ocean of Dakṣa.

The breeze, a kinsman of the fragrance of young *karuṇa* and *mallikā* jasmine, blows as it dallies upon the swings of the Malaya forest; it has been enjoyed and then released by Dravidian women exhausted from the intensity of their lovemaking. ||452||
Those [waves] of the southern ocean which have long followed Dharmapāla with their surges.

Thereafter, those winds— having drunk the remnants [of breath] from the serpents dwelling in the sandalwood trees of Malaya, having wandered within the blossoming creepers at every sprout, and acting as companions to the fire of separation— have arrived. 453.
Amara Siṃha’s [work],
languid with the grace of the rolling waves of the southern ocean gently swaying.

The breezes, made fragrant by the blossoming jasmine garlands tossed about in the amorous play of the Karṇāṭa women, sport repeatedly upon the slopes of the breasts of Kerala beauties and upon the foreheads of Lāṭa women, scattering the jasmine wreaths from the braided hair of Mālava brides. 454.
By the splendors of someone [who resembles] Viṣṇu, the rays of the moon— held for a moment by their lofty [heights]— [are surpassed].
In Dvārakā, the breezes— causing the shores of the western ocean to tremble by their constant impact against the palaces—

serve [the Lord] eternally, filled with fierce *huṃkāra* sounds that fall from the mouths of enraged lions awakened by the dark force of being struck by the hard trunks of the primordial elephants. 455.
Of someone:
92. The Morning Breeze.
This [breeze] at dawn, which crushes the dense beads of perspiration on the surface of the thick, high breasts of sleepless Dravidian women,
is refined by the fragrance of the flowing sap of sandalwood trees.
"O friend, the breeze blows, the remnants of what has been consumed by the serpent. (Su.ra. 1144) — by someone.
At dawn, these breezes— fragrant everywhere with the blossoming jasmine, touching the clouds that rumble softly as they prepare for rain,
and gently caressing the young women exhausted from the battle of love— blow very slowly.
The winds blow, stealing away the drops of perspiration from the forehead. (457) — by Acala (Su.ra. 1139).

At the end of the night, the breeze was sweet with the abundant fragrance of rows of blue lotuses awakened by the rays of the moon; it was heavy with the pollen of those flowers and swallowed the drops of perspiration born from the exhaustion of love-play.
The wind, raining down showers of frost, makes the lotus tremble with horripilation.
In the springtime at dawn, the breeze blows— saturated with droplets of perspiration from the moon-like faces of beautiful women,
swaying their dangling creeper-like tresses, and shaking the garments upon their hips—
as it carries the pollen from rows of fully blossomed lotuses.
The breeze, enchanting with the fragrance of jasmine, removes the exhaustion born of the passion of love. (459) — Amaruka (58; Śārṅgadharapaddhati 3732, Sūktimuktāvalī 83.1).
Whirling far around the region of the breasts,
stumbling slightly at the slender waist, and obstructed by the expansive curves of the broad hips, the breezes blew among the young women.
The morning breezes dispel the exhaustion born of the pleasure of amorous dalliance.
(Ratnākara) (Sv 2167, Śā.pa. 3730)
93. Madana is the kinsman of the moon, the companion of spring, who imparts a charm to the fifth note,
who displays manifold sports, and who is the master of the dalliance of lotus-eyed women.
That god, the lover who dwells within the heart, the wielder of five arrows, ever triumphs as he brings about the sweet transformations of intoxication with honeyed wine.
Rājaśekhara’s [work],
which knows the aesthetic sentiments and dispositions of the three worlds both internally and externally, causes all the multitudes of embodied beings to dance.
May the Blessed One, the Supreme Primordial God, the self-born Great Poet of the drama of erotic passion, grant us security. 462.462
Victorious is that flower-bowed god, the deity of playful amorous dalliances, whose beautiful wife is Madalekhā, who is unrestrained in her love for Bhavānanda.
For him, whose form is that of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), the moon, garlands, and honey serve as an unprecedented instrument for achieving victory over the three worlds. (463)
Of Utpalarāja (Su.ra.
332): At one and the same time, the bodiless god whose bow is flowers strikes the three worlds with flower-arrows that do not even touch them.
Thus victorious is the mind-born one, whose craftsmanship consists of vast and manifold wonderful intentions, and whose form is honored by all living beings.
For someone [else]: (Su.ra.
325) No teacher is to be entreated; the beloved image is the object of worship—[consisting of] gazing, hiding, and kissing.
We pay homage to that initiation of the god Makaraketana, which offers up the self as the sacrificial oblation and conquers the essence of all other vows.
Of Vallana. (Su.ra.
333) 94. I bow to the god Madana, the very bodiless one, who, under the guise of the lotus-petals of women’s eyes, displays his heroic prowess.

By him, with a noose of great length, the three worlds were bound so tightly that even that Lord Kapālī— his body smeared with ashes— was forcibly initiated into the playful vow of bowing at the feet of the Daughter of the Mountain, who was enraged by love. (466)
By Lalitoka. (Su.ra.
328) The bow is the lord of mountains; the string is the lord of serpents.
Bāṇa had the Ancient Puruṣa as his ally, and the gods were his helpers;
the Lord of Cities was the conqueror of three cities, whereas this one, whose weapon is flowers, is the conqueror of the three worlds. (467)
This is that Śaṅkara, whose self-restraint is renowned throughout the three worlds, [who brought about] the bliss of existence for Bhava.
Now, distressed by separation, he supports his beloved with his body;
"By him indeed have we been conquered"—thus laughing aloud, Smara triumphs as he strikes your hand with his own. 468.
Of the blue silk cloth. (Su.ra.
323) The family preceptor [is the authority] for bestowing the initiation of play upon women.

Victorious is the supreme friend of the beloved of Rohiṇī—the bodiless one—who, even with his flower-arrows, is the conqueror of the God of gods; he is the stage-manager for the dramatic play of amorous dalliance. 469.

By Rājaśekhara: (Viśvaguṇādarśa-bhāṇa 1.1, Subhāṣitaratnabhāṇḍāgāra 327, Śārṅgadharapaddhati 3077, Sūktimuktāvalī 1.25) The bow is a garland, the bowstring is a swarm of humming bees, and the target is a young woman.

May that Kāma, whose abode is the side-long glances of his beloved, grant you all your desires— he who, though bodiless, possesses the power to conquer the three worlds with these five arrows beginning with the "mind-piercer" (manobheda). 470.
Of someone; (Sv 82, su.ra.
331) 95. High and low.
O Destroyer of Tripura, from this renewed appearance it is inferred that in previous births I likely never bowed to you;
for in this birth, though I am bodiless, I have not been lacking in devotion even at the outset.
O Great Lord, these two offenses of mine must be forgiven. (Su.ra.
36) — by Muñja.
Neither moonlight, nor jasmine, nor my beloved, nor the fifth note of the lute; neither betel, nor unguents, nor secret dalliance, nor strings of pearls,
nor even the eloquent verses of great poets are able to steal away my mind in such a manner.
Just as devotion to the Trident-bearer, the teacher of all that moves and is stationary, was awakened by merits,
so too [was it] for him alone.
O Goddess, what a wretched state would befall the world, terrified by the wrathful and merciless Citragupta, were it not for you,
O Dharmarāja, who grants liberation from the bonds of karma!
The document concerning the purification of the office of the scribe, issued by Viriñci.
||473|| 473|| Viriñci’s [document].
With his own limbs arranged as a dense couch, with the waves of his breath rising like chowries, performing the function of a parasol with his broad hoods,
and bearing a circle of lamps in the jewels of his crest, he honored the Lord of the Universe.
Śeṣa lives only by means of a mind whose resolve is not fixed for an aeon;
[this is] the teaching of Brahmanāga.
The gods praise his praiseworthy breast; by him his lineage has been purified; even those sages who are themselves worthy of honor bow down before him and stand in awe of him;
the three worlds rest in the palm of his hand—what more need be said? Therein the nectar of immortality is dissolved.

May this first stream of deities, composed by Śrīdharadāsa, purify those who immerse themselves in it—like the Gaṅgā—as it flows like the very nectar for the ears of excellent sayings (*saduktikarṇāmṛta*).

Thus ends the first stream, titled "The Stream of Deities," compiled by the illustrious Mahāmāṇḍalika Śrīdharadāsa in the *Saduktikarṇāmṛta*. Now follow the verses (95 in number). [End of] the *Saduktikarṇāmṛta*.
In the *Saduktikarṇāmṛta* composed by Śrīdharadāsa, may this first stream of deities— which, like the Gaṅgā, purifies those who plunge into it— be auspicious.
Thus ends the first stream, named "The Stream of Deities," compiled by the illustrious Mahāmāṇḍalika Śrīdharadāsa in the *Saduktikarṇāmṛta*.

(2) The waves of the flow of erotic sentiment,
the junction of two ages, the rising state of youth— this young woman is a marvel to the world.
The innocent (mugdhā), the adolescent (madhyā), the mature (prauḍhā), and the newly married woman; the same [woman] when she is confident (visrabdhā);
the pregnant woman (garbha-vatī), the truthful woman (satya-vatī), the wanton woman (svairiṇī), the instructed woman (upadeśa), the concealed unchaste woman (gupta-bandhakī).
The clever woman, the unchaste woman, the woman whose unchastity is observed, and the courtesan;
furthermore, even the young women of the South, the West, the North, and the East may be rustic.
A mere woman, distressed by the marks of another's enjoyment shared with her lover;
a woman separated from her beloved, whose words are those of separation and whose tears are the messenger’s message.

The beloved’s words, the words of her dear friend, the recounting of her gestures, the description of her fever, her agitation, and the manifestation of her various states; ||4||4|| [And] the manifestation of her condition during the moments of her distress. ||4||4|| [Note: The provided source text appears to contain a typographical error regarding the verse numbering.]
The woman prepared for the tryst (*vāsakasajjā*), she whose husband is under her control (*svādhīnabhartṛkā*), and the deceived one (*vipralabdhā*).
[5.5] The woman separated by a quarrel (*kalahāntaritā*); her speech, the words of a female friend, and the slip of the tongue regarding family lineage (*gotra*).

The interruption of the journey, the woman whose husband is away, her speech to her friends, and their response; her conversation with her beloved, the description of her condition, and the waiting for her husband. //7.7//
The crow, the lover's betrayal, and then the commencement of the act of going to meet him;
the woman going to meet her lover during the day, at night, in moonlight, or in foul weather— these are the ways of unchaste women.
The prattling, the form of a woman, the eyebrows, eyes, ears, lips, face, and speech; the arms, breasts, line of hair on the abdomen, and the amorous play of young women.
The types of heroes (nāyakas) are the compliant, the clever, the deceitful, the bold, and the vulgar; as well as the proud, the separated, and the traveler.
Regarding the traveler: the traveler in the rainy season and the traveler's recollection of his heroine.
Interruption of a journey, separation, remembrance of a woman separated from her lover, a glance, a painting, a dream, longing in young lovers, emaciation, and the recounting of virtues. ||11||11||
Agitation, lamentation, the reproach of the clouds that are the memories of the beloved,
madness, the love-letter, and the ornament of the waters of the pleasure-grove.
Conversation with a female messenger, the seduction of a woman by a man, the rebuke of a female messenger,
the arrival of a couple, instrumental music, song, gambling, and the glance.
For women, there is the side-glance and the endearment, the drinking of honey-wine, reclining upon the bed,
embracing, kissing, biting the lower lip, scratching with the nails, and the cooing of the throat.

At dawn, there is the sight of the beloved, then the departure of the women, the praise of lovemaking,
the mutual conversations of the female friends, and the one who feels bashful at the chatter of the parrots.
The dawn, the rising of the sun, midday, sunset, and the darkness of evening; the appearance of lamps and the moon, and the nights— these are the commencement of the season of flowers.
The spring season is its day; the bees are its parrots; the summer heat is its garment;
the passion born of summer is its forest fire; and the onset of the rainy season is its [concluding] state. ||18||18||
The rainy season consists of the rivers born from the monsoon clouds and the days and nights;
autumn consists of the lakes belonging to it and the khañjana birds; and winter consists of the dark nights of that same [season]. ||19||
The winter [brings] the plowman and the traveler; the cold [brings] the crops of that village and its comforts.
Thus, with one hundred and seventy-nine [verses], there is the high and low [variety] of the waves of rasa.

1. The transition of youth:
the eyes of the deer-eyed woman are steady, charming, and upturned; her breasts are not yet prominent, yet they possess beauty.
The movement of her eyebrows was unbroken yet full of intention; her inner longing was directed toward some unspecified object.
With their breasts concealed by the folds of their garments and displaying their circular hips with subtle grace, these secret yoginīs of the practice of love captivate the heart. 477.
Right before those youths, she suddenly became somewhat overcome with bashfulness.
In conversations concerning the amorous dalliances of mature women, the young girl restrains her chest with her mind alone, not with her vine-like arms;

She trembles at the door, she regards the chamber for amorous play as poison,
and she remains only upon a bed spread with lotus leaves; by that very mind, she has been made to perceive your form, brought before her through her imagination.
By Rājaśekhara. (Bālarāmāyaṇa 5.8, Sūktimuktāvalī 208, Viśvaguṇādarśabhāṇa 3.2, Subhāṣitaratnabhāṇḍāgāra 745) Agitated, she does not even look at her own face in the mirror when the moon is present.
Though she is terrified even by the warbling of the cuckoo and does not release her own voice,
and though she harbors hatred for the flower-armed god who inflicts such unbearable burning, that charming girl, O fortunate one, nourishes an ever-increasing love for you at every moment.
Of the Erotic sentiment: (Su.ra.
536) Poison, moonlight, the breeze from a bed of night-lotuses, and fire—[are all unbearable].
That necklace is salt upon a wound, and that sandalwood paste is indeed a cauterization;
O fortunate one, when you are slightly averse, how is it that all these things have simultaneously become, alas, contrary in their nature toward her? (648)
[This is] of Acalasiṃha. (Su.ra.
554) He does not delight in the mountain caves of pleasure-gardens, nor does he approach a window.
From afar she hates her elders and casts aside her desire for the pleasure grove;
O handsome one, that friend of hers remains there, sustained only by the consoling words of her companions,
placing her hope in her, in him, and once again in you.
He seizes the necklace of Dhoyī like a noose, but not the jewel-string which is mostly composed of fire.

O Lord, suspecting you to be Kaṇṭhaka, that young woman does not rest upon the couch of flower-buds; now she is as agitated by the thick paste of sandalwood as if it were mud, and she trembles before the coil of the poisonous vine as if it were a serpent. (650)
36. Description of the state of night:
While this moon of clear luster shines with the brilliance of a blooming jasmine flower,
When you, her beloved, had departed for the eastern sky and had gone but a short distance away,
her breath became like a night-lily bud, her face like a lotus,
her passion like the ocean of milk, and even her glance instantly took on the luster of the moonstone.
By someone [else]. (*Śāradātilaka-pañjikā* 3480, *Sūktimuktāvalī* 44.10; *Padyāvalī* 355, by Bhīmabhaṭṭa):
"The lotus is her face, and the eye is a moonstone."

O fortunate one, when you were stationed far away during those nights as white as the moon of a Caṇḍāla, a transformation born of the flower-bowed god (Kāma) manifested within her, who was like the ocean itself.
By Caṇḍālacandra. (Sūryaśataka 538):
The heat has consumed the outpouring of water; the thickening vapor has been observed by the departing breath.
The wick of her lamp flickers with her sighs, and her body is submerged in pallor;
what more shall I say? Throughout the entire night, she remains by the window facing your path, warding off the moonlight with the parasol of her hand.
By Rājaśekhara. (Viśvaguṇādarśabhāṇa 2.21; Subhāṣitaratnabhāṇḍāgāra 540) Her cheek is clouded by tears that flow incessantly and by anxiety.
O Lord, her heart is distressed and her chest heaves with surging waves of heavy sighs;
thus, in separation from you, either the three watches of the night, or her bed, or the flower-armed god of love alone knows the extent of her calamity, exhausted as she is by such torment.
This forest of lotuses is leafless for its refuge; the earth is devoid of sandalwood.
The waters have become free of mud, and the trees have been stripped of their leaf-cups by her companions;

O fortunate one, those nights—filled with the cries of flocks of longing cakravāka birds and the fragrance of night-lotuses awakening at the sound of her lamentation—are being passed by her in your absence. (655)
Of a certain [woman]:
37. Vāsakasajjā (one who has prepared herself for the lover)
She prepares the bed even though it has already been prepared; she ornaments her body again though it has already been adorned; she personally performs the worship of the Lord of Pleasure;
and as the night passes, she attends to the door for a long time as if it were a loss.
Does that poor girl, exhausted by passion, not do anything at all in the house of play?
— by Ācārya Gopīka.
Seeing her own face adorned with captivating ornaments in the circle of the mirror,
and the house of enchantment made tawny by the flame of the lamp, the gazelle-eyed woman,
filled with joy, thought: "Thus will our union take place after a long time, today."
Slowly, with an intense longing to see her beloved, she fixed her gaze at the doorway in a most graceful manner. (Rudraṭa, Śṛṅgāratilaka 1.76a)
With glances that are tremulous, moist with the moisture of love, repeatedly half-closed,
momentarily turned toward him, flickering with bashfulness, and averted by winking—
as if vomiting forth the inner intention of their hearts— Please perform a final verification to ensure the accuracy of the translation.
"Tell me, O charming girl, who is this fortunate man being gazed upon by you today?
(Amaru 4, Su.ra. 508; Sv 1098, Śā.pa. 3416, Sū.mu. 39.4)

She repeatedly adorns her limbs with ornaments; she suspects even a passing leaf of being you; she prepares her bed and meditates for a long time—such are the hundreds of playful fancies involving her preparations for adornment, the arrangement of her couch, and her mental constructions.
"Though her slender form is distracted by longing, she will not pass this night without you," [says] Jayadeva. (Gg 6.3)
Discontent comes upon me, not sleep;
my mind reckons his virtues, not his faults; the night does not cease, nor does the hope for union.
The body grows thin, yet the passion does not diminish.
(Pravarasena; *Subhāṣitaratnakośa* 723, *Śārṅgadharapaddhati* 3427, *Bilhaṇa*, *Padyāvalī* 214)
38. A woman whose husband is under her own control writes a love-letter upon her breasts, fastens a garland around her neck,
applies a forehead-mark to her brow, and brushes away the curls from her cheeks.
Thus, repeatedly touching her body all over with hundreds of endearments,
her beloved, distressed by separation, does not leave her side.
By Rudraṭa (Śṛṅgāratilaka 1.74a): "O Lord, O playful one, arrange my forehead with its curling locks and its tilaka;
O Master of my life, join back together the necklace broken upon the slope of my breast."

Having spoken thus, she whose face was like the full moon, who had been made happy by the pleasure at the conclusion of lovemaking, touched by him with the words "So be it," her hair standing on end, fell once more into a state of swoon.
Of that very [man]: when the barley-gruel is upon the two lotus-feet of the woman, which possess the luster of fresh lotuses... (Śṛ.ti. 1.42c; SD 3.73, Sū.mu. 80.6)
Even though his passion was equal [to hers], he cast her down,
his purpose being merely to employ flattering words.
Shall I bind these locks of yours, dark and curling like a swarm of bees?
Or shall I place a decorative leaf-design upon this cheek, as sweet and pale as a madhūka flower?
Moreover, having removed this binding [garment] from these lotuses that steal the beauty of opening buds,
I shall place it upon my breast, which captivates the deer of every heart.

He who was of immeasurable weight, whose feet were always the guests of those eager for alms, who was innocent of worldly conventions, unable to endure delay, and addicted to pleasure— [of such a one as Sūryadhara...]
Disregarding my feigned anger, my slapping of his hands, and my forced tears of shame, my beloved plunges me into modesty by force.
Of Ācārya Gopīka:
39. This attendant was seen previously as if possessed by poison, having been deceived; or rather, he was seen with a long-term prognosis, warding [off the danger].
Alas, you who know the sequence of past and future, you have not heeded the words of your friends;
O simple one, you have been deceived by a rogue who, like placing the moon in your hand, has cheated you—fie on that!
Why do you weep? Why do you despair? Why are you sleepless? Why do you grieve? (666)
For someone,
their infamy became known to their kinsmen, and their steadfastness vanished far away.

Shame has been abandoned, immodesty has been displayed even though it was not intended, the status of a virtuous wife has been cast aside, and the path of goodness in both worlds has been lost; a stain has been placed upon the family.
O messenger, what else remains [to be done] such that he still does not come today? 667.
[By someone: "O friend, he has been defeated by a certain other woman with her lute-playing. (Śā. Pa. 3616; Sū. Mu. 71.14)
Surely a wager was made by those two regarding your playful night-strolls;
otherwise, how could your beloved linger even among the *śephālī* flowers where blossoms are falling, even when the moon has spread across the midst of the sky? (668)
By Rudraṭa. (Padyāvalī 213; Daśarūpaka 2.23; Śṛṅgāratilaka 1.78ab) Weeping with longing, trembling repeatedly, departing with tears for a long time...
Her eyes were cast toward the directions with compassion; she conversed with her friend;
yet, even though the time for the evening toilette had arrived, her beloved did not come.
Thus, that deer-eyed woman performed various actions out of anxiety, the full extent of which is beyond the reach of words.
Of that very [place]: "The trysting-house which was mentioned by her beloved after he had himself sent a female messenger, O dear one... (Śṛṅgāratilaka 1.79a).
Having gazed upon that empty place for a very long time, she then desisted in her hope;
and with eyes from which thick collyrium was trickling, as if writing a string of letters upon the ground to indicate her place of residence and worship, she wept slowly and long.
Of Rudraṭa. (Śṛṅgāratilaka 1.78a) 40. Kalahāntaritā (the woman separated by a quarrel).
Because the words of her friends were not heeded in her ear, because the counsel of her kin was not respected,
and because even as her beloved fell at her feet he was brushed aside with a lotus from her ear—
therefore the moon acts like fire, and the application of sandalwood paste acts like sparks.
The night stretches out as if it were a hundred kalpas; even a necklace of lotus fibers becomes a burden.
(Amaru, Su.ra. 702)
"First, my beloved was embarrassed because I, having concealed my anger by a slip of the tongue regarding his family name, did not stop him as he was departing;
yet this man is perceptive of inner intent and skilled in reflecting upon the final outcome."
"Even my friend has become as if painted in a picture; what is this?"—this is Bimboḳa’s [lament] (Sū.mu. 84.4; Su.ra. 656).
As I hurried out from the house, disregarding him who was rolling at my feet, O beloved, I did not consider for a moment that,
alas, you two— the weight of my hips and the weight of my breasts— are exceedingly heavy.
No delay was permitted other than for two existences;
[this is] by Gaṅgādhara.
That my beloved was turned away with harsh words when he prostrated at her feet, that her friend’s advice was not heeded out of dull-wittedness, and that she alone held onto resentment—
all this is now the fruit of that wicked woman's actions, appearing as the radiance of sandalwood and the moon.
The body is repeatedly scorched by frost, water, wind, and lotus stalks. (Rudraṭa; Śṛṅgāratilaka 1.77a, Sūktimuktāvalī 56.1)
It burns the limbs during separations, it stirs jealousy upon reunion;
seen or touched, it steals the heart and renders the body helpless. When it arrives, not even for a moment is happiness found, and when it departs, it cannot be recovered.
What else is more wonderful than this: that he remains my beloved nevertheless? (Amaruka, Su.ra. 734)

41. A statement from a woman separated by a quarrel: "O friend, that he is handsome yet possesses little affection for me—this does not cause me pain, because every person enjoys happiness as ordained by fate."
But this is the torment of my mind: that even though people turn away from me, my shameless heart somehow does not become indifferent. (676)
O Immortal One! (Sv 1118, Su.ra. 694) Sighs burn my face; my heart is uprooted and torn asunder;
sleep does not come; I do not behold the beloved's face; day and night I weep.

My limbs wither away while my beloved, having fallen at my feet, is thus neglected; O friends, considering what virtue have we cultivated that we were made to practice jealous indignation toward our lover? (677)

Of someone: This darkness has arisen from the lights; this fire has been born from the waters; this deadly poison has emerged from nectar; and heat has its origin in shade. (Amaru 98; Padyāvalī 237; Daśarūpaka 2.26)
What indeed could be the remedy for this in times of pacification? This knot is truly very firm; O friends, though it was done out of affection, this unpleasantness cannot be undone by consolations.
Of someone:
Even from that face marked with the lines of lac-dye, why is the moon so unbearable for his torment?
And why is the song of the cuckoo more painful than even the proliferation of her words? (Sūktimuktāvalī 2.63)
O friend, do the heart-piercing arrows of the flower-bowed god not fly forth even from that glance of his, though it is dependent on the slighting of his affection?
O friend, through stories of the moon reflected in water and by some means over a long period of time, the night has somehow reached its midpoint while my beloved remains away.
Then, while I was still angry from a playful quarrel with my beloved,
this eastern direction became as red as a rival wife.

[This is] the speech of a female friend to one who has been separated by a quarrel; [spoken] by someone who, disregarding the consequences of love, has paid no heed to her friends. (Sūryaśataka 1642, verse 42)
O simple one, why have you shown such pride toward your lover at this untimely moment?
For with your own hand, you have drawn these very coals, whose flames blaze with the fire of separation; therefore, enough now of weeping in the wilderness.
Amaru (66; Sbhv 1170; sū.mu. 56.9, su.ra. 659):
I told you long ago, "Do not abandon virtue when there is a quarrel."
In times of fear, he is dearer to you; yet you release him in vain while he is within the power of your own hand.
Having fallen into embarrassment, he will not return again like an arrow;
therefore, my dear friend, he must be brought back by you yourself through the method of pulling him by the hand.
Those many sequences of words from her friends were not even heard by the teacher Gopīka.
O hard-hearted one, this person has not been struck even by the tip of your big toe as you lie prostrate at your feet; due to your addiction to the false vow of silence,
this is merely a means to abandon your attendants, not an assumption of pride.
Of someone: (Su.ra.
687) Her hips are elevated, with a disarrayed girdle.
O fair-thighed one, if that heartless man has departed, having cast aside this face with its pupils darting toward the corners of the eyes,
then surely he alone is the one deceived.
By someone:
"O friend, out of the swelling of pride, I did not take account of the injury to my beloved's affection."
Furthermore, this speech of the circle of friends was not heeded here:
"Now that [the moon] has ascended the peak of the eastern mountain, why will this knot of pride not be forcibly loosened by the rays of the storehouse of digits? (685)
685. Of Jalacandra (43): Mistaking someone's name.
Before the slender maiden, startled by my slip of the name, I stood with downcast face; overcome by embarrassment, I, cursed by fate, began to scribble something or other,
until that placement of lines somehow transformed into her very likeness.
It is evident that it is that same young woman who has returned again with her limbs restored.
(Amaru 46)
"Do not do this; somehow, let your mind not falter even slightly from this point.
Or rather, what can I do here, O beloved, for these words are but a vain knot, a mere tinkling sound of anklets?"
Therefore, let this lotus-foot of yours be my ear-ornament.
(687) [Of Narasiṃha]
"Why have you become afraid when my speech was only half-finished? And why is your throat faltering?
This is no time for such chatter; let this irrelevant talk cease.
Speak now what is relevant, for it is being heard by the ears of your friends."
Satisfaction has already been fully provided for me by these syllables and words; thus says Abhinanda (Sū.mu. 57.26).
When her beloved, having somehow regained his composure,

uttered a faltering reply, she— emaciated by separation— invented a pretext, fearing that her unbearable friend might overhear it and thus suspecting it had been heard, she acted with great agitation.
In an empty house, she sighed again with her eyes rolling [in fear]. (689) By someone. (As 63)
Having approached from afar and warded off her friends with a glance, she stood before you with her arms raised and bracelets jingling, her hips prominent, and her eyes closed out of affection;
she was honored by you when you addressed her by the name of your rival, saying, "I have recognized you."
If he indeed lives, then abandon your haste; surely he himself will entreat you. (690) By Ācārya Gopīka.
44. "O proud one! O young mistress! O proud lady, abandon your anger! What have I done out of wrath?
The distress is upon us; you have committed no offense against me; all the faults are mine."
So why do you weep with a faltering voice? Before whom are you weeping?
Is it not because of this: "I am yours; why are you not my beloved?"—it is for this reason that one weeps.
In one place, sitting together on the same seat was avoided by keeping at a distance due to her pecking [at him];
even the impulsive embrace was thwarted under the pretext of bringing betel. (Amaru 53; Da.Rū. 2.17; Sv 1614; Śā.Pa. 3554; Sū.Mu. 57.1; Su.Ra. 653)
Not even her conversation was mingled [with his], yet by employing her attendants nearby,
the clever woman brought her anger toward her beloved to its intended fulfillment through her indirect behavior.
Fearing that he might prostrate himself, she respectfully covers his feet with the hem of her garment;
under a pretext, she conceals her smile as it approaches and does not look at him clearly.
When I speak, she converses with her friend using contrary words;
let alone her intense affection, even her pride has a charming way of arising.
In his very mind it smokes, in his movements it faints,
in his body it blazes up, and in his consciousness it burns fiercely.
The fire of her great resentment, born from the slight she suffered at the hands of her lover, flickers in her face and bursts forth in her speech.
In someone,
a downpour of tears proclaims the intense paleness of the cheeks,
and the heavy breathing spreads fullness across the jar-like breasts.
Her mind experiences an indescribable longing that makes her limbs thin;
thus, her grief manifests even more intensely than the bloom of her youth.
In someone who considers herself noble,
the moon of her face does not become dull, nor does crookedness take refuge upon her forehead.

Her lotus-eye does not redden, nor does her brow even knit a frown; yet this mere quivering of her lower lip, though she remains impenetrable to a hundred questions, reveals the play of anger within her beloved.
Of Vaidyadhanya: (Su.ra.
688) "You did not show me your face, beautiful with its lower lip quivering in envy."
Not even a single word of reproach was uttered by the innocent girl,
though her state of mind was tormented by my own passionate faults; yet she made her anger known by the tightening of the knot of her garment with her girdle.
Of Kāśmīranārāyaṇa: (Sv 1591) No piercing of the eyebrows was performed, nor has the radiance of the moon-like face ever been such as this.

Your sweet words have not been sullied by turbidity; yet from this, anger is perceived, since your boldness has now vanished and you are once again overcome by shame; and this great reverence for decorum persists, having abandoned all intimacy. (698)
The sighing breaths of someone are crushed by the tremors arising from the swelling of her breasts.
That the external object of sight is lost due to the closing of the eyes, and that tears flow when the eyelids are raised— these states, O fierce woman, announce a heart broken by grief. (699)
Although your disregard for ornaments bestows splendor upon someone else, [it does not do so for you].
Nevertheless, it seems to tell me, as if from within, that someone harbors resentment.
46. O friend, let my glance—proudly attached, tremulous, bold, and yet sharp—turn back; let my girdle slip down from the quivering of my breasts, and let it tear through my bodice.
Even so, I cannot believe that my deceitful lover will appear again;
otherwise, my heart would have burst from silence within this very moment.
From Amaruka (Su.ra.
636): Even when a frown is formed, her gaze looks up with even greater longing;
even when her heart is made harsh, her body takes on a thrill of horripilation.
Even though her speech is restrained, this scorched face is smiling;
when that person is seen, how will there be any conclusion to her pride?
By her alone was the knitting of the brows fashioned, the closing of the eyes practiced for a long time,
laughter learned with care, and an effort made toward silence.
I have somehow steadied this mind to maintain my fortitude; I have girded my loins to uphold my honor, yet success rests in the hands of fate.
Dharmakīrti’s (Amaru 92; Su.ra. 645; Padyāvalī 231):
My face was turned away from her face, my gaze was directed elsewhere, and my ears—most eager for the sound of her speech—were covered by me.
Though restrained by my hands, the bristling of my skin and the breaking out of sweat on my cheeks increase; O friends, what can I do, for the seams of my bodice are suddenly parting?
(Amaru 11; Sv 1581; Śā.pa. 3535; Su.ra.
640) "O friend, let my heart burst as it may, and let my body wither away as much as it will; I shall have no further concern with a lover whose affection is fickle."
Having thus spoken impetuously out of a swelling of pride,
that doe-eyed woman looked toward the path of her lover with apprehension.
47. A speech by a proud woman (*māninī*) to her lover (*nāyaka*): "Why do you lie prostrate at my feet with a dejected mind? For masters are independent. (Amaru 71 [61]; Su.ra. 666; Sū.mu. 55.1)

If you were delighted there for some time in some place, what offense have you committed? I am the one here who has wronged you, since women have their lives in their husbands; therefore, surely you must be entreated by me alone in our separation. 706.
Of Bhāvadevī. [Su.ra. 643; Vākkūṭasya; Sū.mu. 57.14; Padyā. 381; Kasyacit] Thus it was: at first, this body of ours was undivided.
Therefore, you are now my beloved, while I am one whose hopes are destroyed;
you are now the master, while I am but your wife. What more can be said?
This is the fruit I have reaped for my life, which is as hard as a thunderbolt. (707)
Amaruka: (Amaru 66, Sv 1622, Su.Ra. 646) "Let it be known; enough with these deceptive words, my dear, you may go."
Not even the slightest fault is yours; rather, fate has turned its back on us.
Since your love has reached such a state, what pain is there for us when this wretched life, inherently fickle as it is, has departed? (708)
In that [love], anger consists of the knitting of eyebrows, and restraint consists of silence. (Amaru 27; Sv 1617; Sū.mu. 57.6; Su.ra. 657; Padyā. 223)
Where there was mutual smiling and conciliation, where there was a look of grace— behold, now this very same love has become perverse:
you roll at my feet, yet for me, a wicked woman, there is no release from my anger.
When you were the moon, with a body beautiful in its fullness of digits— (Amaru 34; Da.rū. 2.19; Sv 1630; Śā.pa. 3562; Sū.mu. 84.7; Su.ra. 648)

I was born cool and moist by nature, like moonstones; now you are the sun, possessing harsh rays that have driven away all moisture, and I too am fashioned from the stone of the sun, emitting flames of anger. (710)
Of Acala. (Śā.pa. 3564, Sū.mu. 57.20, Su.ra.
647) 47. A Friend’s Awakening of a Proud Woman.
O noble lady, how small an offense is this slip of the tongue?
This man has been rolling at your feet for a long time; do not persist in your pride, abandon your anger, release him, and favor your beloved for his own future welfare.
Listen to what we say, dear friend; do not set your mind on pride. (Manokasya, Su.ra. 680)
"O friend, this beloved is not ill-behaved, nor is he devoid of virtues;
this pearl necklace has fallen at the base of your feet.
Take it, O charming girl, and let it find its place of affection upon your neck."
For no one else exists any other means for the pacification of the torment of the heart. (Sū.mu. 56.10; Su.ra. 658)
The beloved of my life sits outside, bent over, scratching the ground;
my sisters remain without food, their eyes swollen from constant weeping;
and by the parrots in their cages, all singing and reciting has been abandoned.
And such is your condition; now abandon this stubborn pride. (Amaru 7; Śāradātilaka-pañjikā 3551, Subhāṣitāmṛtasaṃgraha 56.5, Rask 2.206a)
This silence of yours, this smile that does not arise upon your face, this indistinct gaze, and this flavor of composure while standing with your face turned away—
these are due to the loss of courtesy in those who, though worthy of worship, possess such contrary inclinations.
O dear friend, the new servant goes far away from my heart. (714) —
Umāpatidhara.
O slender-waisted one, why do you bring about such withering upon your slightly pale cheek—resting on your red palm—with tears from eyes smeared with collyrium?
O charming girl, let the bee indeed kiss the kandalī flower here and there out of its fickleness; what does it matter?
Is that fragrance of the newly blossoming jasmine forgotten by him? (Su.ra.
651) — Pāṇini.
49. O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, cast a sidelong glance; let the God of Love vainly aim his arrows and momentarily cast aside his bow;
for your moment, raise the creeper of your brow!
Moreover, O charming girl, utter words that are sweet with inward passion and whose sequence of syllables is indistinct; let there be a delusion of drums among the lutes of the world.
Of Bherībhramaka (Su.ra. 450):
"Why is her braid so disheveled? Why are her eyes without collyrium?
And why is there no application of musk-paste or decorative leaf-designs upon her cheeks?"
O moon-faced one, why does this friend of yours weary herself at an improper time by failing to remember you, while your articles of adornment rest in her hands?
Of Abhinanda:

(Sahityadarpaṇa 4.193, Subhāṣitaratnabhāṇḍāgāra 731) O beloved, abandon your silence; let my hearing drink the stream of nectar, let these two eyes of mine be opened, and let the world become composed of blue lotuses.
Be gracious; let even love quell my restlessness entirely,
for surely this attendant is beyond reproach and free from fault.
Of the child: (Su.ra. 670) If your gaze is cast down and vacant, why then does it remain fixed with curiosity?
If you have made an effort toward silence, why then does your lower lip quiver?
If the eye is fixed in meditation, how can there be the rising of horripilation? Pride has been displayed through gestures; be gracious, tell me what is to be said. (719)
Of Amaru: (Sv 1625, Su.Ra.
638) Upon her cheek, the decorative leaf-pattern has been crushed by the pressure of her palm;
this nectar-like essence of her lower lip has been drunk in by her sighs.
Again and again, the tears clinging to your throat cause your breast to tremble;
O you who are devoid of courtesy, it is resentment that has become dear to you, and not we.
By someone. (Amaru 67; Su.ra. 664, Sa.ka.ā.v 489, Sv 1627) 50. The shattering of pride:
When [the lover] is seen, [her heart] is slightly bud-like, like her eye; when he stands at her side, it is like her face.

When her lover touched her feet, the beautiful-eyed woman’s anger— which had been subdued, remained on the outside like a bristling thrill, spread a touch like the knot of a sash, and then became slackened as she spoke— departed from her as if out of shame.

Of someone: [Love] has sprouted in the mind; it has become two-leaved in the pair of spreading eyes. (Sakalāṅkāravidhāyinī 15.496, Śārṅgadharapaddhati 3581, Sūktimuktāvalī 58.2, Subhāṣitaratnabhāṇḍāgāra 699)
In speech, the tree of pride of the indignant woman has sprouted; on her cheeks, it has grown thick;
in her various gestures of anger, it has blossomed; but when her beloved has prostrated at her feet, that tree of pride has borne fruit and become barren at its very end.
By Rājaśekhara (Su.ra.
679): Of two who are suffering in silence on a single bed, turned away from one another...
Although each remained in the other's heart, the couple preserved their mutual dignity through courtesy; yet, as their glances slowly mingled with sidelong turns,
the quarrel of pride was broken by a sudden burst of laughter and a firm embrace around the necks.
By Amaru (Amaru 19, Sv 2112, Śā.pa. 3715, Sū.mu. 81.8, Su.ra.

3429) "O Bhadra, you dwell in this village; therefore, through your acquaintance, you know the news."

My companion, emaciated by the pain of long separation, has plunged into the fire of spring.

For a flock of cuckoos, there is emaciation when afflicted by disease; for one wounded, there is blood; and for one bitten, there is the flow of saliva.

Ah, it is understood! While the honey-seeking bees have begun their clamor, some reckless person must surely have cast his gaze upon the mango bud. (905)

While the village sleeps and the clouds thunder,

at midnight, women whose husbands are away— whose minds are overcome by swelling longing— sing songs that are beautiful because their rhythmic beats have ceased; the travelers weep with tears born of compassion for their own misfortune.
It is heard that someone, with eyes motionless due to absorption in meditation, is weeping. 906. 906. [Of someone.]
O traveler, do not go by this path if your life is dear to you, brother;
for here stands before you a most terrible Rākṣasa in the form of a mango tree,

"It is heard that the caravan of travelers has just now been destroyed by one of pitiless intent. (907) [By someone.]
O travelers, leave the path along the banks of the Godāvarī;
meanwhile, let another road be sought by you here,

The fresh sprout-sheath emerging from the placement of his lotus-like feet—
[this belongs to someone].
From where do you come? Where indeed is the face of happiness seen? Where does the darkness dwell?
Where has the smoke-bannered god of love arisen among women? Where have those youths been seen?
Where will he go? And where is the fifth? Where is *ṇasakṛt*? And from where has *saṃkura* emerged?
Where is the arising of the single flavor of bliss, where indeed is the virtuous woman, and what talk can there be of a traveler?
(909) [Of someone.]
"O traveler, no lodging is given now to a wayfarer in this village;

263): O brother Magha, upon the neck of Vyāsa—which possesses the splendor of the throat of Śrīkaṇṭha, dark as the collyrium of a playful lotus—hangs a necklace as beautiful as the bow of Indra.
Roar at your leisure for just a moment and show her mercy; that young girl, her eyes filled with tears, her slender body as delicate as a young lotus stalk, is not able to endure it.
Beholding from afar someone delighted by a rain-cloud, alas, he does not move even a single step forward.
Why does he, whose life is ruined, sigh so long and hot through eyes like unceasing rain-clouds?
At midnight, the emperor of poets, that traveler of aesthetic sentiment, beheld with upturned eyes the treacherous expanse of clouds and the lightning flashes suddenly lurking within them.
There was no longing song, nor was there weeping with trembling agitation; no sighs were released, nor was any sign of consent given—rather, it was only the heart [that betrayed her].
Of Vāhlīka (Śā. Pa. 3892):
Having heard at midnight the sound of a steady rain-cloud pouring down water, [the lover] meditated for a long time upon his young, separated beloved, sighing deeply with tears in his eyes.

[Amaru 11] 89. Remembrance of the Beloved while Abroad:
"By us, who take delight in the practice of the Supreme Person through discernment..."

How these days pass for her— struck even by the arrows of Rati’s lover (Cupid), yet due to her youth and this fresh separation from you— we do not know, alas, how they pass for that body of yours. 916

From the heart of that one filled with sorrow, sorrows break forth like sprouts from a tree.

[I salute her] whose ornaments have been cast off and whose lips are moistened with the water of tears. (Sv 1152)

When the sun has set, alas, I seem to see my beloved standing far away, her face weary with double the grief, her lotus-like hand pressed against her face, as if she were inscribed upon the wall of my memory.
920 Of someone 90. Refutation of the commencement [of motion]

She steals away his departure with childish talk, accompanied by tears falling from her eyes.

The beloved has been held captive by the slender woman with the flood of a river fashioned from her torrent of tears.

A fresh cluster of nine buds, placed upon her hand, brings an end to the journey—

"O beautiful one, you have gone far from the house; here is a milky tree—
turn back from this very spot," the traveler said softly to his beloved,
whose bodice was bursting open across the expanse of her pair of breasts heaving with the weight of her indignation.
Beholding the chest [of the son] with eyes filled with tears, she brought about the cancellation of his departure from the son of the Sun. (Sv.

Of a certain person.

"I am removing this bark garment and placing a fine silken cloth upon your breasts;

980. Śāntyākaragupta’s 102. Candropālambhaḥ (The Refutation of Candra)

that emaciation of the ocean which was dispelled, and that [closing] of the night-lotuses which was taken away— [all these were accomplished by you].

Umāpatidhara.

O wretched moon, do not touch me even in play with your scorching rays, for the lines of soot from the fire of separation from my beloved turn into ashes upon contact with you; indeed, those who roll here in your light undergo a state of being consumed by heat.
The rays [of the moon], charming like the stalks of lotus fibers that are half-ripe and half-old.
