the fifth note dwells within the hollows of the throats of the sweet-voiced cuckoos.
For the Lord, who delights in adorning the three worlds under a single umbrella, the month of Caitra suddenly became a marvelous thing— a warrior who was a world-conqueror.
The surface of the pond is bristling with the knots of lotus leaves and sprouts,
while the bees, clustering upon the buds of the mango trees, remain in a state of utter stillness.
Moreover, today the Blessed One, whose weapon is the flower, bears his bow with pride,
wipes the string, and desires to conquer the world with five arrows. (1235)
(From the *Subhāṣitaratnakośa*, verses 173ab, by Vīryamitra; also attributed to Abhinanda):
153. It is a spring day; the lotus pond is bristling with reddish sprouts, and the night is not yet long.

The days are arriving—days that pierce the vitals of young women separated from their lovers; when the light of the sky-jewel has become slightly bold as it releases its frost in small measure, and these days are made resonant by cuckoos emitting the fragrance of mango blossoms. (1236)
To the Saṅghaśrīs: (Su.ra.
152) They gently summon the southern breeze with the cries of the male cuckoos.
These days adorn the forest groves with sprouts used as ear-ornaments by bees perched upon them;
they beautify the moon with moonlight that has shed its mantle of frost; and they both increase and repeatedly intensify the god of love. (1237)
1237 (Kasyacit; Su.ra.
161) These [clouds] now incessantly and without hesitation spread despondency.

The days delight the bees with the fragrances of lotuses in the wilderness; the forest regions of mango groves resound with the cries of vocal male cuckoos, while travelers flee in all directions upon hearing them. 1238.
These [songs] of Yogeśvara delight the ears with the humming of bees intoxicated by passion.
The days of spring have hearts that travel the path of ascetic purification (dhūta),
and breezes that proudly share the intimacy of the fragrance from the lotus-faces of women whose faces are like spotless moons. 1239.
(For someone) [there is] a new lotus-pond, with its cool waters emerging little by little as they recede.

These days delight us, as bees alighting upon the faces of the quarters form rows of curls; and the minds of travelers are agitated by the explanations provided by cuckoos—the kinsmen of Love—who have begun to expound upon the sprouts of seeds [of passion]. 1240.
1240 (of Hari) 154 spring trees

Even here, this glorious tree, now densely budding, has its breeze perfumed by the fragrance emerging from the sap poured upon its sprouts, which have been broken by the weight of bees eager for mutual play.
"Alas! This young mango tree bestows madness [upon all]," says someone. (Su.ra. 187)
The *vicakila* flower now attains a likeness with six-month-old pearls;
the *aśoka* tree is honored by petals redder than the scars left by the teeth of a Vāhlīka woman;
and this *kiṃśuka*, its tips brushed over by bees, begins to droop slightly from its stalk.
A certain script has indeed been inscribed by the crimson buds of the *pāṭali* tree;
[this is] by Rājaśekhara. (Viśvaguṇādarśabhanitīśataka 1.25; Subhāṣitaratnabhāṇḍāgāra 165)
I believe the fire has taken refuge within the *kiṃśuka* trees out of fear of the cold water;
for indeed, it makes the forest dark with its smoke known as buds—
otherwise, how could it serve to torment the wives of travelers?
Under the guise of flowers, it emits a dense, crimson streak from its crest—[the work] of someone [Pautāyani]. (Su.ra. 176)
Now, the bud of the *plakṣa* tree, skillful at parting its inner petals, unfolds like the beak of a parrot; ah,
it is indeed capable of rivaling the loveliness of women’s lips!
The sprout, clearly red with beauty, emerges from all sides. (1244) —
Vāmana.
Smeared with pollen that resembles finely ground vermilion, the *palāśa* trees— whose branches sway in the wind and whose songs are the humming of bees—
are clothed in garments as red as saffron.
These trees shine, bearing the delightful festival of honey-filled days;
[this is] of Vasantasena.
155. These cuckoos in the midst of the forest captivate the heart, their throat-sounds surpassing the dense resonance of the fresh mango buds.

By the mere glance of whose eyes, the sparks from the embers of the body of the god of love— made terrifying by the mass of flames from the fire of the eye of the Lord Bhūteśa— appear as if they were shining.
Of someone: (Su.ra. 171) With cries that are sweeter than anything, uttered from tasting the tips of mango sprouts shaken by the Malaya breeze at its first rising;
In various places, the cuckoo recites, as it were, a *sāmidhenī* verse to kindle the fire of Love for the sake of consuming the lives of travelers.
He who,

by merely accepting the shade [of Hari], brought about the state of being tearless in the five-arrowed god (Kāma), who otherwise causes a flow of nectar to his ears through devouring mango sprouts and kandalī shoots.
This very fifth [note], having pined away from wandering through the narrow caves of the palate’s lofty peaks, now uproots itself from the throat-cavity of the female cuckoo right to its very root.
By Bilhaṇa: (Vc.

7.76) He who is the elixir of the erotic sentiment for deer-eyed women, the fever of detachment and anxiety, the drum that expels the affliction of worldly peace, and the syllable of the instruction in truth from the Teacher of Desire; [he is Śiva].
Victorious is the fifth note of the cuckoo, which possesses the power to shatter consciousness in a wayfarer’s wife who is overwhelmed by the heavy fever of intense amorous longing.
For someone,
the *oṃkāra*s are a restatement of the mantras of the *upaniṣads* of the flower-armed god;
for the recitation of love, they are the fragrance-delighting Veda at the rite of rebirth.
The sound of the cuckoos— a nectar-sprinkling upon the mango groves— is a fever for the ears of travelers whose hearts are captivated by the unattainable woman.
Dhvani 156: Vasantabhramara [says]:
O you whose eyes are like the red and elongated flower-arrows, possessing the dark luster of smooth collyrium—

Upon the crest-ornament of the *karṇikāra* flower, as red as Kashmiri saffron, and amidst the blossoming *tilaka* mark, the swarm of bees belonging to the Goddess of Spring bears a beauty like that of a most charming woman, resembling moist dots of musk-paste upon her forehead. 1251.
1251. Of Umāpatidhara:
The tip of the mango bud was severed by the scissors-like beak of a cuckoo.

Now, the breeze, trembling as it stirs the flowing streams of milk and wine, and filled with the joy of the fragrance of blossoming spring flowers, sets the swarms of wandering bees humming, which spreads an inner longing within me. 1252.
Those who once found joy in the jasmine and the honey now find no delight in them, for their essence has been consumed and discarded.
Having been repelled by the lotuses in the forests whose pleasure remained unchanged,
the bees now direct their intense, passionate intent toward the fresh honey of the mango buds.
In the bud of the jasmine flower, the humming intoxicated bee shines like a nine-fold [jewel].
As if filling his conch shell at the departure of the Five-Arrowed One (Kāmadeva). (Sā.da. 4.9, Śā.pa. 3786) [Attributed to Kasyacit]
Thirsty female bees plunge into the forest’s edge— a river of nectar with sands of dense pollen— where the breasts of young female cuckoos serve as its bathing ghats.
In the beginning of the summer heat upon the earth, the breeze stirred by the wind serves to remove the torment of Āvantikajahu.
The sky bears a mass of dust shaped like a cloth-canopy;
the bees, their minds suspecting it to be a forest fire among the *mandāra* trees, do not suddenly approach the nectar of the Protector. (1256)
In Bhavabhūti’s *Uttararāmacarita* (200):
"The entire water of the ponds is agitated by herds of buffaloes."

The cakravāka bird enters the umbrella of lotus leaves; at every step, the female elephants, having repeatedly sprinkled their lordly elephant with water from their trunks due to great fatigue, lead him into the shade of the groves.
Rolling about on the edge of a certain leafy, muddy spot, the young elephant spends the heat of the day.
Thirsting, the buffalo stealthily searches for moss in the ponds;
the porcupine, fanning with breaths cool and fragrant from its habitual consumption of medicinal roots, settles within the belly of a forest mountain cave whose heat has been dissipated. 1258.
While the Lord of Yoga and the Ocean remained asleep even as the water-machines in their palaces were in motion, [the world was awakened].
The heat shatters the dense embrace of Śrī and Nārāyaṇa;
moreover, the rays of the sun—cruel as parched grain in a frying pan—torment the moon, whose beauty now remains only as a skeleton upon the scorching skull-plate of the sky. 1259.
By someone [possibly Nārāyaṇalacchi]:
A stone acts like a thunderbolt; the city street acts like heated iron.

In this intense heat of the fierce midday sun, where even a windless spot acts like a fire and gravel acts like dense glowing coals, the earth everywhere withers and the sands of the rivers act like sparks of fire.
1260 Bhavānanda’s [work], 158. The Summer Attire.
Their upper garments are moist with water, their play-bracelets are made of lotus stalks,
their head-ornaments are fashioned from *śirīṣa* flowers, their necklaces are composed of *vicakila* blossoms, and the bodies of these dark-eyed maidens are wet with sandalwood paste.

The ritual for conquering death through the delight of sexual union, performed without [the need for] Tantra or Mantra, belongs to someone [unknown]. (Viśvavidyābharaṇa 4.3, Surata-ratnākara 212, Rājaśekhara)
The braid, having emerged from the water, takes refuge upon a crest of *saptalā* flowers;
the *pāṭala* garland around her neck sprinkles coolness over her breasts;
and the delicate-tipped *śirīṣa* flower settles upon her ear.
He distributes his ascetic merit across the limbs of women, marking them here and there with the signs of his own self—thus [says] Madhuśīla (or Madhuraśīla). (Su.ra. 209)
Ear-ornaments of *śirīṣa* flowers possessing the playful charm of young female parrots, necklaces of fragrant jasmine with their inner threads intact,
and lotus stalks white as pearls with tips sprouting like shoots for the fashioning of bracelets— [these are the offerings].
At the onset of summer, fresh adornment delights amorous women. (1263) By someone.

The *śirīṣa* flower at their ears vying with fresh blades of *kuśa* grass, the *kuravaka* garland upon their bodies, the *pāṭala* wreath around their necks, and the blossoming [fragrance] moistened by thin, fresh water— [all these belong] to the beautiful women.
A certain attire, born from the transformation of the day,
shines forth upon Kamalāyudha.
Her breast-slope is immediately covered with *campaka* buds; *mallikā* flowers serve as a cross-strap, while *vairakila* blooms form her girdle.
Her bracelets are made of lotus fibers, her necklace of *kesara* filaments, her braid is adorned with *cāmpeya* and *pāṭala*, and her ear is graced by *śirīṣa*.
If this is merely a disguise among women, then who are the servants of the Bodiless One?
(1265) [Of someone.]
159. Summer, whose very essence is the erotic sentiment,
[is characterized by] breasts that bear slightly blossoming jasmine buds, belonging to those who have just bathed at that season and whose bodies are moist with sandalwood paste.
The embrace of gazelle-eyed women slowly causes the god of love to sprout anew, even though his power was withered by the heat of the summer sun.
By Maṅgalārjuna. (Su.ra. 192, Śā.pa.
3834) It was once nestled at the root of a water plant, momentarily acquainted with sandalwood paste, and had set its light foot upon necklaces of lotus stalks and the moon.
Having rested for a moment on the bank of the grove of fresh plantain trees,
coolness now finds its place in the embrace of my beloved’s neck.
Of someone: (Su.ra.
201) Upon this [mountain], she whose body is moist with thick sandalwood paste, her eyes reddened by sleep, repeatedly yawns under the guise of her soft, playful, and swaying vine-like arms;
At the close of day, the fawn-eyed women emerge slowly from their vine-cottages, their expansive breasts unevenly covered with drops of perspiration. (1268)
The flutes of Kalidasa’s Nandin steal the hearts of men, for they are cool to the ear; and the wine,
when mixed with cold water, is worthy of its price.
And the breasts of the fawn-eyed women become like snow,
for the heavy favor of the Lord of Love rests upon their pure surface.
By Rājaśekhara.

(Viśvaguṇādarśabhāṇa 4.4; Surathotsava 211) Upon the breasts of the long-lashed women, there hang clusters of *kadamba* flowers, dripping with abundant liquid nectar, which have been heated by the sun.
The breezes, their heat forcibly snatched away by the embrace of beloveds emerging from water-sports, bestow an indescribable majesty as they become cool.
For someone,
the forest fire climbs the tree, enters the chasm, and vies with the mountains.
He licks the sky, he writhes upon the surface of the earth, he hides within the interior of a thicket,
he wanders inside a hollow, he stops, and he clings to the creepers— what is there that the fire in the forest does not do when it has fallen under the power of the wind? (1271)
Of Yogeśvara (Sūktimuktāvalī 34.7, Vasundhara; Saṃketa-kalpadruma 1.82): The beasts and birds have been destroyed, and the deities of the land have been reduced to helplessness.

The quarters of the sky, scorched by the earth and veiled by smoke naturally sooty, have been rendered like anthills— the forest reduced to such a state by the extinguished forest fire after it has consumed those various great trees along with their flowers, shoots, and fruits.
In this [verse], it is of that very [type] where the *nīṣadha* is slightly interrupted and bent by the expansion of the *vitatta*.
Slightly gathered and then bent, then heaped up and rising,
the dark smoke of the forest fire— resembling the shoulder of a young buffalo—
creeping at its own will across the sky, creates fleeting leaf-patterns.
By Bāṇa. (Sūktimuktāvalī 1.85; Subhāṣitaratnabhāṇḍāgāra 1174. Both anonymous.
O young girl, this high mountain range of clouds that pervades the sky is not [merely] a garland of clouds.

Why do you vainly soil your face with streams of tears falling from the corners of your eyes? This is a column of smoke rising from a forest fire— resembling the stones of the Vindhya mountains crushed by the trampling of a rutting elephant in rut— that darkens the entire circle of the quarters.
By someone [Dhārākadamba] (Sūktimuktāvalī 2.203;
Śārṅgadharapaddhati 3829): The quarters of space possess the sky of the rising twilight as their crimson blossoms.

As the fire blazes upon the mountains, it causes the bamboo thickets to burst into flame— thickets where the trees are entwined with *kiṃśuka* creepers blooming in dense clusters, their peaks embraced by fluttering saffron-colored banners.
The commencement of the rainy season for someone in the year 1275 [of the Śaka era].
The female crow, languid from pregnancy, desires to remain in her nest for the entire day;
the bee, having tasted the bitter sap of the *nīpa* creepers, abandons the crimson *pāṭala* flower;
and now the peacocks withdraw their brilliance, their work of burning [the forest] having come to an end.
The cuckoo slowly approached a rose-apple tree from a mango grove, its fruit near ripeness;
[this is] by Abhinanda.
At the onset of the rainy season, on the mountain slopes where the ground has become firm earth, the new grasses— like a mass of bristling hair—
manifest through the hundreds of blossoming buds of the *kuṭaja* trees,
while the waters of the cascades flow down toward the beloved.
Through the perspiration from its drainage channels, it manifests an indescribable softness;
[this is] of Narasiṃha.
The trees, thickened by droplets of water mixed with dust raised by the wind, have spread out their bark-like leaves like umbrellas; now the sprouts of young grass emerge from the ground,
while the clouds are gazed upon by the swiveling necks of peacocks, dark and glossy.
The eager peacocks cause the faces of the quarters to resound with their cries, as if for the sake of the lotus. 1278 1278 [For] the lotus.
With their dust slightly settled, gazed upon with joy by flocks of peacocks,
and shattered by the sighs of housewives whose dwellings have been destroyed and whose young *haridrā* plants have withered,
these drops from the fresh clouds fall now that the onset of the rainy season has begun.
These drops [of rain] have rendered the moon-like faces of women separated from their lovers lusterless; [this is the work] of someone [named Bindu]. (Śārṅgadharapaddhati 3872)
Terrified by the thundering of the massed clouds rising at the onset of the rains,

the summer season has retreated; in some places even the objects left behind are covered in dust, while in the *ketakī* buds there is pollen, and in the hearts of those separated from their lovers, there is a forest fire.
The circle of stars in the flickering of fireflies, and the reddish light in streaks of lightning—
[these belong] to someone.

162. During the rains, the cranes— eager to swallow the rows of young grass with the greediness of newly arrived locusts— plunge at their will along the riverbanks, near the mountain slopes, close to the nesting grounds of herds of female buffaloes.
In a certain corner of the field, the pigeon somehow swallows grains of *kodrava* while warding off the danger posed by scarecrows made of grass and reeds placed within.
While this cloud— the lord of yoga—
intensifies its state of stillness with the low, rumbling sounds of its thunder, which are worn out by intoxication, it brings about an unsteady stupor in the mind.
Resting the quarters of the sky upon his lap and making them resound with the roars of the rain-clouds,
I believe even the sky— its eyes of moon and sun closed— is now falling asleep.
For one of windy temperament: (Su.Ra.
229) Songs that move forth, marked by the victories of the God of Love, with the sweet warbling of intoxicated cranes breaking forth clearly.
Moreover, the peacock, longing for the thundering of the clouds, dances with its tail-feathers spread wide like a parasol and its plumage raised high.
The entire circle of the sky was pervaded by clouds that had risen unexpectedly;
neither the cool-rayed moon nor the Lord of Light appeared within the range of his vision.
What further purpose can now be served by these broken and soiled things, since the hailstones fall so thickly and these clouds discharge flashes of lightning?
The fragrance-laden Bakula trees and Kadamba buds of the wind-swept grove seem to have their hair standing on end with joy;
they are densely covered by masses of clouds as if clad in a dark blue upper garment.

Having driven their enemies far away as if they were anklets, the quarters of the sky, like longing women going to meet their lovers at the arrival of the clouds, have departed somewhere while uttering the cries of swans.
Once, during the rainy season, while the enemy of the Daityas— the sovereign of the three worlds— was sleeping upon the couch of the lord of serpents, a cloud appeared.

Having reached the rainy season, which is like a night of darkness, the thundering clouds— stationed at every quarter and clearing the walls of the directions on all sides with the lamp-like flashes of lightning— remain awake like sentries bearing bows.
1286 Oṃ! Having forcibly diminished the nights of Kaṇṭha and having violently carried away the waters of the rivers—
Having scorched the earth and utterly destroyed the dense thickets of forest trees,
the clouds wander in every direction with the light of lightning-lamps, as if intent on searching for where the hot-rayed sun has now gone.
Oṃ to Kaṇṭha. (Su.ra. 251; Kasyacit; Śā.pa. 3869; Sū.mu. 61.18—all attributed to Pāṇini).
Having drunk water at will to his heart's content due to the power of destiny...

Despondent from excessive distress, with his body clinging to the rocky mountain peaks, his girdle entwined by flashes of lightning, the cloud vomits forth its burden of water under the guise of thundering, as if repeatedly belching it out. 1288.
The moon reflected in water pervades the sky, the quarters, and the peaks of mountains.
Roaring through nights dense with thick darkness, like a cloud with the lightning-flash as its lofty lamp during the rains, who here remains alive among those separated from their lovers? 1289.
To this fool who considers himself omniscient, the moon seems nowhere to exist, and the sun is as if gone abroad.
The wheel of planets and constellations in the sky is as if being drawn and erased;
day or night—both are obscured from discernment by dense, massed clouds. What is this? Such is the terrible resolve [of fate]. (1290)
Of someone: (Su.ra. 262) 164. A river in the rainy season.

Today, the banks of the water are resonant with the cries of water-fowls, where cobras sleep upon the tips of reeds, where flocks of geese call out, and where herds of deer have formed their haunts; the waters are rising, and the greedy ants are swarming toward them in great throngs.
Pervaded by intoxicated peacocks, they cause the restless mind of the Lord of Yoga to yearn for the rivers.
(Su.ra. 221) / 1291) Yogeśvara.
These rivers of the coastal marshlands, with their muddy banks overgrown with stalks of *nalada* grass, where conchs resound and shoals of crabs sport, and whose waters are turbid with tangled reeds,
produce longing in the heart— especially those with frogs leaping from their upturned mouths.
The riverbanks have their edges pitted with mud-blisters that are scattered and then disgorged; these belong to the Supreme Lord. (Su.ra. 254)
Devoid of dust, fragrant with the scent of blooming *sarja* flowers, their ridges resounded with the cries of peacocks dancing in intoxication,
they stole away the very perception of the forest regions with their surging currents.
On the slope of the mountain, the rivers create a sound with their gurgling waters for the sake of the Kāpālika.

Now, at every riverbank, the regions where fresh *nicula* thickets are blossoming everywhere long for a swift breaking of the exhaustion caused by the excessive length of the summer heat, which was like the constricted throat of a tortoise.
Of Hari, whose friend is the dātyūha bird vocal with the joy of playfully spreading its wings. ||1294||1294|| Of Hari.
Here, with their interiors filled by the heavy burden of water,
possessing a many-fold and terrifying speed as they whirl through ravines and caves, the river channels clash against the slopes and ridges of the banks.
The rivers of Tripurāri [are] terrifying with twice-great roar.
165. We surely pay homage to those days of the rainy season, which pour forth nectar, as they spread across the sky clouds that serve as masters of the peacocks' dance.
In those [ladies] with eyes like fresh blue lotuses, the knots of the stubborn obsession of pride— which are deeply rooted and cause extreme exhaustion— break apart of their own accord.
In some places,
the regions of the horizon were within arm's reach, the sky was contracted by the mass of dense clouds, and the surface of the earth was strewn with falling torrents of water.
How indeed have these days been endured with wonder by the wives of travelers— days made cruel by the roar of unrestrained thunder, while their bellies were covered by masses of fresh clouds?
For someone,
these days are heavy with separation; the oceans surge with mist,
the sky is blue as clouds dark as the Vindhya mountains, and the air is fragrant with the scent of *nīpa* and *arjuna* trees.
Even the crow, seeing his mate exhausted by her approaching delivery and seeking a nest,
becomes agitated as he busies himself gathering bits of straw with the tip of his beak— such are those [trees].
These dappled rays of Rantideva’s ascetic heat, now arising here and there with fragments of clouds, manifest the hospitality of darbha grass mingling with ketaki petals.

O friend, these days are delightful: the minds of people rejoice at the contact with rice seedlings and young barley sprouting on the outskirts of the villages, and the quarters of the sky are filled with the long-drawn songs of cattle-drivers. (1300)
For someone,
it was the night of the rainy season, when the sky was overspread with clouds and a gentle breeze blew at the end of the downpour.
How were those nights passed by those away from home—nights during which the quarters of the sky were momentarily illuminated by flashes of lightning, while the moon, stars, and planets lay dormant;
nights when the air bore the fragrance of nectar-like Kadamba blossoms drenched by rain, and where the croaking of frogs spread far and wide, uninterrupted by the passage of travelers? (1301)
By someone [else] (Su.ra. 220; by Yogeśvara):
The masses of darkness are streaked with fireflies, and vivid lightning flashes clearly.
With the swelling roar of great clouds made manifest by their resonant sounds, with their conchs blaring,
and with the eastern winds scented by the opening of *ketaka* flowers,
these nights— raining down hailstones— I cannot believe that they will be endured by people separated from their lovers. 1302
Of someone: (Su.ra. 228) With droplets of spray scattered by winds blowing in all directions, and with far-flashing lightning bolts...

With the air anointed by the fragrance of ketaka blossoms that have just opened, with the quarters resounding with the cries of gallinules, and accompanied by the deep, heavy thundering of clouds, these nights agitate the hearts of those dear to travelers. (1303)
For someone,
the burden of the croaking of frogs was [drowned] by the sounds of clouds heavy with water.

How do these rainy nights pass— terrible as they seize the life-force of young women separated from their beloveds, streaked with lightning amidst masses of darkness, raising roars of profound depth, and possessing the power to uproot all stability? (1304)
[The clouds] of Mādhava,
filled with continuous masses of darkness made most terrifying by the piercing flashes of lightning...

The nights— whose skies are crowded with dark clouds that have obscured the luminaries, whose nearby trees are illuminated by fireflies, and which resound with the chirping of swarms of insects intoxicated by the rainwater— exude a profound depth.
By someone; (Su.ra.
252) the beginning of autumn.

In some places the sky is bright with clouds; in some places there are groves of blooming kāśa grass; in some places the ground at the edge of the fields is matted with lotuses whose tips have emerged from the water;
and furthermore, in yet another place, there are the moist impressions left by the beautiful footsteps of cakora birds.
The charming fragments of sandbanks, released by the river, are seen;
Behold, having spent the night elsewhere, he now arrives at dawn and gently soothes this lotus plant, whose limbs are distressed by separation.
O slender-limbed one, by falling at his feet, the thousand-rayed sun [was propitiated]—
[this was said] by someone.
With smoke-grey wings and pale bellies, the wagtails flying about on all sides scatter the approaching autumn like women joyfully scattering parched grain;
and the night, with a smiling face, bears the auspicious crescent-moon as its bud-like lip.
He places the moon-jar, white as a mirror of moonlight, within the courtyard of the sky—[this is] by someone [unnamed]. (Su.ra. 269)

Those sprouts of the tusks of young female elephants, which now rival the tips of the tusks of non-tough female elephants, and by swallowing which among flocks of swans a certain gurgling sound is produced from the friction against their rasping throats— those very sprouts [are now being consumed].
The knots of the sprouts of lotus-roots have emerged from the beds of lotuses.
(Kamalāyudha; *Sūktimuktāvalī* 284; *Dhvanyāloka* 4.7)
The swans have departed; instantly, the impurity of the waters has vanished; the moon is clear; the rays of the sun have spread forth with increased vigor;
the quarters of the sky have expanded, and the vast firmament has become the color of a sword.
That bull among sages, renowned as the master of yoga, has arisen as the controller of the Vindhya mountain.
168. O moon-faced one, although I possess the splendor of the stainless autumnal sky and the beauty of fresh sprouts in the form of lips with the luster of bandhūka flowers;
"Fie on me!"— thus, as if because her full breasts have withered away, this autumn bears a great heat.
From *Manovinoda* (Su.ra.
267): Now, eager for the pleasure of devouring grains of rice, the boars have been driven by their owners toward the boundary to drive away [other animals].
The trees have their branches occupied by pigeons who have built dense nests for the sake of their young;
the anthills have their interiors dug up by the sharp claws of jackals.
By Śatānanda (Su.ra. 285):
The sun burns fiercely like a low-born man recently enriched;
the ruru deer sheds its antler like an ungrateful friend.
The water becomes clear, like the contemplation of Dharma in a sage;
the mud, like a poor man driven by desire, goes to its drying up.
Of Bhāsa: (Su.ra. 276, Sv 1821, Śā.pa. 3907, Sū.mu. 62.3) Now the moon bears the luster of the honey-like faces of beloved women;
the rows of sporting *khañjana* birds spread the beauty of the eyes of those with deer-like glances.
The lotuses rival the fragrance of the breath of those fair-browed women, and the female royal swans practice the gait of those with full breasts. (1314)
The *kāśa* reeds, resembling Indra and bearing white blossoms, serve as garments for the rivers; appearing like *kāśa* flowers, they shine upon the new sandbanks like the swans of the river Śrī.
Resembling a swan, joined with the rising sun, pure and sharp as autumn, the moon of the earth,

Yet we are truly unable to praise each of his individual virtues; therefore, O King, for the great festival of those who hear of them all, we praise You alone. (1387)
These [verses] of Chittipa are born of the lineage of the autumnal moonlight; they are siblings of the Ocean of Milk.

By whom here have your virtues not been placed upon the ear— virtues that are friends to the serpent Śeṣa, that radiate the splendor of rows of blossoming night-lotuses like the cool-rayed moon, that were companions in childhood dust-play with him, that are kin to the celestial river Gaṅgā, and that are brothers to the snowy mountain Himālaya? 1388.
1388 While the quality of the god Hari, whose splendor is like the laughter of the destroyer of Tripura, is being extolled...
Drawn by affection and by a curiosity to hear,
the Lord of Serpents himself assumes one thousand eyes with eyelashes bent; yet another set of a thousand eyes is excessively dilated due to the rolling of their sluggish pupils.
If for someone Mount Meru were the staff and the circle of the earth were the cloth-covering, [he would still not be satisfied].

O Daughter of the Earth, only when this Vindhya mountain becomes as level as a measuring cord, and when its mother, the Triple-City Conqueror, or Keśava himself should appear, could the multitude of your virtues be measured. (1390)
1390 [In the year] of Pravarasena 5: Dharma.

O Lord, if you were not a lame and crippled man in the Kali age at Utkala, then how could the world have been deluded— by four feet in the Age of Truth (Kṛta), by three steps in Tretā, and somehow by two in Dvāpara?
How can this Dharma, being like a lame man standing on a single foot, wander about? (Su.ra. 1455, by Cittūka)
In the Kali age, the very lineage of the Bull’s feet having been destroyed, you have fashioned it anew and once again set the wheel of his station in motion;
this was indeed proclaimed by those who, guided by your weapons, shattered the sun.
Having heard this, O Lord, Anūru will abandon Mihira and serve you.
(1392) [By Ācārya Gopīka]
When the earth had been made firm by him through four well-performed steps, why did he resort to asceticism,
touching the ground with only the tip of his big toe?
Even Adharma, emaciated, assumed the state of an ascetic.
(Śrīharṣa)

While he, devoted to righteousness, was ruling the earth which was filled with the heat of asceticism, the sacrificial altars— with their rising columns of smoke produced by the sacrifices— were like trees with uprooted thorns, or like blinding medicinal herbs that caused pain in both his feet and his eyes.
Let alone attacking him, Kali was clearly unable even to look at him. (1394)
— Jayadeva’s.
By his very nature, he moved upon the earth swiftly, leaning upon rows of sacrificial stakes that had been offered without weariness.
Even a single word of the Dharma [is precious] according to the sequence of time;
this is by Umāpatidhara.
O Śrīmadrūpaviṭaṅkadeva, crest-jewel of all sovereigns,
it is fitting that your presence should wander here even at night, like the moon.
Let not the moon become embarrassed and abashed by the sight of your face;
let not this venerable Arundhatī become a vessel for ill-repute.

As the Creator fashioned the very body of the Goddess of the Three Worlds, with her face like the moon, the entire treasury of his luster was exhausted; yet, even in the creation of the unfathomable universe, he did not become diminished.

Was his remaining body, consisting only of hair, fashioned from masses of blinding darkness because it was so difficult to perceive due to the total disappearance of the entire orb of his radiance? (1397)
O Śrīharṣa, this face of yours possesses the lovely luster of the full moon;
your eye is indistinguishable from a blue lotus; and your lip is as red as the bandhujīva flower.
O Lord, tell me, how could the deer-eyed women not meditate upon your creeper-like brow, which is the vine of Cupid’s bow and a fellow student of graceful play?

Was she not overtaken by wind? No, no. Was she not afflicted by the great elements? No, no. Was she not exhausted? No, no. Was she not vomited forth by the waves of a derangement of the humors (sannipāta)? No, no.
Why is it that, upon seeing Śrī Bhojadeva—his unprovoked enemy—she faints, weeps, sighs, and yet wears a smiling face? How could this be?
O King of men, that the deer-eyed women drink in the essence of your form with the cupped hands of their eyes, exceeding all measure—this is the very essence of your mind's vision. (Su.ra. 749)
Then, under the guise of perspiration, they seem to vomit forth colors resembling *kadamba* flowers, wandering about as they are shattered by the arrows of the Bodiless One.
O Lord of Beings, this gaze of Śaṅkaradeva produces [this] vision.
Your splendor, as delightful as a fresh blue lotus,
brings prosperity to those who seek you as friends and misfortune— the bodiless god of love— to your enemies and to women. 1401.
Forcefully uprooting knowledge from its very roots upon the mountains of the Pratyak-khala (the wicked who turn inward).

O fortunate one, your glances are like trees of nectar to the circle of friends, radiant as rows of flaming fire to the forest of the mature armies of your enemies, and are the sole elixir of the sentiment of love. (1402)
O best of kings, wherever the lotus-pale [complexion] of Mādhava [is seen],...
As your eye moves here and there as you look with favor, Kamalā, who dwells within the lotus forest, indeed runs after it in her desire for it. ||1403||
Of someone: (Su.ra.
1450) Those whose only wealth is their loincloth are indeed the ones who eat the supreme *dhātrī* fruit.

At their gates, throngs of horses neigh; by them alone has the earth been won, and by them this very family has been adorned—what more need we say of those who have been beheld by you, the Supreme Lord, whether you be pleased or enraged? (1404)
Jayāditya’s [verse]: (Su.ra. 1410, Śā.pa.
1224) At their gate stood lordly elephants, the subduers of those [elephants], who themselves were the sustainers of the universe.

The palaces of those houses, with their jeweled steps shimmering like scales, dance as they are adorned by golden parasols that color the quarters of the sky; such prosperity attends those whom you favor with the grace of a glance out of affection. (1405)

8. Arm.

"O sir, who are you? Are you one of Vālmīki’s disciples, or perhaps of Vyāsa, that you have undertaken this praiseworthy effort to praise the pillar-like arm of the Bhoja king? You are like a cripple wishing to climb a mountain, or one seeking to touch the moon with his hand."
If you wish to cross the ocean with your two arms, what answer can we give to this? (1406) —
by Chittapa.
The mountains rise exceedingly high on all sides, and the oceans are vast;
yet you, bearing even these, are not at all weary—homage to you!
As I repeatedly offer this praise in wonder, O Earth, Please provide the text you would like me to translate. I am ready to assist you with your request.
"Only so long as your arm was remembered while wielding this [sword], were my words sealed.
(1407) By him alone. (Kp 118, Kuval 183, sū.mu. 97.10)
O King, it is false that the tree of paradise (kalpadruma), possessing limited power, vies with your arm;

In this regard, you yourself are the tree of paradise to be meditated upon, since even when the world was a single ocean, this [sword] remained.
At the end of the eon, Hari, having withdrawn the entire universe into himself, sleeps in the shadows. (Sāṅkhyakārikā 3.101)

The Lord of Mountains was lifted up by the ten-headed Rāvaṇa; Arjuna Kārtavīrya bound him in prison; and the sage Paraśurāma cut down his forest-like arms—a tale whose thorns of doubt regarding the nature of his prowess have thus been tied into knots.
The arm of that monk was like a magnet-stone pillar for attracting the realization of the three worlds.
With hands that trample upon skulls and the severed heads of elephants, adorned with the intestines of hungry ghosts as crowns,

and with beloved women standing at their sides whose words falter with intoxication— even as they cry out "O Yama, ward off the mace!"— your broad right hand, which effortlessly repels the maces of Yama, is praised.
His arm was [the guest of honor] at the drinking parties for blood, hosted by *vetālas* at every battle.
Possessing the beauty of the tender calyx of an upright red lotus,
his forearms bristling with thrill from grasping the hair of his beloved, he was the refuge for the circle of friends, the twice-born, enemies, and courtesans.
Your hand [is the cause] of honor, gifts, fear, and enjoyment; such is the hand of knowledge. (Sū.mu. 97.50)
By whom has this hand of his not been raised— this hand that scatters heaps of pearls from the hollows of the frontal globes of enemy elephants shattered by his sword,
and which, amidst the battle of the fourfold army, is stained by the hooves of galloping horses?
As if scattering a multitude of seeds for the earth-born [plants] upon the trampled lands, [he established his fame].
(Śrīharṣa) (Nc 12.66)

O ornament of the earth, our hands— intent on upholding the Vedas and purified by the water of charity— have praised only your hand, the lord of the spreading pearls from the surface of our crowns trembling with smiles; yet, forgive us, for what indeed is not perceived by poets?
That fish was seen even more clearly, hidden in your hand as well—
[this was said] by the teacher Gopīka.

For those whose virtuous conduct is devoted to uplifting the wretched, even that tree of paradise is but a trifle; the wish-fulfilling gem does not even enter their thoughts; and fragrant with the fulfillment of desires, it is no longer a source of longing for them—once they have gained even a slight degree of favor.
O Lord of the Earth, O you whose beautiful fame is well-guarded, this right hand of yours [is victorious].
(Jayadeva)
O King, may your sprout-like hand be victorious— its power surpassing that of the Kalpavṛkṣa through its tireless play of bestowing gifts, radiant with the blossoms of fame,
and from which the waters of rutting elephants flow under the guise of the water poured during acts of charity.
The lines of letters of wretchedness were inscribed upon the foreheads of the wise by the very streams [of his tears].
(1415) Of him alone.
Victorious for all time are the dust-particles of your lotus-feet, which are like a powder for subjugating the Goddess of Fortune.
Those ill-fated syllables inscribed by fate upon the foreheads of men, which are erased by the marks formed by prostration. ||1416||

Of Abhinanda: (Sahityakaumudī 5.467; Subhāṣitaratnabhāṇḍāgāra 1391) [The dust of the lotuses that are the abodes of Lakṣmī are like the sands of the river of moonlight formed by the rays from the jewels in the crowns of kings who bow down in service.]

May the dust of your feet— which, at dawn, trample the multitude of trembling pillars that are the hollow bellies of the wood of poverty belonging to King Karṇa, the very embodiment of the Kali age— be victorious!
By Vallana: (Su.ra.
1416) Having created an exceedingly wonderful confluence of the celestial river and the Yamunā by means of the luster of his own crest-jewel sapphire upon the radiance of the Lord’s toe-nails;
O Venerable One, what king indeed did not leap forward, performing as it were an expiation for the immersion of his accumulated evil deeds through the worship of your feet?

O Lord, who indeed— desiring the protection of prosperity and longing for refuge— would not go for shelter to Your feet, which are as beautiful as the very abode of the playful grace of Fortune? They belong to one who is praised by all.
Having properly followed you into the shade, your enemies now wander the earth— though it is pervaded by the heat of the sun that is your valor— without their parasols, having been rendered fearless.

From the eastern mountain whose peaks are moistened by the ichor of Indra’s elephant up to the western ocean whose waters are drunk from the navel of Varuṇa’s excellent bride— this [is the land] of Jayadeva.
From Mount Meru to the Bridge [of Rāma], those kingless monarchs, whose garlands of flowers were falling from their heads as they touched the surface of the earth, worshipped his feet.
O ocean of benevolence, beloved of the wise, wall of virtues, and tree of dharma— this is the pleasant account of Vasukalpa.

O Lord Muñja, you who are affectionate toward those seeking advancement, a great renouncer, a refuge of discernment, an abode of Fortune, a master of the initiation into the workings of the God of Love— why do you not deign to touch this person? (1421)
Of Bhojadeva:
(Sūktimuktāvalī 1.86) "The crest-jewel of women, the beautiful essence of all stories, the lovely root-stalk for the sprout of kindness..."

O you who are the mantra for captivating the mind, the friend of the god of love, the beloved of the surging waves of speech, the sole abode of good fortune, the repository of tender words, the ocean of fortitude, and the tree upon the mountain of Dharma—O Poet Rājaśekhara, we have seen you; now we must depart. 1422
Of Abhinanda. (Su.ra.
1714) Sprouted in the act of resolve, it then has two leaves at the time of departure.

O brother, as I entered the city, the tree of my desires sprouted on the road; it rose up with a hundred branches when you were about to appear; it budded when you were seen; but now that you, the Lord, have been beheld, it has today blossomed and borne fruit.
Of Chittapa: (Su.ra. 1435) The world appears as two moons, the sky as three abodes, and the universe as four deities.

O best of kings, while you shine forth, this world possesses the five traditional lineages, the sixfold collection of sacred speech, the six-arrowed god of love, the year with its seven divisions, the circle of the earth vast as the eight oceans, and the wheel of the directions with its nine leaders. ||1424||
O mobile abode of the serpent of Lakṣmī’s amorous play, O wish-fulfilling tree of one’s intentions! 1424.

O you who associate with those who accomplish the highest good, O son of Gaṅgā whose limbs are adorned with the arts of battle, O lover of the Vaṅgas, O ornament of the assembly of kings who are rivals to the lords of Gauḍa, O protector of the earth against hostile monarchs, O protector of the virtuous—you have been seen; we are satisfied. 1425.
Jayadeva’s 12. Hyperbole (atyukti)
Wear the immeasurable lotus upon your head; display your own prowess; bear the wheel-marked lotus-foot; lift up the earth with your arm;
place Lakṣmī near your brow; and become superior even to the Lord of the Gods.
O sole thief of the inner hearts of all beings, even so, you are indeed known as Hari. (Cittapa; Sūktimuktāvalī 97.6)
On this sandy bank of the Sarayū, white as lilies in the firm moonlight,
a game of dice was played for a long time by two perfected youths;
one says that Kaiṭabha was slain first, while the other says it was Kaṃsa.
Therefore, tell me the truth: who was killed there by you previously?
Of that very [person]...
In your hand [hold] the wish-fulfilling tree, in your mouth the moon, in your arms the one named Ananta;
in anger, indeed, that Kālakūṭa poison, and in satisfaction the beloved of Hari;
in vigor, invoke by name this submarine fire, breaking open its bounds.
O Ocean, O Lord of the Forest, this sound of yours is but the exertion of one who has assumed a disguise out of magnanimity.

O Lord of the Earth, today as I lay awake, this thought occurred to me: "The ten incarnations of Hari have been described and celebrated; why are you not mentioned there as the eleventh? Even though I know that your life story is beyond the reach of poets' words..."
I do not compose this out of fear; for who else would speak such things as the poet Bhārata? (1429) — by Ācārya Gopīka.
Conquer all with prosperity, uplift the world, and let your foot— disguised as a nail but bearing the crescent moon— be placed upon it;
fix your gaze clearly in your heart, become the support of the bull, abandon the double-tongued serpent,
and, filled with wrath and devoid of attachment to Durgā, burn down the hundreds of cities of your enemies.
Nevertheless, O Lord of the Earth, you are known as the Lord of Bhavānī because of your noble deeds.
Vasantadeva’s.
13. How is it that virtuous men are thrilled with horripilation [at your praise], if the earth has been made free of thorns?
And if your virtues are renowned, why then does the common folk still proclaim your faults?
O King, if you are the foremost leader in policy, why is it that the conduct of your subjects is contrary to policy?
This is indeed not surprising; for if it were not surprising, how could you have ordained such a thing?
O Lord of the Earth, when Samantabhadra abandoned his forbearance toward you in battle, even those renowned for their strength became intolerant toward the enemies;
yet as their bodies trembled, you too were overwhelmed with trembling.
You take tribute from the earth, and these [kings] as well from the heavens;
yet what is it that you, who are superior even to them, are praised for by those possessed of virtues?
It is a marvel that Dhoyīka alone dwells eternally in three ways within the hearts of his enemies, the learned, and the deer-eyed women alike.
Spreading heat, the essence of joy, and delight through the fervor of his heroism, his discipline, and his grace; 1433,
[By someone] (Su.ra. 1438, Śrī Hanūmat):
You walk two or three steps; your enemies leap over the earth as they flee. You discharge five or ten arrows; they discharge many weapons.
"Those lords of goddesses have been slain by you, yet you are the husband of human women;
you are censurable—how can there be praise for you? Let this be decided, O illustrious Karṇa.
Of the Lord of Knowledge:
(Sv 2516) The ear is situated at the head of all; what in the three worlds has not been heard by the ear?
It is not surprising that even the glances of fawn-eyed women come to rest upon the ear somewhere or other.
But even more wonderful is this: that this circle of the world, though itself a flawless orb of excellence, supports the earth girt by the seven oceans.
O you who possess pride in your own deeds,
you are vast in virtues; by your fame, you are Rāma, Nala, and Bhārata.
"O Śatrughna, you are always Yudhiṣṭhira in great battle"— bearing such a likeness to ancient sovereigns through your noble deeds,
O King, how could you not be Māndhātṛ, even though you are the ordainer of the three worlds? (1436)
Of Vīryamitra: (Sv 2502, Su.Ra.
1417) "O Lord, if you are the moon, the treasury of arts, then we are the oceans."
If you, the Lord of Waters, are a treasure-house of boundaries, then we are the clouds;
if you, O rain-cloud, are the fulfiller of all hopes, then we are the trees; and if you are renowned for standing upon the path of the righteous, then we are the travelers on that path. (1437)
By someone: (Su.ra. 1392) "If one's desires are to be obtained at the confluence of the Yamunā and the Bhāgīrathī..."
O Lord, your own servant desires only to be maintained by you;
indeed, is this not better than death? For death is merely the departure of the mind from the body.
Live long, O Mind! Our body here is but yours alone at your lotus feet. (1438)
For one whose mind is focused on the Lord, He is to be served like the wish-fulfilling gem, the celestial tree, or the Rohaṇa mountain among mountains. (Sa. Ka. Ā. 2.356)

When you have aroused his anger, O hero whose valor is proven by every great gift, your husband alone becomes devoid of consciousness and does not abandon his hardness; another bears the pain of being cut, while yet another is the lord of the Kinnaras—whom else could you possibly entreat? (1439)
O Lord, you are delighted by the words of the Vedas for Śaraṇa, but for me, O Protector, there is only the discourse of boundless world-weariness.
"You are full of intent regarding the arts, yet my livelihood is deficient in them day by day; you alone are my goal through the purity of my devotion, yet for me, some inexplicable absence triumphs.
Thus, O Kaurava, how can you, who are a garden of play for virtues, be worshipped by me, a treasury of defects, through any means? (1440)
1440 Of that very [mind],
15. the basis of place.
What kings born of the lineages of the Moon and the Sun have not been won over? Yet,
we consider you alone to be the true lord of the earth— O noble one,
by whom the body was massaged, the hair drawn back, and the long [garment] cast aside.
Having reached Cola and Madhyadeśa, the hand [of authority] was soon brought down upon Kāñcī through learning.
Of learning.
O you who have effortlessly conquered the form of Kāma, having suddenly thrown the Kuntalas into turmoil and swiftly accomplished the destruction of the Colas as well as the subjugation of Aṅga,
you have indeed conquered the Madhyadeśa and, before long, laid your hand upon Kāñcī.
Thus, having brought [all] under his control through you, his beloved lord, the earth is enjoyed by you, O Abhīka.
(From the *Śabdārṇava*)

"O King, you indeed take delight in seizing her hair; casting aside her girdle, you have withdrawn your hands from her grasp, yet the striking upon your limbs has already begun"—when the bard, perceiving your inner intent, had spoken these words of praise, [the queen said: "Enough! [and she struck him].
The young women feel bashful upon looking at one another, while the enemies tremble with fear; [this is] by someone [namely, Śrīharṣa] (Su.ra. 1430).
By a mere knitting of his brows, he conquers and utterly defeats the Goddess of Gauḍa; by a mere sport, he subdues the Kaliṅgas.
O King of the Cedis, he scorches and consumes the wicked like the sun, and he brings about the destruction and subduing of the Mlecchas according to his will, as well as the pride of Kāmarūpa.
He who steals away the splendor of the Lord of Kāśī and sports upon the head of the King of Magadha—
[salutation] to Śaraṇadeva.
You display the playful tossing of the Colas' waves; you perform the drawing of their locks of hair;
you are capable of bending their girdles; and with impetuosity, you effect the contact of your limbs [with theirs].
Thus, O Indra among kings, today [the ocean], its long [surges] filled with trembling at the praises of the bards, [is agitated].
Even the hearts of women who are enemies are moved toward the worship of your feet.
(Jayadeva)
In how many instances was generosity not practiced? Who were not honored with the power of speech?
And among the wise, was there no one who, out of love for virtue, gave even a blade of grass?
Here, like an unseasonal rain-cloud, he shattered the mass of the flames of supreme suffering with pillars of streams of golden water.
A full water-pot at the forefront, a graceful woman with a smiling face,
an elephant with temples moistened by the flow of rut-fluid, a white-complexioned cow, and a bull.
O ornament of kings, as you depart, the crow on the *kṣīrī* tree utters sweet words, and the female jackal cries "Śivā"— surely these portents appear for the sake of those who seek you.
Of the Supreme Lord. (Su.ra.

14.49) A vast, difficult path strewn with hundreds of thorns in the form of adversaries has been traversed; a forest of rocks and mountains, crowded with tens of millions of cruel beasts of prey, has been crossed.
The river at the edge of your camp has arrived; the handful of water for the funeral libation has been offered to Poverty.
O King, who are mute with the syllable "No," you are wicked, but we are satisfied.

The residence of the king is in golden palaces; his friendship is with the immortals; his sport is in the groves of wish-fulfilling trees together with hosts of celestial nymphs; and nectar is joyfully drunk until the throat is full.
"O Lord, this was done by you when you were angry; I know that you are pleased with your servants after slaying your enemies in battle, but tell me further, O King of Gauḍa, what will you give?
For you, the Lord of the Yoga of Dharma, Lakṣmī— the one whose nature is drawn by her friendship with the smiling lotus— is present in your eyes, in your face, in your hand, and even in your feet.
That she has been brought to her true nature by supplicants through the glances of your eyes, through your instructions,
through the movements of your hands, and also through the grace of your feet— [this is the wonder].
17. The Sustenance of the Poor:
In whose houses the harsh sound of conchs, bowls, and moving pestles is difficult to hear;

O Lord of Men, whereas previously there was nothing, now, by your grace, the sound of lutes played by those sweet-voiced women is heard— rich with the resonance of the sequence of notes beginning with *ṣaḍja*, as their hands move over the frets and their rows of bracelets jingle upon their trembling fingers.
Of Bhāsoka. (Su.ra. 1394; of a certain [author]):
The dwellings of destitute Vedic scholars are filled with heaps of cotton seeds.
By your grace, now those very mansions whose courtyards and small inner chambers were once filled with gusts of wind have such that, in their surrounding grounds,
the pearls from the necklaces of young women— snapped during playful battles— fall to the earth. (1452)
Of Śubhaṅka (Su.ra.
1390): The young palm trees with their thick, glossy leaves stand in the courtyard of the house.

From their subtle [ears], they send you this message for a long life: "O you who are gracious, those merciless lovers of destitute Vedic scholars, adorned with golden shimmering earrings, do not remove the tender leaf from your ears. (1453)
The Lord of Umā,
the sky-clad one, has no garments; his half-body is the very garment of his own mistress.
The hundreds of beauties of the fair-browed women, whose bodily splendor was enhanced by jeweled ornaments,

and the opulent cities of the citizens— none of these could rival the glory of the one who dwells in the cremation ground and subsists on alms; for the lineage of Sena is ignorant of the burden of poverty.
1454. Umāpatidhara’s pearls [were made] from cotton seeds, emerald fragments from leaf-shoots of vegetables, and gourds [from]...

By your grace, the women of the learned Brahmins who enjoy great prosperity learn from the pomegranate trees how to wear silver ornaments through their blossoms, from the pumpkin vines how to wear jewels through their broad bellies, and from the nagara-creeper how to wear gold through its fully opened flowers. (1455)
1455 Of that very [person],
18. excessive giving.
O Lord, the wish-fulfilling tree, whose sweet warbling of cuckoos is a delight to the ear, sleeps;
the divine cow of plenty, satisfied with mere young grass, practices rumination;
and you, who always grant the desired fruit, are fixed upon the eyes of supplicants.
Thus, a sprout has been planted for a long time upon Mount Rohana by the wounds of the chisel of Kāmadeva.

While this [king] who bestows excessive gifts stands here, let that wish-granting tree (kalpadruma) somehow remain bent over under the pretext of the weight of its fruit, which increases as it is plucked by supplicants;
for how can a beggar compare to him, who rises preeminent through the emergence of an inexhaustible abundance of jewels?
But Ratnācala, his shame thickened by the ill repute of abandoning his guild, [remained steadfast]. (Śrīharṣa)
I know, O Vikramavardhana, that while you bestow wealth upon supplicants,
you will become like the unfathomable ocean— once shallow with stones, now deep with jewels;
and I foresee that its belly will weep with tears in the form of the weight of gems from the Rohaṇa mountains.
In a few days, it will become like a pomegranate fruit squeezed by ripening;
[this is] by Ḍimboka (Suvarṇarēkhā 1437).
"Brother, cast away this grief born from separation from your beloved;
indeed, mental anguish and physical illness shall not afflict you again once night has arrived.
Know that no one else can equal the Golden Mountain (Meru) in the excellence of its gifts."
In a few days from now, the realization of non-duality with the ocean will come to pass for me.

O Lord, if supplicants were to seek you out with great difficulty after a long time, you would be hard-pressed to grant their requests; yet you, on the other hand, daily and with effort, search for those very supplicants,
giving them far more than they had even imagined when they first thought of you upon their attainment.
If, upon beholding you, the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) does not shatter, it is surely no stone at all. (1460) —
by Chittipa.
19. O Valor! You who take singular delight in reckless daring, you fearless hero, now with your boundless expansion and unrestrained intellect, you are somewhat merciless toward knowledge.
That entire royal assembly exists without prosperity, without weapons, without food, without territory, without an army, without splendor, and without support. 1461,
To you, who have conquered the earth as far as my very borders and who are like a second Vasu, pearls and other jewels were already offered by me;
yet here I am, now become utterly destitute.
Thus, O King, at dawn this ocean before you bears a heated axe in the guise of the solar orb rising from the horizon, its waves appearing like uplifted arms.
Of someone:
Why do you still torment those two lovely hands, which bear the marks of royalty, with these scriptures that are sharper and more brilliant than the blade used for severing the heads of enemies?
O Lord, what king on the surface of the earth could endure your bow-like brow, curved in anger, with its string meeting [your eyes] in such a cruel, sidelong glance?

the ocean is consumed deeply under the guise of the fire named Vāḍava.

1045) If the ocean did not possess such vastness, if it did not have such depth, or if its compassionate favor toward all living beings were not so universal; ||| [then this work would not exist].

Salutations to that Agastya, by whom that very Lord of Waters— who once sported as the boar Hari causing the delusion of Śumbhara and whose waves filled the quarters of space— is thus drunk up; yet even when drunk, his belly was not filled.
Of Vācaspati, the ocean of words: (Su.ra.
1201) Shall we speak of Hari, who holds the universe within his belly, or rather of the hood of this serpent?

Of someone:
Having bowed one's head to the very command of the Sage, one should remain on the Vindhya mountain. (Śā.pa. 4025, Sū.mu. 109.49, Su.ra. 1209)

Furthermore, you who desire a very high station must not overstep this [limit]: for what distress could possibly arise on the surface of the cheek of Him who drank the ocean—finding its refuge in mountains such as Maināka—as He swallows you? (1703)
Of Śālūka: (Su.ra.
1123) Hari was not remembered as being sleepy, nor was the fire, which consumes the universe, taken into account.

What more need be said? Have those waves, which once licked the very sky, not been observed by the sage whose belly was emaciated by his vows, as he held them for a moment in the hollow of his three joined fingers?
It is a marvel that he drank up that ocean; was it perhaps an auditory illusion on our part? ||1704||
Let this eye of someone’s remain veiled by a certain distance, yet even the mind [reaches it] through its own vast powers.
O Sage, this ocean, whose essence is beyond all hope, has been reduced to a mere mouthful by your great asceticism;

you ought to desist from this very act. Beyond this, there is no further fame for you to gain from drinking it in a single draught, for its loss would be like the depletion of the entire treasury of the rain-clouds.
1705. Water of Gaṅgoka of Tailapāṭīya, 14 [māṣas].
Your depth is terrifying; by the power of your essence, you possess a manifold variety that is also wondrous.
There is no stability in you, even when held upon the head, and your mouth is utterly irresistible.
Your power is great enough to cause even the massive mountains to split asunder; tell me, what is this water?
What indeed have you gained by abandoning your wicked brothers, since you have acquired their virtues? (1706) Keśaṭa.
Your independence is like the crawling of a lowly serpent, and your submissiveness when placed in a worthy vessel is likewise strange;
this turbidity produced by another reveals that your affection does not find its true place within you. Alas! O Water, I ask you about this.
"O friend, is your master far away, or is he your own teacher? [He replied:
"It is indeed his."
For you who dwell among the four castes, the touch of water does not cause reproach;
in a worthy recipient, nobility of birth does not exist, for dignity arises from your own excellence.
Thus, even if your conduct is censured by the world, you are the very embodiment of the Lord.
Who, indeed, is able to fathom the conduct of one who is adorned by the Lord?
1708 Of him alone...

From the lotus came the lotus-born Brahmā, and from him, from this cosmic egg, arose this entire universe consisting of the moving and the stationary; yet its root is you. Shame on you! Like a thief, you depart in secret, having slipped out through the lattice-windows.
Living beings, having taken refuge in you and being solely dependent on you, are bound helplessly by that very [bond]. (Śā. Pa. 1166; Sū. Mu. 36.19)
Coolness is indeed your innate quality, and your transparency is natural;
what more can we say of your purity, for others become pure by contact with you?
And what further ground for praise could there be for you than that you are the very life of all embodied beings?
If you go by a lowly path, who is able to obstruct you, O Water? (Śā. Pa. 1165; Sū. Mu.
15. The conch was born from the ocean; its luster is as bright as the moon;
yet its chest is naturally crooked and hard.
The rightward movement of the conch shell was a source of great honor, yet even so, it was struck by the saw-like blow of its left side.
To someone who has known its whiteness, the sound of you being heard delights; O Sindhu-rāja, your birthplace is truly beautiful.
Even that secret must certainly be told to one person; O Kamboja, who can conceal the crookedness of your heart?
There are thousands of blue conch shells in the ocean, struck by the spray of its waves, which roll along the shores, their hundred petals staining the surface of the earth with variegated hues.
There arose a certain singular conch, the Pāñcajanya, which was a source of wonder for the virtuous,
for it is filled by the breaths of the Enemy of Mura, which are capable of bearing the dissolution at the end of an aeon.
By Kaviratna: (Sv 917, Śā.pa. 1119, Sū.mu.
29.7) In the interior of the belly of the ocean, conch shells have arisen, are arising, and will most likely arise again at every step in numbers beyond counting.
Was there even one such as he here [in the past], other than the wielder of the Pāñcajanya conch,
by whose roar these women of the enemies of the gods now become so that their eyebrows droop with fear?
A right-spiraling conch shell, brought to the shore by waves surging high from the gusting wind of the Gosoka river, was carried away by the power of fate.
Is he burnt, or has he become ink? With such doubts,
the common women lead him away to be served by the female snails.
Of Anurāgadeva (Su.ra. 11|18, by Sucarita):
16. A jewel is worthy of being set in a collection of golden ornaments.

Of Acala: (Sv 898, Su.ra.
1672) Even from being struck by a thunderbolt, even from being trampled underfoot.
If they are indeed jewels, they endure [all things] out of a longing for virtues.

O jewel, abandon your grief here thinking, "I was situated within the ocean and have been cast up onto the shore by merciless waves"; for surely someone whose heart is drawn by acquaintance with your virtues will appear.
"May the Lord of Men make your splendor kissed by the makara on his crown.
(Su.ra. 1073) — [Attributed to] Someone.
"O brother, one must not abandon one's birthplace; enough with these heaps of jewels here, by which this ocean—even though it has sunk to the bottom—was made a 'mine of gems' (ratnākara).
For these [other jewels], there is no appreciation of their qualities here, no renown for their weight, nor even a mention of them."
Having been born from another, they once again occupy the summit of the mountains. (1719)
— Tilacandra.

As long as there is no one to take them up, the virtues of those possessed of such qualities remain like non-existent things; even the Kaustubha gem, though worthy of honor, was [as if] non-existent before it came to dwell in the heart of the Enemy of the Daityas.
Did he not exist in the ocean, and was there ever any scriptural authority for him, that Rudra who presides over the administration of dharma?
1720.1720. Dharmādhikaraṇikarudrasya.
17. O Lord of Merchants, we say something regarding the emerald; do not feel shame here.
How is it that this conduct is so unrestrained in your city at present?
When there was doubt as to whether this might be an emerald or glass,
the task of examination was entrusted to the salt merchants. ||1721||
This familiarity with the ocean of Nārāyaṇa is not for those born blind;
you, who possess eyes, have utterly mocked those who are truly possessed of vision through their discernment of virtues.
O emerald, the false outpouring of faults by miserly merchants will serve only to diminish your virtues and bring you ill repute.
O moon reflected in water,
abandon your pride in your own qualities;
you have fallen into the emerald of a merchant full of envy.
Even the price you receive for a glass trinket is better for you than that [other thing]. (1723)
O emerald that kisses the crest of the world, what humiliation is this to you— that some base person has cast upon you the stain of the delusion that you are mere glass? (Śāpadeśa 1104)
That we stood here in silence within the range of your vision was determined by the wretchedness of filling our insatiable bellies.

By whom were you, Vallana, brought here from that place with such care by one devoid of compassion? And by whom have you been presented for sale in this foreign land? How did you come to be sitting here so comfortably?
Let alone a buyer who can bear the burden of such an expenditure on this [emerald],
O brother; there is not even one capable of testing you, emerald jewel.
Of Maṅgala: (Śā.pa. 1110, Sū.mu. 28.11, Su.ra.
1023) 18. "Tell me, what are these various jewels? What is renowned by its genus? What is its value in cowries?"

"By how many [steps] can this be reached, or what is the purpose of this? What is the use of every single step?"—thus belittled by the crowd of villagers, alas, the merchant holds the jewel in the palm of his hand and yet desponds. ||1726||
Is this not a fragment of crystal belonging to the physician Gadādhara? Or is it a stone, or perhaps one from Sindh?
"Will this hailstone not become paralyzed with fear?"— O Moon-jewel, through such sudden imaginings of the villagers, these days of mockery shall pass away. (1727)
That which was smelled, kissed, repeatedly licked, and chewed by the moon reflected in water— 1727.
Or if you were cast down because this sapless one was provoked to anger, do not feel distress;

Of Dūnoka. (Kuval., 153):
Others cook their own bellies as pots over the ocean.
The world is surpassed by the mass of radiance from these hard gems;
yet, O Lord of Lakṣmī, what is this clamor in the three worlds?
Ah, how great is the noble reception accorded to this jewel, the dear friend of the Lord! 1729.
O pearl-jewel, at the house of the cowherd, shine forth outside, illuminating the dwellings.
Make even the virtues of the lords of the earth bear fruit for yourself;
why do you waste your life here in vain within the hollow of a mere oyster shell?
This ocean is vast and deep; who here would take you into account? 1730.
Of Murāri. (Su.ra.
Let these merchants of the jewel have their heads dancing with the introductions to its multitude of virtues; but we, O Gold, are the bards of your fame.
And yet, alas, by you whose face is never withered, they are made to feel the pain of burning and cutting!
For, having accepted [this], they are made to sit comfortably upon the crest of a king. (1731) Of the Water-Moon.
Hymns have been recited, offerings presented,
hands joined in supplication, and prostrations performed many times;
yet what can we do, O Treasure of Gold, before You?
Even that burnt yakṣa is not able to behold him here,
[the son] of Vaidya Gadādhara.
O goldsmith, grind me mercilessly on a whetstone, burn me with fire, or pierce me with iron; do not weigh me against *guñjā* seeds. (1733)
O, what is the use of this vain pride in one who, though rendered exceedingly pure by burning, cutting, and rubbing, remains as he was?
That you have been placed upon the scale together with golden *guñjā* seeds. (1734)
Of Bāṇa (Su.ra. 11.17):
That which is tested on the touchstone yet remains unstained; that which remains unaltered even during the merciless operation of the chisel; and that which, when cast into fire, does not wither.
Alas, O gold! Having placed you on a scale alongside this perfection of purity, that you were judged by the virtuous to be equal in rank to mere *guñjā* seeds—what can be done?
O Śoṇa, by whom— driven by a passion for the misfortune of the Goddess— were these two rivers, the Nanda and the Nandā, bestowed upon you for Balabhadra?
I know that you were once delightful, with water only reaching to the knees;
but now, with forests on your banks falling away due to your current, with waves and eddies difficult to cross, and with turbid waters that breach the shores—whom do you please? (1736)
Of Śatānanda. (Su.ra.
1509) These trees that have stood here since birth have been uprooted from the bank.
The waves, fragile as they are, are suddenly raised to the highest height;
within lies a collection of rocks, yet on the outside even the fragrant trees fall away.
O brother Śoṇa, there is no one who does not laugh at the ruin of your prosperity.
1737. By Amarasiṃha. (Śā. Pa. 1122, Sū. Mu. 30.5, Su. Ra. 1028) [In that which] lasts for only a few days.
In youth, which causes intoxication, the wicked commit such offenses that their very birth becomes in vain. (1738)
By Bhojadeva. (Śā.pa. 1124, Sū.mu. 30.2, Su.ra.
1110) There are indeed hundreds of rivers whose waters have passed beyond the path reached by the eyes; yet...

yet she is that very Jahnavi who, when seen, purifies the entire universe.
She is now divided, turbid in some places, and in others pitiable with extremely meager waters. (1739)
1739. Of Umāpatidhara:
The waves have become calm; the water is still, smooth, and clear.

This disciplined appearance speaks of tranquility, as it were, like that of rivers; nevertheless, by means of those various trees fallen here and there along their banks, that very same lack of discipline manifests itself before the mind, even though it has been restrained.
1740. Composed by someone [else].
(Sū.mu. 30.4, Su.ra. 1111, Śabdārṇava) 21. Lake.
The birds are sweet-voiced, the descent is auspicious,
and the grassy meadow beneath the trees on the bank is delightful—
all this and more is excellent for Kamalākara.
But the water of Maṅgala has been made turbid by the fresh rainwater.
1741.1741. Maṅgalasya.
In every forest, how many tanks are there not, possessing waters of blameless sweetness and abundance, and capable of sustaining vast multitudes of excellent birds? But for this swan—
Whose excellent mind does it carry? What is the foundation of your mind? 1742. 1742. Of someone.
The holding of water is for the relief of travelers distressed by the journey;

the cluster of lotuses is for the joy of the swarms of bees; the grasping of lotus stalks is for the delight of the white-winged swans—what indeed can be said of that lake which is so highly esteemed, even though this [swan] was born upon its very shore?
Even from afar, this tree with its glossy appearance removes the fatigue of our eyes;
thus says Vaidya Gadādhar.
Through familiarity with these masses of rays from the hot-rayed sun,
let not your nature become sharp and pungent; for indeed, your innate coolness is [your true self], while these wicked ones merely lick a few drops of water.
Repelling travelers, they bring about an indescribable withering within you.
(1744) — Umāpatidhara.
Where a flock of swans drinks the pure water with graceful play,
in that beautiful lake, a young cātaka bird— whether by delusion,
nature, or pride— does not drink its water along with those birds.
What does this matter? For you, there is either height or lightness, O lake of Śakaṭīya Yaśavara! (Su.ra. 1070; by someone)
22. When the water had been drained from the dried-up lake, the lotus stalks were devoured by the herds of boars belonging to the circles of farmers.
O friend traveler, today when the trees on the bank are consumed by fire,
this lake was seen by you as nothing but a cause for sorrow.
In the lake of Vaidya Gadādhara,
the water was drunk up to its very banks by herds of elephants intoxicated with rut; by the surging of his powerful waves, the entire world was pervaded.
In that very same [time], when the waters have been drunk up by the fierce rows of the sun's rays,
the midday grounds have arrived at every step, scorching the nails of travelers. (1747)
Mādhava’s land is covered with nooses; the lotus groves are swept away by powerful winds; the waters are nearly exhausted; and the flocks of birds have taken refuge in their burrows.
Now, in this lake, there will surely come about for those birds who have long cherished the affection of service to it that process of being cooked in a sealed vessel (puṭapāka). ||1748||
Having attained supreme bliss by means of breezes raining down fine droplets, the melodious cries of rows of swans pleasing to the ear, fully blossomed lotuses, and pure waters;
Later, when his wealth was exhausted, the blessed lotus-pond carried away his own body and, under the guise of lotus stalks, gave his bones— white as the new moon— to those who sought them. (1749)
Of the Fortunate One: (Su.ra.
1657, by Kasyacid) Where, due to the impudence of its excessively hot waters, herds of wild elephants with upraised trunks plunged fearlessly right near the shore of that pure [lake].

Of Madhuraśīla (Su.ra. 1043, by someone):
23. Where are the swarms of bees in the full lake, the lake of the rainy season?
O birds, do you remember those words of your kinsmen at that time? Cruel and parching as she was,
this very same lotus stalk has once again appeared beneath your very heads.
By the heat of the forest fire, whose body was being scorched by the intense radiance of the sun, [the body] of Viriñci—
O traveler, having come far along the path, repeatedly fainting from affliction,
wandering with a piteous gaze, and longing for even the water of a puddle due to the agony of thirst—
by my past merits, I have reached this lake where elephants are submerged and birds are falling. (1752)
O most excellent lake, may you remain for the lord of the earth as one who has obtained the nectar from the ocean of milk.
The waters, shimmering with clusters of lotuses that rival its own sweetness and adorned by swans as their crest-ornaments,
have dispelled all heat, parching, and fatigue through the touch of breezes saturated by showers of cool, gently tossing droplets— breezes truly enchanting to the mind. (1753)
Gosoka’s mind was drawn even to wells where not a drop of water remained, having been hidden deep within.

O pond, because my gaze has now repeatedly fallen upon you— who possess smiling, upturned white lotuses and consist of the play of waves— even though your excavated basins contain but a little water, mud, and distress, that fever of the summer heat within me is now stilled.
The physician Gadādhara was as if dead, hidden within the earth by frogs dwelling in hollows and by tortoises.

In that very lake where the pāṭhīna fish repeatedly fainted from wallowing upon the surface of the thin mud, a cloud out of season arrived and performed such a feat that herds of wild elephants, submerged up to their frontal globes, drink its water.
1755 Chittapa’s. (Bp 201, Sv 843, by a Southerner; Śā.pa. 777, by Akālajalada; Su.ra. 1059, by Dvaṃdūka) 24. The Fish.
O Pāṭhīna fish, release the water from the Kunda lake that you have drunk here,
mixed with the mud of the constantly falling riverbanks;
it will fall upon your tender body as you emerge.
A deep wound upon his body from the arrow-like beak of a kurara bird;
[this is] of Vasantadeva.
Where is the deep-water lake, the birthplace of you, O young *śakula* fish, and where is this encounter with the shore resulting from your new engagement in water-sports? Therefore,
lead yourself here into this opening that is devoid of crabs (*kulīra*).
Let the family of cranes pass the day as long as the sun-god remains. (1757) [Bhāskaradeva]
In this lake, so intensely terrible with venomous serpents, you are indifferent even toward life; O fish,
spare this body of yours.
For one who contemplates stability, where is there no happiness? — thus says the Emperor of Poets.
