Being bound in a braid, why do you swell with pride while experiencing such a state?
(1760) [Of someone]
25. Having observed this skill of yours in tracking out vulnerabilities, the serpent has adopted crookedness in its gait and poison in its mouth.
I think you, O serpent, have been appointed by fate to the unworthy task of taking the lives of human beings. ||1761||
O snake-charmer, do not thrust your own finger into the mouth of this creature out of pride in your mantras; for this is surely some kind of serpent.
Right here, a thousand like you, scorched by his virulent poison, have fallen down lifeless.
That you gaze with ease upon the peacock of Aśoka,
or that you look down with utter contempt upon Tārkṣya;
O serpent of Śiva, we revere your very birth, since you have by chance become the sovereign of the licked medicinal herbs.

Enough with these coils coiled in front of Gadādhara; enough with the whirling circles that blind the eyes; enough with the incessant outbursts of thundering roars; and enough with the showers of venom.
Why, O serpents, do you harbor these unbridled outbursts of anger?
Are we not indeed the reciters of praises for the Blessed Tārkṣya?

O brother snake-charmer, those very same petty serpents now bow their heads when you take hold of them, for their poison has been neutralized by the dust of your mouth, permeated by the power of your mantras.
But this serpent is worn out; even from the mere act of running across the earth crowded with throngs of great lords of virtues such as yourself, his head does not bow down. (1765)
Umāpatidhara’s 26:
O frogs, even you may croak as much as you wish; what is gold?
Though brought to a state of great splendor by the fresh floods of water,
this pit will soon perish; yet it shall remain a source of sorrow for a long time, for your former purchase alone remains within its boundaries.
This much is the earth belonging to Nāka; and following that, the celestial sphere is this much.

"Such is the extent of the underworld, and such is the amount of water upon the earth"—having realized this regarding the well, this frog, who has learned its depths, does not merely croak; rather, he lets out an exceedingly powerful sound. ||1767||
O frog of wicked resolve, what indeed is the name of this evening [of yours]? Victory to Nandin!
Why do you emit a cry while pressing against your body as if in anger?

that I consider to be the playful sport of some blessed master of poisons. (1770)
1770 Of that very same [author].

we praise your behavior from its very root,

yogeśvarasya.
Fie upon the conduct of this honey-bee,

It was not even from the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas)— which were cooled by shade, where seekers of their fulfillment sported upon golden slabs, which possessed houses of various painted clusters of blossoms, and from which celestial beings gathered for play— that [the breeze] drew its waves of wonderful fragrance.
It runs swiftly and warbles most charmingly; what is this *indindara*? (1783) [By Ballana]
He who has no desire for the dust-powder on the lotus of Śrī’s playful sport,
who does not wish to drink the stream of ichor from the elephant of the gods, and who has abandoned attachment to the fragrance of the flowers of the thirty [deities].
O friend, O bee, how truly auspicious is your state, for you are indeed contented! (1784) 1784 Maṅgala’s.

Finding no joy in the *kunda* flower, feeling distressed by the honey, and lacking support in the mango, he does not take even a moment’s pleasure in the clove; he forms no attachment to the *priyaṅgu*, nor does he frequent the *cūta*.
Remembering his drinking of the honey from Lakṣmī’s play-lotus, the bee [remains there]. (Chittapa; Sūktimuktāvalī 19.8)
30. O bee of the lotus,
even if the lotus-pond has been destroyed by a rutting elephant agitated by your playful movements, if your own life-breaths are dear to you, why then is the earth devoid of lotuses?
O bee, having cast aside the lotus, that you are instead intent upon the ichor from its very temples— oh, at this we feel ashamed even to speak!
When the sun, possessing the luster of a flame of fire, has settled upon the peak of the western mountain as the moon in the water,
the thirsty bee enters the lotus to reach its filaments.
A person seeking wealth does not take into account the confinement within that [palace], nor indeed does one intensely parched with thirst consider the exhaustion born of the time of twilight.
Of someone:
Let the madhūka flower indeed fade away; alas, let the mango tree reach its full maturity!
I suspect that the honeybee is not poor in honey; it triumphs in the lotus.
In every forest, these [trees] of Jahnu’s lineage met with many blossoms in full bloom, their union made lovely by the affectionate fragrance [of the flowers].
The thirst for the lotus never ceased; however,
these bees drink its nectar freely until their bellies are full.
Wherever the fragrance of the *śāṭīka* flower is manifest here, there is no honey from the beauty of spring;
and where the honey is abundant, there is no richness of scent.
Thus, censuring the *maruvaka* flower and losing all interest in the *kunda*,
the bee desponds as he repeatedly recalls the lotus.
Umāpatidhara’s 31. The Mango-Bees:
O mango tree, you are fortunate now, filling both crows and parrots with your fruits.

But that blue jay, which formerly sported incessantly upon you when you were blooming with a heavy burden of jasmine blossoms, does not come now that you have borne fruit; for he eats only the flowers.
Is such a devotion to one's own desire for fruit ever found even in a wish-fulfilling tree?
Of Vallabha. (Su.ra.
1103) To discern the lake of lotuses produced by the joy born from drops of nectar...

Why would the bee not suddenly hasten toward the mango tree— its mind indifferent to play due to its lack of desire for sport, yet full of longing for the fragrance arising from the abundant, emerging burden of unprecedented blossoms? (1792)
1792. Here, this deluded bee has abandoned the clusters of mango blossoms for that very [lotus].
It pursues the branch of the *śākhoṭaka* tree, which is crooked, tasteless, and pithless.
[1793] Of someone.
Let the cuckoos indeed savor the mango buds for a long time, provided that some fortunate honeybee perceives such fragrance as well. (1794)
In the spring of Vasukalpa, there truly exist in every forest blossoms that never fail to bloom, whose lovely beginnings are the friends of the abundant, sweet honey.
There are hundreds of thousands of trees here, yet the bee, full of passion, playfully and impetuously drinks the essence of the nectar from these mango trees alone. (1795)
O bee of the *ketakī*, you who wear a forest garland,
having abandoned this lake of blooming lotuses— a dwelling place of nectar— why do you seek it out?

O you restless bee, that you are repeatedly pricked by thorns while kissing the fresh ketaki flower— this is the fruit corresponding to your deed, you who are wandering, soiled, noisy, and mad with passion! 1796.
Having abandoned the delightful taste of drinking honey from lotuses, O noble one, [he now drinks]...
Since you have flown toward the flower of the *ketakī*,
alas, this is the very fruit of your misconduct; why do you grieve, O bee, with your wings pierced by thorns?
The leaves of a certain [plant] are difficult to approach due to their thousand thorns.
There is not even a rumor of honey amidst the darkness of pollen; O Ketakī, your flaws have not been perceived by the bee, who finds delight in fragrance alone.
1798. Of Sarasvatī. (Śā. Pa. 1012) Having abandoned that forest of lotuses which is the abode of Madhu, [the bee] was drawn away by its mere fragrance.
O bee, why do you run in vain toward the *ketakī* flowers in hope of honey?
These flowers bear a core that is crushed within a vessel-like calyx crowded with the tips of thorns, and filled with filaments soiled by masses of pollen. (1799)
The thick fragrance of the *narasiṃha* tree, possessing the luster of moonbeams, is a mass of petals.
The collection of filaments is soft; the pollen of the *ketakī* flower is like the powder of sandalwood. All this is excellent, yet there is only one fault:
that bees, being barred by the thorns standing at the entrance, cannot enter.
1800 of someone;
33. Mountain.
O Kailāsa, you mountain who have grown arrogant merely by being the vessel for the residence of Paśupati— abandon this pride here at once!
Have you not seen [the Lord] when He rose up with effortless grace?
Resembling a lotus upon the lotus-hand of Paulastya,
[this is] Dāmodara’s.
The enemy of Mura obtained Lakṣmī; the conqueror of Tripura obtained the moon;
and the lord of Paulomī obtained the king of elephants from the ocean—tell me, what was obtained by you when Mount Mandara was churned?
This abode of jewels, which mercilessly [crushes] the mountains, is the refuge of Kāmadeva. (Śā. Pa. 1068)
I have never beheld a herd of elephants, nor have I ever enjoyed the breeze from yak-tail fans;
nor has the moon ever served as a parasol near my head,
nor have mountains been brought to serve as footstools— fie on fate that I am now in the ocean!
O Maināka, son of the lord of mountains, your life has indeed passed in vain, despite your greatness. (1803) —
Vaidya Gadādharasvāmī.

This moon rises upon the summit of one mountain and, in due course, sets upon another; between these two, which mountain is truly praised? For who does not make the crest-jewel of the rising one shine, yet causes that of the setting one to fade?
He who acts like you is difficult to find; this high-peaked mountain [is such].
(Puṇḍarīka; Śā. pa. 1079, Sū. mu. 36.15)

May the eastern mountain place upon its crest the sun— the life-giver to the world whose eyes are overwhelmed by darkness— as he rises with increasing brilliance; for it is no wonder that he reaches this sun when his day has ended and his rays have faded away.
The final mountain, performing [this], places it upon its crest; how wonderful!
(This is the seal-mark.)
34. What is the use of that golden mountain or the silver mountain? For those trees which stand upon the Malaya mountain are truly trees indeed.
We pay homage to the Malaya mountain alone, by depending upon which even the śākoṭa, nimba, and kuṭaja trees become sandalwood.
It is indeed appropriate that the *śākoṭaka* tree should rival some young *campaka* tree.
On this Malaya mountain,
it is said that all the trees are indeed sandalwood.
From the elephant Muṣṭika,
you shall obtain hundreds of young female serpents;
satisfy your desire for sandalwood from the Śrīkhaṇḍa mountain by gathering hundreds of Gaṇṭadṛṣad stones.
Your fame has manifested from the heavenly realm down to the surface of the earth and even into the netherworld; yet, no tree other than the sandalwood tree is observed to be its source. (1808)
O brother Candanaśaila, abandon your dullness; let this breeze, spreading fragrance as it moves,
be embraced without hesitation by the graceful women.
Even while standing still, he is satisfied by the mouthfuls from the hollowed palms of thousands of wide-expanded hoods raised by the serpents dwelling within the hollows of the sandalwood trees.
For someone here,
O Malaya mountain, there dwells a boundless ocean, a treasure of waters, entirely dependent on the affection for your feet.
Then why do you not remember yourself as a mountain of noble lineage? Why do you carry the banner of infamy upon the branches of every peak with swarms of serpents? (1810)
35. Of Vasukalpa, another serpent, Dhara, [seized] Śarabha as he was leaping from a mountain peak that had been snatched away by Unmuktakrama.
O foremost of the assembly of young śarabhas, who here is capable of restraining you?
Therefore, depart from this surface of the earth with your skill in leaping and soaring;
for that very Lord of Mountains, whose fame is like the golden moonlight, is the fit abode for you.
Of Vallaṇa. (Su.ra.

1056) He, by the fear and pain caused by even a tiny particle of whose fierce scent-wind, various caves— Please note that the provided fragment ends abruptly. The full verse from *Sūktimuktāvalī* (10.56) continues as follows: yasyānuddhuragandhavātakaṇikātaṅkārtinānādarī- kroḍākṛṣṭakuraṅgasaṃgatigataḥ kodaṇḍapāṇiḥ patiḥ | tasyaitat tapanīyadānavidhutaśrīgarvasarvasvakaṃ nāsīraṃ purato 'bhyudastakaravālavyālavalgitam || **Translation:** He, the Lord who holds the bow in hand, has entered into the company of deer drawn into the embrace of the interior of various caves, which are distressed by the fear of even a tiny particle of his fierce scent-wind. Before him is this vanguard, which has robbed the pride of the beauty of molten gold and in which fierce swords brandish like serpents.

What praise can I offer to these herds of lions, whose heads and tails are hidden by their chests as they crouch in the corners, having been uprooted from the pride of defeating insolent and invincible scent-elephants?
This śarabha, smiling with newfound arrogance, feels only supreme compassion in his heart.
Of that very [person]: (Su.ra.
10.46) "Even by the lord of beasts, the frontal globes of the king of elephants..."
For he is indeed the universal emperor of the Śarabha clans, by whose manliness arising from his temples their gaze, startled with fear, has utterly vanished. 1813.
In the year 1813 of Mādhava,
he whose lightness of fame reached the very limits of the circle of the earth—

How could that Sarabha— who, in his play, humbles the wind-god, who possesses a boundless fever of pride like the king of beasts, and who is such a source of wonder to the lords of the quarters with his various rising and curved leaps— ever come within the range of our words? (1814)
1814. Of Makaranda’s [elephant],
which split the temples of the herd of elephants bathed in clusters of moonlight from his claws—

O Sarabha, when the lord of dogs has been slain or driven away by you— the conqueror of lions in the fields of battle— by the hundreds, he has indeed fallen into a most pitiable state; alas, there is no occasion for your impetuous fury now.
1815 Of a certain person 36. The Lion
Let people call him the Lord of Beasts, the Foe of Beasts, or Hari; for both titles are mere playthings for him who crushes elephants as if in sport. (1816)
Of someone [it is said]: (Śā. Pa.
901) "What does a doe accomplish with many sons who are incapable of action?
She trembles along with even one son wandering in the depths of the forest."
Even with a single son, though he be but one, who possesses a soul capable of splitting the temples of lordly elephants and who is strong with long-reaching prowess, a lioness exults in pride. (1817)
The sun has risen, capable of scaling mountain peaks; your claws possess the essence of a diamond, your splendor is formidable, and that great roar of yours shatters the mountains.
By the lion, who was drowsy and failed to leave his mountain cave due to indolence,
this entire world— the sole means for universal conquest— was obtained, yet nothing at all was achieved. (1818)
Of someone:
his body is foul-smelling, his hand is intent on killing others, and his discrimination between good and evil is known only through his animal nature. (Su.ra. 10.35)
Thus, there is nothing at all beautiful in the lion;
yet his splendor is such that it renders the world wretched.
Of Vasundhara: (Su.ra.
10.91) Indeed, these collections of water, fire, wind, and smoke are naturally roaring; but under you, the world is free from pride and intoxication.
Be gracious; desist from this undertaking and restrain this anger of yours,
O Hari, for this [roar] has arisen from the clouds, not from elephants.
By Amarasiṃha.
(Su.ra. 1071) 37. A lion cub has not yet practiced its assault; its fangs have not yet sprouted.
His body is not yet full-grown, his claws have not attained firmness,
and his roar is still so soft; nevertheless, O lion cub, he possesses some such power by which even rutting elephants are rendered devoid of pride.
Having reached this forest, the herd of elephants wanders about in fear, thinking, "This is a young lion."
This [lion], too, shaking off that flank of flesh where the mane has not yet grown, employs his claws— even though they are ineffective— out of greed for meat. (1822)
Shaking their shoulders whose manes have not yet emerged, emitting loud and sweet sounds,
scratching their paws upon the rock with claws that are not yet fully visible,
and bearing eyes that are red and squinted in anger— such are the lion cubs.
By good fortune, they gaze upon the sky where the clouds roar fiercely;
their shoulders lack the rising manes of hair, and the sprouts of their claws are not very distinct.
The budding of the sprouts of his teeth is slight, his roar from his mouth is soft;
yet even now, the lion cub has not ceased his activity appropriate to his lineage,
which dispels the blindness of the elephants caused by the great scent of rut.
O young lion, if you indeed abandon your anger, then we shall speak.
"Having thus slain an entire thousand elephants, what has been gained by your long-lived self?
If you say, 'I am indeed capable of doing such a thing,' then fie on you, fool! Is the ocean not able to flood the world on all sides, that you still rely upon such fortitude? (1825)
[The work] of Vīryamitra. (Su.Ra.
1060) 38. Jaratsiṃha.

There is no power for an assault here; the tusks and claws have stripped away the rows of flesh to the root, the eyes are dim and sightless, and the body is worn out by the exertion of violent play. Therefore, O lords of elephants, roam at will within this forest of deer!
The lion, having by the power of fate reached the miserable state of old age, has abandoned his pride. (1826)
— Nākokasya.

Alas, the time has ripened for this world, which once resounded with the slightly unsteady and heavy trumpeting of rutting elephants roaming in the sky; what is this that is now being struck by a herd of female elephants?
That lion hears the sounds of the trees moving within the prison on his side—
[this is] from Vaidya Gadādharasvāmin.
A mouth without fangs, the decay of claws,
and a voice that is unstable and rattling— alas, the lion bears these signs of the onset of old age!
This bank is being enjoyed by young elephants;
it belongs to him alone.
Having heard from afar even the mere warbling of the throat-sounds of one languid with sleep,
that entire herd of scent-elephants fell down here one by one in a swoon;
yet today, before this very lord of beasts, they have let out a fierce roar.
Jackals, intoxicated by the smell of raw flesh, roam about unflinchingly. (1829)
— Gosoka.

Let alone the ancient renown of Hari, who possesses boundless prowess and whose exceedingly wonderful undertakings were performed with great honor; for even he was rendered incapable of descending through the doorways of the caves and caverns of the Vindhya mountains, though they were already worn away.
The scent-elephants are startled by the fragrance and tremble slightly with their limbs as they encounter the limbs of the body-bearer.
(1830) Vallana’s.
39. O elephant, why do you suddenly strike the tree by the road as if mad? Why do you shatter the lake of blooming lotuses with the blows of your trunk?
Then, O best of elephants, we shall recognize your incomparable outpouring of rut,
if you touch the mane of even a sleeping lion cub.
Of Nārāyaṇa: (Su.ra.

1072) His fever has not subsided, his thirst has not ceased, his body is not emaciated, the dust from his frame is not washed away, and he has not freely swallowed mouthfuls of fodder; what talk can there be of sport?
Alas, has the lotus not been touched by the elephant with its trunk extended far out? Oh, the bees have begun a causeless clamor of humming! (1832)

Of Ācārya Gopīka. (Śāradātilaka-pañjikā 923; Sūkti-muktāvalī 23.10) Wherever it may be, even in that bower, a line of antelopes, a multitude of rabbits, a cluster of porcupines, and a troop of boars experience happiness.
Alas, what tree indeed is there in this ruined forest so tall that the lordly elephant, afflicted by the heat, might dwell within its shade?

There was a certain one whose playful dwelling was in the midst of the Vindhya forest; for whom the course of worldly existence always provided sustenance through the bulbs of beautiful lotuses growing at will, and who had a hundred female elephants as his playthings.
That scent-elephant, having by fate reached the shore of the desert where the leaves of the *śaivalinī* serve as his bed,
languishes daily, yearning for the Vindhya mountains.
Whether seeking to seize the fangs of Narasimha or merely to kill an elephant,
that outcaste hunter does not calculate the loss of his own gain.
Indeed, by selling even a few fresh fruits here for an old one,
how many hundreds of thousands of coins does that lord of serpents not obtain while living? (1835)
40. Here, the wild elephant of the protector of Tripura’s enemy [is like] a multitude of hunters equipped with weapons fashioned from powerful machines.
Here is a herd of lions with leaping, sharp claws;
here is a mountain impossible to scale; here is a river of thick mud;
and here is a blazing fire in the middle of the forest—alas, what a calamity for the lord of elephants! 1836
O elephant,
do not trumpet so loudly; here dwells the lord of deer in close proximity.
"You have been seen! By fate, depart from here very far and quickly!
Do you not see before you this mountain ridge, whitened by rows of scattered bones from elephants torn apart by sharp claws? (1837)
In this forest lap, richly endowed with dense abundance, Saṃgrāmacandra [dwelt] in the year 1837, amidst fresh warmth.
For how many years have you not wandered at will in comfort upon elephants?
Fie on you, O elephant, that you were born here at this time of destruction, when there is neither water, nor trees, nor grass—only this forest fire plays! 1838.
O King of Serpents, the mountain of Vaidya Gadādhara’s Pulindapattana is very far from here, on this side.
By placing your foot upon this anthill, do not assume a different form; rather,
adopt compassion for the female elephant submerged in the forest, lest the waves— whose masses of foam are already crumbling against the city walls— should first destroy the dry land.
In 1839, [this was written] by Gāṅgoka of Tailapāṭī,
who displays playful grace through bees blinded by the rut-fluid.

Go to another forest, O elephant, where there are trunks of fierce trees and which is intensely delightful with thick foliage; for here, in this grove of plantains, you will certainly find no relief for the itching of your temples.
1840 of the Guru [year]:
41. Mattagaja (The Intoxicated Elephant)
A noose around the neck, firm shackles on both feet,
a tight girth-band, and a most cruel blow from a goad upon the head;
alas, the man is mounted upon the shoulders even at a time fit for pleasure!
"O fool, O excellent elephant, we do not know why you are intoxicated," [said] Laṅgadatta. (Śā. Pa. 931)
O intoxicated elephant, this young bee, wandering far and his mind distressed by intense thirst, has alighted upon your cheek;
you too, therefore, abandon this addiction to swinging on the cradle of your thick ears.
Relinquish your self-will and, for now, dispel this thirst for the fragrance of the Surabhi cow.
He who, in his childhood, was nourished by mouthfuls of handfuls of wild rice shoots,
and by whom the milk remaining from the oblation was drunk from the hollow of a lotus leaf—
him, that elephant, with temples quivering as he is intoxicated at the time of giving gifts; [the bees swarm around him].
Standing at the door, the ascetic looks on repeatedly with both joy and fear. (Manoka; Sv 637, Śā.pa. 918, Su.ra. 1689)
If even tens of millions [of coins] are exhausted through the unrestrained feeding of a lordly elephant whose temples are moist with rut, what loss is that to kings?
For by him alone, who delights in the field of battle, having conquered the position of the enemy—
The splendors of sovereignty over the circle of the earth are bestowed upon their own lord by Vāsudevasena.

By him who first brought a village elephant before you and bound you with snares,
by whom your head was crushed by harsh goads, and by whom you were made a mere beast— you whose heart is now subject to the command of his big toe— look upon those blameless ones who long to see you.
O lord of elephants, you alone are truly blinded by rut as you advance to slay living beings.
(Umāpatidhara)

42. An elephant fallen into the mud, emaciated by hunger and distressed, beheld from afar trees consisting mostly of *karañja*, *sarja*, and *sarala* species; he then set out toward the foot of a mountain.
Having come here out of delusion into this impenetrable and difficult mountain cave, supportless and submerged, what can this Blessed One do, whose fate is adverse? (1846)
The bees, intoxicated by the play of Śaṅkaradeva, possess the splendor of the moon through the luster of his teeth's radiance; yet,
because of his movement, even the mountains fall away from him.
Do we not know the qualities of the sudden ferocity of fate, by which that elephant was submerged in an instant on the bank of the lake, mired in the mud of its sporting waters?
This clamoring of yours is unbecoming to a lotus-root; what occasion is there for clapping your hands?
You have shaken yourself excessively for the sake of washing your limbs.
Somehow you have fallen into an impassable mass of mud; O noble elephant, maintain your fortitude, for the way of destiny is difficult to overcome.
The female elephant of Pāmpāka did not come when summoned,
nor did she, out of affection, stroke her young calf with her sprout-like trunk as he sought his share of the fodder.
That lordly elephant, rushing out of pride and with the impetuous desire to conquer a rival elephant, was miserably submerged in the waters of a lake.
The protector of the enemy of Tripura does not even look toward the [other] directions; he does not resort to despondency;
nor does he, in his mind, reckon any other on earth as capable of subduing him.
Sunk in the mud, with the bristling of his hair caused by the intense force of his own profound majesty, the elephant lets go of the essence of life.
O bound elephant,
you whose body is addicted to the pleasures of the banks of the Revā, do not grieve in vain.
O Kumbhin, drink the water drawn from jars; let your memory of the Vindhya mountains be as barren as a childless woman.

For you have now been driven far away by fate from those female forest elephants, and your dalliance belongs only to the bowers of forest creepers and *śallakī* trees where the shoots are swaying. (1851)
O young elephant, take a mouthful of fodder from the bracelet and abandon your bond of affection for the female elephant.
Now, constantly apply a coating of mud to the wounds caused by the knots of your snares;

for those foothills of the Vindhya, grey with the pollen of flowers fallen from the banks of the Revā and once gazed upon by the wandering eyes of the beautiful wives of the Śabara chiefs, have now receded far away. (1852)

By Bhartṛmeṇṭha (in *Subhāṣitaratnakośa* 640, attributed to Hastipaka; in *Śārṅgadharapaddhati* 928, attributed to someone). The Vindhya mountain, like a father, has been abandoned; the river Revā, like a mother, is the Blessed One.

With minds tenderly bound by affection for you, these elephants—equal to you in their noble birth—have surely offered this very body for the sake of binding themselves to you, O elephant; yet you remain far away, while harsh goads rest upon the surface of their heads as they wallow in the dust. (1853)
In this very matter,
I do not consider this to be the loosening of the knot, but rather the further wounding of that which is already firmly bound.

Those young elephants, timid and terrified by the roar of lions in the forest, who— when remembering their own herd— conceive in their minds thoughts of humiliation from being mounted, beaten, or driven to other lands, to whom will they go? (1854)
Of Pāmpāka.
(Śārdūlavikrīḍita, verse 934) O friends, let there be no pride in the greatness of your own intellect in your minds.
An elephant that goes toward captivity is one who possesses discipline; here, this [elephant] is victorious through its discipline.
If, however, puffed up with anger, it abandons discipline under the sway of intoxication, then does it not throw the entire military camp into total turmoil? (1855)
In the year 1855 of the reign of Tripurāripāla,
[the month] Mṛga, 44.
Even when the forest fire has itself subsided, and even when the cruel lord of the Kirātas draws his bow while the hunter loosens his snare,
the deer, not seeing its companion and with tears of grief welling up, does not look [at them].
The body is consumed, the vital organs are struck on all sides, and movement is broken— such is the state of the moon reflected in water.
O deer, that you do not eat green sprouts anywhere, that you do not find stability,
that your eyes are agitated as you gaze at the quarters while crying out piteously,
and that you are emaciated every day— by this, it is clear your beloved has been separated from you by fate.
"O you who run toward every forest, toward every river, and toward every dawn! (Keśaṭa; *Subhāṣitaratnabhāṇḍāgāra* 756).

"Among the wild creatures in the forests, the deer is its own enemy; the cruel forest lord is the foe of its body; therefore, here there is refuge in the peaceful sage who dwells nearby"—thinking thus, this man approached him, yet by his own ill fortune, he fell [into danger] right there.
Then Ratnamālī, though he had spoken the words "Do not fear," became pitiless and remained silent. 1858. [This was] of Puṇḍraka.
Afflicted by thirst, he does not give his gaze even to a nearby meadow of young grass, nor does he cast his tongue toward the crystal-clear mountain streams; alas,
being ill at ease, he cannot even remain in the company of friends out of curiosity.
Meditating upon the forest of Mekalakanyakā with an unceasing torrent of tears, the deer [perished]. (1859)
— by Bhaṭṭaśālīya Pītāmbara.
Having slept in the thick shade of trees within difficult forests and caves, and having eaten his fill of grass, this deer— satiated by waters easily obtained from clear springs—
is now a fellow-student with the side-glances of fawn-eyed women.
Alas, like a deer hostile to its own flesh, he was among families of cruel hunters for the sake of the Lord of Dharma.
(1860) 1860. [For] Dharmayogeśvara.
45. Like a deer struck by a hunter, he has abandoned his birth-forest as if it were mere blades of grass; the open ground has become like a mother who has been left behind;
and the trees, which served as the cause for his rest, are no longer reckoned as kinsmen.
With her face distressed by the separation from her young fawn, the doe was abandoned halfway along the path; yet even so, the pitiless hunters do not release me as they search for her tracks. (1861)
Of Dharmapāla (or Muktāpīḍa): Having cut the snare, cast off the trap, and forcibly broken through the net,
he emerged from the forest far away, having escaped from the mass of snares as crooked as a bordering mass of fire.
Leaping with extreme speed beyond the range of the hunters' arrows, the deer fell into a well; what can human effort achieve against adverse fate? (1862)
By someone [Muktāpīḍa; Śāp. 940; Su.ra. 1493].
While his beloved was acting according to her own will, she became languid due to the excessive heaviness of her pregnancy;
meanwhile, a Kirāta, bow drawn to his ear, was running right behind her.
Distraught by the fear that his beloved’s love for him might be lost,
the deer looks back again and again while he moves forward repeatedly. (1863)
By Kālidāsa (Su.ra. 1169; attributed to someone):
This young deer, submerged in the wilds of the earth and unaware of any danger, is trembling with fear as its slayers draw near.
O merciless one, alas! Even as you repeatedly gaze upon your own face reflected in the boat, you still strike me; how can your intellect be so deluded?
If this forest of Tilacandra has perished— alas, what is this? If that lake has been destroyed,
then why indeed does this powerful twang of a bow resound from ahead?
Today or tomorrow, the deer— his mind exhausted by anxiety over the movements of the does that are about to give birth— is gasping for breath with his neck slightly bent down.
In that very place,
there was a deer struck by a forest fire,
languid from the heavy exhaustion of pregnancy, as the dense wind fanned the blazing wildfire.
Beholding his mate, whose eyes were rolling and who was overwhelmed by a mass of flames, the deer—though having fled far away with speed—immediately turned back and ran;
yet as she went, he was reduced to a mere memory. What is difficult for love to accomplish? (1866)
The doe lingers for the sake of her young, while the hunter takes away her life.
"Alas! The arrows of the Śabaras and the fires of the trees are flashing!"—thinking thus, the deer enters the depths of the forest for a moment, desponds, faints, and flees. (1867)
O Moon reflected in water,
abandon your despair; O deer, leave the burnt anthill.
This fire, with its bursting, pungent stench,
is perishable; meanwhile, the sky is now thick with garlands of clouds that shatter the thirst of the deer longing for the streams from the rain-bearing clouds.
On one side is the forest fire of Dharmayogeśvara, and on the other side is the earth entangled with a web of flames.
From here the hunter rushes, following closely with his bow drawn;
from this side stands that python ahead with its mouth wide open.
Where can this young deer go, and what can he do, being subject to the power of fate? (1869)
1869. By someone: (Su.ra.
1508) The sun blazes in the middle of the sky, and the forest is consumed by forest fires.

The quarters of the sky do not shimmer on all sides with smoke, nor are the paths bristling with stones; rather, as the deer runs toward its life-breath with the corners of its mouth drenched in blood, even the hunter out of compassion has not fixed arrows upon his bow. (1870)
1870. By Umāpatidhara. (Sū.mu. 26.8) 47. The Deer Woman.
Show favor to these children; having transgressed the forest regions where the Śabara women sport in the waters,
cast off your timidity— here it is before you.
The penance grove of the compassionate one is like a doe. [1871] By someone.
O deer, go now to the lake crowded with the assembly of Bhillas; why do you linger here,
not entering from the penance grove to drink the water?
Even a tawny cow is unfit to be eaten; this is the view of Capaladeva.
O doe, roam upon the mountain peak devoid of humans; abandon these young ones,
for the interior of your belly is already agitated by the presence of a hyena.
What joy indeed can there be in one who bears the earth?
It belongs only to him [who is free from such burdens].
Here, the Kirātas, with their bow-vines drawn into circles, move with silent steps and suppressed falls, being unaccustomed to your languid glances.
"O wife of the deer-catcher, they are attacking; go far away!
[Thus spoke] Mandoka.
"O hunter, having taken all the flesh from my limbs except for my breasts,
release me; grant me this favor,
for these fawns of mine are perishing, being unaccustomed to taking mouthfuls of young grass."
My children are intent on beholding my path. (Chittipa; *Śruti-svādhyāya* 660, *Śārṅgadharapaddhati* 4015, *Subhāṣitamuktāvalī* 90.1)
48. O buffalo, enjoy various animals and water for as long as you desire; do not cause this forest to tremble with your frantic dancing.
By this evil deed, although his intention toward you is utterly ruined, he becomes free from stain, like a pond.
The tree of Vaidya Gadādhara finds no stability on the ground because of these fruits that have fallen of their own accord;
its branch-tips, heavy with fruits matured by ripeness, are unable to ascend further.
Enraged that his own prowess was not recognized, and wailing in fury,
this son of a monkey, desiring to seize it, drags the lavali tree. (1877)
That Umāpatidhara’s dwelling is in the courtyards of outcaste houses, his birth is in the lineage of dogs,
his belly is filled with the remains of offerings, and his body is unfit for touch.
O dog, you have today enjoyed all that delicacy by the command of the king, since you ascend the palace encircled by golden chains. (1878)
He who was purified by the rites of the Vedas and consecrated for the sake of removing all obstacles;
he whose companion at Gayāśiras was praiseworthy; he who was equal to the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Alas! After a long time, the bull—marked with the discus and trident, the carrier of the sacrificial liquor, and the vehicle of Śiva—has been seized in the house of the Turuṣkas; fie on their deeds!
The height of that camel causes fear among people; its excessive deformity is its long neck;
it possesses a cruel stride at every joint; and its place of birth is the desert.

Alas, what a tragedy! That camel, a mere beast, which possesses such a fondness for high and sharp thorns, has been taken into the royal service and has become the recipient of two great titles. (1880)
49. From afar, the quarters of the sky were seized by birds perched upon the branches of Govinda’s tree.

While the monkeys stood watching with fruits already released, and while the travelers— exhausted by their journey— remained merely casting off their shadows, they protected themselves at the cost of others; for on that tree, one’s own self was surrendered to the axe of the night’s darkness as it fell upon the branches.
by the small birds in every direction who were quickly honored with the crowning of Abhinanda’s head, [the world was filled].
The timid deer have fled, their burden of exhaustion dispelled by the gift of shade;
alas, what a pity that the restless monkeys, greedy for fruit, have also departed! Only this single tree has endured the calamity of the forest fire.
By someone [else]. (Su.ra.
10.24) With beautiful shade, its summit bowed down by the weight of fruit, it bestows the pacification of all afflictions.

Having beheld you, O fair-thighed one, we have indeed left the path and come here; yet if within you there be the terrifying sight of a circle of serpents moving in the hollow of your trunk, vomiting forth the fire of poison from their throbbing mouths, then you shall truly be blessed. (1883)
Of this tree of knowledge, why should we ever elaborate so much? (Su.Ra. 1050) We shall explain it. Always...

Alas, that innate essence of benevolence toward others, though uprooted by the wind in the mountain fortress of the clouds, has nevertheless reached the path of other people as it passes along the way. (1884)
Of someone: (Su.ra.
1090) Having gradually endured the fatigue of intense frost, the leaves [fell] down.
Some trees, bound by the vow of ingratitude, do not even acknowledge the ground beneath them— the very soil that provides their shade— out of a mere desire for the prospect of future offerings;
yet others, who practice gratitude, remain at the foot of those same trees even while they wither away.
By Acalasiṃha. (Sū.mu. 33.8, Bilhaṇa; Su.ra.
1042) 50. The Wish-Fulfilling Tree (Kalpataru).
O wish-fulfilling tree, although you bear the desired fruits for all seekers, you are not to be worshipped by those possessed of pride,
because you have not granted them their desires in their entirety, even though you are wise.
Their effort was rendered fruitless; [the effort] of Nāka was fruitful.
||1886|| 1886|| [The effort] of Nāka.
What is the use of even the fruit obtained from that stiff wish-fulfilling tree which, having been bowed to by children, dwarfs, and the elderly, does not grant its fruit? (1887)
First the leaves of King Kubjaka were devoured by insects; then the roots of the Kalpa-tree were uprooted by the Vikula trees; subsequently, that tree fell, and a hundred creepers were broken.
Furthermore, from even those [seeds] that have perished, the multitude of sprouts grows forth vigorously,
provided that Hari, the compassionate Lord who is the sovereign of the eastern quarter, is pleased. (1888)
How many trees indeed have grown near the city of the gods belonging to Balabhadra?
Yet, among them, that very wish-fulfilling tree alone is praiseworthy, wherein these virtues reside.
His intentions were the longing for fruit; the fruit was jewels; his livelihood was the world; his eminence was the cause for cutting through affliction; and his glory was invincible. (1889)
The trunk of this refuge-tree is gold; its sprouts are brought to life by emeralds;
the beauty of its clusters is formed of pearls; and the swarms of bees are sapphire-blue.

Who can equal him whose fruit ripens in accordance with his very intention? Fie on his birth among the discourse of trees, since even he is but a tree, though he is the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma).
By Gadādharanātha. (Śā.pā. 988, Sū.mu.
33.11) 51. O traveler, resort to the shade of the sandalwood tree in order to dispel your fatigue.
Do not indeed fear that there is a swarm of serpents here once again;
for now, peacocks have made their dwelling in this place, by whose delightful cries the snakes have fled away to some other spot.
drawn from afar in every direction by the fragrances of Acalasiṃha, they departed.
"O sandalwood tree, we have come here expressly to see Lakṣmī;
what do we see? O fortunate one, a serpent is playing right on your chest! May it be well with you; let us go—release us, we must depart. (1892)
O Lord of the Malaya mountain, if that very [wind] of yours, which subsists upon your feet, were cast away— (Śā.pa. 998, Sū.mu. 33.24, Su.ra. 1078) [his own...]

Having uprooted the sandalwood trees with the floods of water from their groves and waterfalls, let them emerge; let them abandon the host of serpents, let them destroy their heat, let them assume prosperity, and let them attain the state of being worshiped by the three worlds, thereby unveiling your fame. (1893)
wandering again and again in every direction, he gazed upon what was seen.
No tree has been seen by us that is equal to the *malayaja* (sandalwood), which,
when its sap is gathered through burning, cutting, and rubbing against stone surfaces,
spreads an ever-increasing and captivating fragrance. (1894)
Bhāmaha’s. (Su.ra. 1082) Where is the Malaya slope, the place of your birth, and where are you forest-dwellers?
Where indeed is the cutting by an axe, and where this journey to distant lands?
Where is the rubbing upon a slab of hard stone, and where this state of being like mud?
O friend sandalwood, do not fall into despair; your very virtues are your enemies.
1895 of *malayaja* (Su.ra. 1053); 52. *aśvattha*.

"O Lord of Elephants, having previously enjoyed hundreds of branches drawn from this very Pippala tree while resorting to its shade, why do you not rest here out of shame? Fate has indeed ordained such a conjunction that even by tens of millions of beings like yourself [this tree remains untouched]."
Having been made such and such by him, it has once again become like this with its sprouts. (1896)
— by Īśvarabhadra.

Truly, O best of Pippala trees, this path of the righteous has been adorned by you with your lofty and dense shade; what more can be said? You are a manifestation of Hari himself, and furthermore, the birds, drawn by the enjoyment of your fruit, have taken refuge in you.
That the male cuckoo utters its song is not at all appropriate [for the season].
(Śālikanātha; Su.ra. 10.61; by someone else)
Let the sprouts, which rival the palms of beautiful women, not close their eyes; let the glories of the flowers, sweet as the sound of a lute, not rise up in welcome;
and let there be no abundance of fruit dripping with sweet juices—nevertheless, [the mango tree is still the king].
The birth of Aśvattha, who is worthy of worship by the worlds, has occurred with ease. (1898) —
Umāpatidhara.
This [place] does not directly produce any joy, nor does it dispel calamities by disregarding them,
nor does it delight the wise even with its consoling eloquent verses; yet,
through the mere presence of that Blessed Lord, the husband of the Daughter of the Ocean, this [joy arises].
The aśvattha tree growing on that very ground removes the evil dreams that have been reported.
||1899|| Of that very [tree]...

The leaves of the *pippala* tree have been torn by swarms of insects; its branches have been uprooted from the very base by wild elephants; its bark has been stripped away by young elephants after they tasted it;
only the trunk remains—and even there, it is being gnawed by those suffering from the cold.
The villagers perceive on all sides the onset of the falling of axes;
it is that very [tree] of his.

53. The mango tree, having been watered again and again with various long-cherished cravings known since its birth, was somehow revived by waters released from a water-wheel before any [human] effort could be exerted.
O gardener, having brought the mango tree to a state fit for the attainment of a full abundance of fruit, why do you abandon your affection for it in an instant?
Some were burnt by forest fires, some perished from the tossing of violent winds,
and some gave up their lives due to the pain of being struck by the edge of a sword.
O mango tree, you alone among the lords of the earth triumph as a refuge for weary travelers;
yet fie on fate, for even you have been forced to admit swarms of insects within your core!
O mango tree of Vaidya Gadādhara, why do you in vain gratify the bees? Why do you [gratify] the cuckoos that constantly chatter sweetly? These are not pure, nor are they long-lasting.
Make those sprouts flourish day by day, bearing which you shall maintain your loftiness, and through fruits produced in abundance at every joint, you shall attain great height.
That sprout of coral which was seen by Vaidya Trivikrama, emerging from the mouth of a splitting joint of bone,
was obtained; and through the sequence beginning with the two halves [of the seed], it ascended to the height of a hundred palm trees.
Glossy with budding sprouts, dense with opening buds, flowering with wide-spreading petals,
and now bearing fruit with great excellence and bending low— what an extraordinary mango tree this is!
Of someone [Śā.pa. 1019, Hetuka; Sū.mu. 33.17, Harṣa; Su.ra. 1104]: In the season of flowers, some tree may be fragrant; in its unripe fruit, some other may be full of scent;
and when the fruit has matured, yet another may be sweet-smelling.
From the first appearance of its blossoms until the ripening of its fruit,
the fragrance of the mango tree alone manifests throughout the world.
Of Umāpatidhara:
54. The Aśoka tree, with its dense and cool shade and fresh sprouts...

O Aśoka tree, whether you remain with your glossy, charmingly fragrant clusters of blossoms, or whether you bear fruits that resemble them, we shall be free from sorrow merely by beholding your face. 1906
May the trees of Nāka possess a hundred sweet fruits and rows of blossoms praiseworthy for their fragrance.

In the spring season, there are hundreds of trees with particularly dense thickets; yet what other sight can rival the beauty of this *kaṅkelli* tree, which, with its fresh, dancing creepers radiant with garlands of blossoming clusters, displays such splendor? (1907)
Of those very trees, how many are there in this world? There is none other than this.
For the sake of its flowers, the practice of serving a woman’s feet became its course;
O Aśoka tree, if you turn inward out of joy because of a desire for fruit, then tell me, which method of *dohada* (fulfilling a longing) would be more praiseworthy? 1908.
for some [it was] after the arising of the flower of Jalacandra, and for others even without that.

In just two or three days here, the rows of fruits on the trees swell forth upon leaves that bear the likeness of rubies amidst their clusters of blossoms; alas, the very birth of the *kaṅkelli* tree has passed away, for its beauty lies only in its flowers, devoid of fruit.
O Umāpatidhara,
what use have you for humility, what use for loftiness, and what use for dense shade?

O Aśoka tree, what is the use of your playful foliage or this beauty of your flowers, since the multitude of travelers sitting at your base, though weary, do not daily eat their sweet and soft fruits to their heart's content while praising you with longing? (1910)
1910. By the poet-king Śrī Nārāyaṇa. (Śā.pā. 1004, Sū.mu. 33.32, by Śrī Bhojadeva; Su.ra. 1038, by someone).
55. The Silk-cotton Tree (Śālmali).
Let the *puṣpa* protect itself with thorns, gladdening the *ketakī*s with its fragrance;
moreover, this *panasa* possesses a fruit exceedingly pleasing to the heart, as sweet as ambrosia.
Yet you, *śālmali*, have neither scent in your flower nor flavor in your fruit—so why do you exist in vain?
O Nāgoka tree, you completely cover your trunk with poisonous thorns from the very root.
Its root is nourished by thorns and potsherds; its interior is pithless;
its flower is scentless; its fruit is useless for hunger; its leaves are never pleasing;
its growth serves only to attract vultures—alas, this is one thing, but the other must be told!
O brother Śālmalī tree, there is nothing in you worthy of your great size. (1912) [Of someone]
O wretch! Summoned from all directions by the magnificent display of its branches reaching to the ends of the horizon,
why do you run so swiftly with the vain hope of finding the fruit of the *śālmali* tree, when that very fruit is as fragile as a cluster of cotton-wool ready to burst at a single touch?
Even the paths ahead should not be looked upon by one who wanders with eyes closed, like the moon reflected in water. (1913) 1913 [This is the verse concerning] the moon in the water.
The spreading of its branches, which possesses the majesty of covering the vast expanse of the sky;
the abundance of its blossoms, which resembles a forest of red lotuses; and the supreme beauty of this silk-cotton tree (*śālmalitaru*) are beyond the reach of even the most eloquent words.
Nevertheless, alas, this fruit consisting of a mere succession of rays is not to be enjoyed.
(1914) — Umāpatidhara.

Thinking that from this flower, which is great by its very nature, a most magnificent fruit— charming, sweet, fragrant, and cool— is likely to be obtained, the parrot remains there, awaiting the perception of the time for the *śālmali* tree’s ripening.
...until he sees the cotton-wool emerging from the seam of its pod from within the fruit— this is by Śālikanātha (Su.ra. 1063).
56. O tree of the path, that you spread out such vast shade; that you satisfy [beings] with your sweet fruits;
that you are bowed down and yet you are lofty; and that you abide skillfully upon the road—[for these things, we offer praise].
O Lord of the Earth, that which you are generally extolled by other travelers along every path is precisely what you yourself are thought of by wayfarers for the sake of rest.
For someone, the sun is cruel overhead; the ground beneath his feet is harsh and stony; the wind blows, sweeping up clouds of dust; and the essence of the lake has grown thin.
Aha! Why did these travelers not lose their lives at that very moment, had they not entered beneath the tree whose leaves served as a parasol? (1917)

That young son of yours, Puruṣeṇa, who was covered with only three or four leaf-sprouts, whose sole means of sustenance was the water released by the clouds, and who had found his footing on the path of the virtuous— [he has been taken away].

Now, after a few days on this path, he has arrived at a place where the ground is overspread with the shade of a dense mass of leaves bent down by fruit— a result produced by his accumulation of demerit. (1918)
Tell me now, in this time of calamity, where are those birds who were formerly protected by Surabhi with fruits, leaves, and shade— that very tree of rest? Where are they for you now?
Blessed indeed are these tree barks, which show honor merely by being in proximity;
for it is without cutting them that this axe has fallen upon you. (1919)
Vittoka’s:
(Śārdūlavikrīḍita 985, Subhāṣitaratnabhāṇḍāgāra 1099) Why were you born at a crossroads? If you have dense shade, why?
If you are endowed with shade, why bear fruit? If you are richly laden with fruit, why are you bowed down?
O tree, endure now the pulling of your tips and branches,
the shaking, the crushing, and the breaking [caused] by people through their own wicked deeds. (1920)
Of someone: (Sakalāstaka 4.93, Śāpava 971, Sūktimuktāvalī 33.4) 57.
The tree of the wind-god [the *marutaru*], with its body densely covered by swarms of insects in the hollow at its root, is like a serpent.
O tree, we know that your head is distressed by rows of vultures and your lower parts are covered with thorns; thus, for a long time, you have been a dweller on the wrong path.
Nevertheless, even in this earth, you alone are the refuge for this plant. 1921
Where, in the *marudruma* [tree], was the very first teacher of Vaidya Gadādhara?
Even that sprout, which had quickly been plucked from somewhere by young women during a time of distress, was soon swallowed up by most terrifying camels. ||1922||
Alas, for Capaladeva,
the beauty of the flowers has become a mere memory, as their petals have withered and fallen away.
Though the birds have flown in every direction, despairing of any fruit from its sprouting,
and though the desert tree remains silent with its mass of roots exposed and its fibrous roots withered down to the underworld, it nevertheless meditates upon the untimely cloud.
In 1923, for Bhaṭṭaśālīya Pītāmbara,
the wind [was] at the tip of the nose, the water in the eyes, and the fire in the mind.
Are these desert lands not known for their stability even under the weight of conflagrations,
where travelers, in the frantic search for water across hundreds of directions,
long for the very trees they find to provide them with a state of irrigation through the clusters of sweat-drops from their own bodies? (1924)
1924. What greater blessing could there be for us than this, that we have endured Govinda for the sake of our very lives?
Having stripped the trees, alas, you burn them, O charcoal-maker! But what remedy is there for travelers distressed by sunbeams as fierce as thunderbolts in this shelterless desert wilderness? (1925)
1925 Gadādhara’s [verse] (Śā.pa. 1183, Sū.mu. 33.6, Su.ra. 1039).
58. Various Trees.
On a banyan tree rich with fruit, some fruit ripens with its essence fully manifest; among those fruits, a few seeds reach the stage of sprouting;
even among those, only one becomes an excellent sprout and attains that height.
That which the sacrificer runs toward to dispel his fatigue, as if toward his own mother—this is by Śālika (Śālikanātha). (Su.ra. 10.62)
Alas, by whom were you, O Campaka tree, planted here in this narrow lane near the vulgar folk of a wretched village, where greed increases through the growth of newly sprouted vegetables?
You are a sprout fit for the construction of a path broken by cows—
[this is] for the hero.
Outweigh the trees with the abundance of your fruits; touch the sky with your loftiness; and shroud all the quarters of space with your vast dimensions.
Yet, even so, no bird other than the crow can ever equal you.
Seeking its fruit, the *nimba* tree joyfully runs toward you, though you are by nature bitter—
O Lord of the Universe! (1928)
Because of their breadth, fragrance, and exceedingly sweet nature, those who are tormented by hunger and intent on filling their bellies have performed service to you here; yet,
being deluded by immediate gratification, they daily produce a state of ill-health.
O Panasa tree, we have not seen any lack of sweetness in you at the time of ripening.
(Umāpatidhara)

He who undergoes suffering for the sake of others is naturally sweet; indeed, even his transformation here is welcomed by all. Yet, due to cursed fate, he has not suddenly attained his appropriate maturity.
Is this a fault of the sugarcane, or rather of the desert land which lacks its virtues?
59. There is a desert, then a thicket of śamī trees, and beyond that a grove of khadira; further still is a dense thorn-bush where the cries of insects resound.
From here is a grove of jujube trees, and beyond that a stretch of barley fields;
where, O traveler, is that auspicious path? This is the desert, a land of ruin.
O Cloud, while you were sprinkling the entire universe with your common showers,
who indeed was not struck down by the sudden storm you brought about at that moment?
Even the heat of this very Mareṇa river was not dispelled by its shores, which were ignorant of the grace of sporting female swans and whose sandy banks had dried up from the subterranean depths.
O deer, after wandering here and there in the vicinity of King Anaṅga,
remain as a resident and do not again entertain the desire to set out upon the desert path.
In this place, where only a few men— those with weak arms and those whose hands are occupied with various vessels full of virtues— can obtain mere drops of water from the well. (1933)
O traveler, brother of Umāpatidhara, why do you run toward this [desert], which is filled with a flood of false mirage-waters, blinded by the affliction of a fiercely spreading thirst?
Indeed, these are the borders of the desert lands where, by cruel men, the entire water at the base of Pātāla— which benefits both oneself and others— has not been protected. (1934)
Drinking it again and again, drink this milk; sprinkle it on limb after limb; O friend, perform plungings and emergings from it over and over again.
O traveler, for these weary wayfarers who suffer intensely from the exhaustion of their remaining journey,
the desert— devoid of kinsmen— is now far ahead, and the path grows distant.
Of Dhanapāla. (Śā.pā. 1151, Sū.mu. 30.3) 60. O cloud, you are lofty; you are filled with waters.
These thirsty birds entreat you;
O cloud, this is your time for the service of others.
Where are you now in the midst of this fierce windstorm, and where are they?
O cloud,
beloved of the longing one,
cover the other quarters here and there!
Abandon this territory; the Sage born from a jar dwells here,
for even that ocean will not remain for you when his wrath rises, since you display your valor here only by drinking water again and again.
O Physician Gadādhara,
even if you were to rain down thousands of torrents every single day until the end of time, still—
O cloud, who can measure the exhaustion you endure within the unfathomable belly of the ocean?
If you were to release even a moment’s worth of your water upon the peaks of the mountains, would not your glories then spread forth in the guise of mountain torrents and rivers? (1938)
O Vāsudeva,
these are those fierce forest fires of the desert lands before you.

O cloud, it is not fitting for you to depart while sporting with the fierce winds of ill-nature, disregarding these trees whose leaves are scorched by the harsh rays of the sun licked by flames— trees whose bodies are withered and which are now bathed by the waters at the shore.
O Lord of Yoga,

"Let Kṛṣṇa be placed in the mind; let the Supreme Brahman be contemplated. (Bhartṛhari, Śatakatraya 3.11)

Those who accomplish the welfare of others even at the cost of their own self-interest are truly skillful; but those who exert themselves for the sake of others without contradicting their own self-interest are merely human rākṣasas— those by whom the welfare of others is sacrificed for the sake of their own ends.
But as for those who pointlessly destroy the welfare of others—who are they? We do not know.
Of that very [person]...
Is that even discernment where compassion does not flow spontaneously?
Is that even yoga in which there is no taste for benefiting others? Is that even dharma in which the cessation of malice toward others does not manifest?
Has anyone heard that which is the actual state of tranquility, yet does not lead [to it]? (Su.ra. 16.29, Ss 2.25)
A dog, with a mind focused on a swarm of worms, greedily eats a human bone— foul-smelling, loathsome, and drenched in saliva— yet, out of delight for its incomparable taste,
it does not hesitate even when seeing the Lord of the Gods standing nearby.
For a base creature does not take account of the worthlessness of its possessions. (2340) [Śūra, *Nītiśataka* 9.30; *Subhāṣitaratnabhāṇḍāgāra* 1628; *Sūktimuktāvalī* 2.9]

69. Now, for one who knows the inner self, this forest of existence is terrifying; this body is a house full of many cracks, and powerful Time is a thief, while the night of delusion is inevitably dark.
O people, take up the sword of wisdom and the shield of renunciation, don the armor of ethical conduct, and remain vigilant with steadfast vision.
O Silhaṇa,
my heart, which had long wandered astray and roamed at will along the perilous paths of the forest of sense-objects, is now distressed.
In this waveless, eternal ocean of supreme bliss— wherein all transformations have vanished through the loss of discernment, and which consists of the constant, unwavering delusion of stability—
(2342) [Note: The provided text fragment contains two verse numbers (2342) twice, indicating it is part of a larger work.]
Meditating upon that Primordial God on some bank of the celestial river, he was weary because his mental faculties were stained by the impurities of worldly existence.
With the movement of his fingers stilled by practice, his progress toward the senses subdued by the gentle sound of his lute played with world-weariness, he was absorbed in the supreme Brahman.
What need is there for a mere lump of earth for Śaṅkaradeva, or for Mount Meru following that,
or even for those called gods, who are but insects in the hollow hut of the cosmic egg?
Even within the three worlds, this is a further marvel: that he, who is graced by the bliss of compassion,
plunges into the flood of the nectar-filled ocean of the meditative absorption on non-duality of mind.
Not even one among the many names of Ballaṇa is here; that which is the small lotus in the water,
whose dwelling is in the drop, for whom even the nectars do not taste sweet in the process of experience.
O heart, bow forever to that eternal Brahman, by whose unfolding even the rays of the sun become as darkness.
For someone,
destiny first creates one who is a mine of all virtues.
If that jewel among men, the ornament of the earth, should then perish in an instant—alas, what a tragedy! What a lack of wisdom on the part of Fate! (2346)
Of someone: "The feet for the fatigue of the road; the wife for the sake of separation. (Sv 3126, Śā.pa. 4000, Sū.mu. 131.39, Su.ra. 1473)
If the Creator felt no shame while always bestowing upon me these things— speech for the sake of petitioning and a body subject to decay— is it not also a source of great weariness?
By Rājaśekhara. (Su.ra. 1321) The earth is not for support, nor are the realms of the Nāgas.

And for him whose human effort has been brought under control by previously accumulated non-virtue, there shall be no dwelling even among the inhabitants of heaven; even the wish-fulfilling tree does not fulfill his desires. (2348)
Of someone: (Su.ra.
1097) O you who are turned away from the side of the virtuous, and who are intent upon the destruction of your own family!
"O divine Destiny, enemy of the lineage of heroes, you are victorious!
— Umāpatidhara.

If erudition were not conjoined with wealth, it would not endure for very long; and if the moon, whose form is as beautiful as moonlight, did not possess its full orb in every direction, it would not exist;
likewise, if the fair-browed women did not possess the intoxication of youth born from their breasts until death, [their beauty would not persist].
"Fie on the Creator, by whom that Gaṅgādhara was made deformed in this world!"—
this was said by someone.
71. Let fate indeed act; however, let the wise man exert effort here and there, for the fruit that comes to him is only that which resides in the mind of destiny.
Of someone: (Sū.mu.
112.10) with a bent face, body hunched over a basket, and senses impaired by hunger.
Having dug a burrow himself, a rat fell at night into the mouth of a serpent;
satisfied by its flesh, the rat quickly departed by that very same path.
Remain well-settled: fate alone is turbulent in both the prosperity and the destruction of the world.
Of someone:
"That very Creator is to be revered, by whom the creation of the world was made exceedingly brilliant."

The wondrous variety of the arrangement of unprecedented objects in every single form is most marvelous; moreover, what else could be more extraordinary than this: that for Śakra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, [this world] serves as the key to the fruits of karma existing within the belly of the three worlds, brought directly before his eyes. (2353)
He who was the sole supreme friend of Daśaratha and the one who brought joy to the worlds.

Alas! That very moon—the possessor of digits, the glorious one, the auspicious jar in the rite of love, the source of nectar, and the crest-jewel of the Destroyer of Tripura—is now setting; indeed, the ways of fate are inherently treacherous.
Of someone: (Su.ra. 1370) "That the Lord's bow was broken by a child, and that the son of Jamadagni was conquered..."
That the earth was surrendered at the word of his preceptor, and that the ocean was bound by him—
each one of these deeds of Rāma, the destroyer of the ten-necked Rāvaṇa, how can it be described? Describe fate instead, for even he was suddenly reduced to a mere memory by it.
2355 Śrī Hanumān.
(Su.Ra. 1359) 72. Time.
Time alone, moving on with utter indifference, destroys many great men simultaneously, like an infinite force crushing mountains.
Of Bāṇa:
(Hc 5.2) Even birds that roam exclusively in the sky encounter calamity;
fish are caught by skillful men even from the ocean, despite its unfathomable waters.
What is ill-conducted here, and what is well-conducted? What merit is there in attaining a high position?
For Time, stretching out its hand in calamity, seizes one even from afar.

Here Bhīma displayed his prowess against Vasubhāga; here Droṇa released [his arrows] out of grief for Karṇa; here his horses were slain; and here Bhīṣma, the lord of charioteers, stood ready to fight.

The universal form was shown here to Arjuna by Hari out of curiosity; these are merely its outlines, for those who have performed meritorious deeds do not behold it, for Time indeed grinds everything down.
Nearby, the stream of Time flows incessantly, bringing terror to all, as it carries away the banks of day and night with its falling currents.
For here, as one falls, there is neither support nor even a turning back;
yet you remain so unperturbed—what is this delusion of yours? (2359)
Of someone:
(Ss 3.2) He is not compassionate toward the ignorant, nor does he delight in the assemblies of the virtuous;
indeed, he finds no relish in the amorous dalliances of women.
Time devours the entire world without agitation; alas, the acquaintance of those naturally cruel is surely never moistened by compassion. (2360)
73. The cremation ground of the Lord of Yoga was half-burnt; having joyfully brought much corpse-flesh from the funeral pyres, [he offered it].

A hungry ghost (preta), whose body is parched and bound with clearly visible veins due to his excessive consumption of food, threatens with a crooked and harsh gaze; he repeatedly strikes with fragments of bones, dried by the extraction of marrow, at the jackals that rush toward him out of greed for food. ||2361||
A certain ghost bites Jayāditya’s head with the tip of its fang.

One desires to lick the brain and seizes the head, while another, shaking his hand again and again, plucks away the raw flesh from a corpse cooked in a funeral pyre, its fingers like blazing flames of fire. 2362.
The vast outskirts of Nīlāmbara’s [palace] were encircled by rows of dancing, terrifying vetālas, and were exceedingly fierce and formidable.

How can the cremation ground, when beheld, not produce delight? There, *ḍākinīs* frolic at every step; there is the playful leaping of *pūtanās*; vultures, snatching morsels of food-remnants from the sport of *kolas*, tear away bones with joy as they feast upon them. (2363)
Of Umāpatidhara:
When the trees, filled with dense darkness produced by night, have awakened far away—
Look, the rows of jackals, their necks outstretched as they bend the earth with their two fore-paws,

drink the thick, dripping fat-water from the circles of boiling corpses— circles that have been stared upon by the jackals with the light of their flickering torches streaming from the caves of their own mouths.
From Pāṇini: (Su.Ra. 1529) [He emerged] from the funeral pyre, which possessed the intense radiance of a fire kindled by the striking of his flapping wings.
Having violently torn the corpse from its chest and, through a frantic scramble,
instantly devoured the abundant flesh as if it were glowing with heat by seizing it with fierce beaks, the old vulture— seeing the half-burnt meat still burning within him— quickly enters the water.
2365 Of that very [subject]. (Sū.mu. 94.6, Su.ra.
1528) 74. The Summary.
By travelers whose throats cannot reach the water and whose palates and gullets are parched,
who spit and vomit as they cry out, the salt-ocean is reproached:
"By whom was this false name of yours created in vain upon this pit of brine?"
Pāthodhi, jaladhi, payodhi, udadhi, vārāṃnidhi, and vāridhi are synonyms for the ocean.
[2366] Of knowledge:
Ah! Who is this blessed woman, standing at the window of the white palace, who,
with the tinkling of her anklets, awakens the god of the uneven arrows (Kāma),
whom the flower-bowed god previously roused when her lord of life had departed?
Emaciated by sleeplessness, she was mercilessly tormented day and night by showers of arrows—by someone. (Sū.mu. 49.11)
Those heads that once shone upon the head of Hara,
O Śiva, Śiva, now roll at the feet of vultures; alas, truly, the fruits of deeds committed in the past are indeed harsh.
The ripening of karmic actions manifests among living beings for some person.
Due to the expansion of the powerful bows of the Śārīs held aloft above them,
those fierce [birds] perched near the riverbanks were unable to plunge into the waters of the rivers at all when he set out.
The elephants drink water with their trunks extended straight upward—
[this is] of the Lord who bears the Gaṅgā.
In Sītā’s heart, which was as delicate as a śirīṣa flower, it struck with great force;
yet in the chest of Rāvaṇa, which was always blunted by the thunderbolt yet superior to a diamond,
it sank as deep as its feathers— oh, how we do not understand this!
O friend, which tree was it whose flower became the weapon of the Flower-Armed One? 2370 75. Of various kinds.
Does the wish-fulfilling cow not desire to stay there?

Does the wish-granting gem not respectfully long to take its place in the palm of the hand? And does the celestial kalpa-tree not strive to adorn the courtyard of the palace? Why then does he not wish to remain in the midst of his home?
When, it is said, the Creator becomes obedient to the command of some meritorious man. ||2371||2371|| Of someone.
Why do you hate us, who have exhausted the multitude of our faults?
For the discernment, purity, devotion to humility, and mastery over the senses found in the wealthy— who behold the rising fortune of the ignorant— are [the very things we lack].
Indeed, we have not acted out of partiality toward Cittapa, nor are we intent upon any ulterior motive.
Cittapa’s.
When the mind of one with dull intellect delights again and again in evils,
and when there is neither agitation nor peace, nor even a sense of revulsion while performing such censurable deeds—
will that not become like a blazing fire at dawn, the fierce hell known as Raurava?
The capital city of the illustrious Puruṣottamadeva resounds with the sharp noise of iron wheels and saws.

Vālmīki bound the ocean with mountains brought by monkeys, and Vyāsa likewise [bound it] with the arrows of Pārtha; yet, even so, no exaggeration is attributed to those two, for their words and their meanings are like things held on a scale. Nevertheless, this [work of mine], compared to our own compositions—
The world has extended its mouth to defile you; homage to you who stand firm against it! ||2374|| By Dharmakīrti. (Su.ra. 1726)
Palaces, with clouds resting upon their spires, and moats that rival the ocean, eventually attain equality with the ground over time— even those belonging to kings;
yet the fame of even a humble poet, consisting of the composition of true meanings, remains immortal in the realm of speech.
Unless one has witnessed the dissolution of the age (yuga), this [merit] is generally not exhausted again—
at the feet of Puruṣottama. ||2375||
76. Praise of the King:
The prostration at the lotus-born feet of the glorious primordial Boar repeatedly spreads joy to the wise and causes a fever in the ears of his enemies.
A true kinsman, an ocean of virtues, a staff for the blind,
and the very arm of the righteous King Lakṣmaṇasena, he was yet harsh in his punishment.
The court of law,

which had been suppressed by the humble words of the wealthy, found its way back through the weaving of speech from agitated mistresses, further nourished by the cries of children distressed by hunger.
O best of moving kalpa-trees, having drunk this nectar-like speech of yours which flows in harmony with the truth, may that fever in my ears— which has long been intense— be stilled, O servant Baṭu.
The ocean was the very limit of his lower lip in its extent and its wealth; he was the slave-boy of the great kings and the boat for the lords of bards in their battles. (2378)
Enough with Rājavetāla and Ādivarāha; we praise Baṭudāsa alone as supreme.
By him who uplifts the world, his face was not turned away.
(2379) — Umāpatidhara.

The wish-fulfilling creeper ascends to the very threshold of his courtyard, and the thought-gem rolls at his feet— he by whom the one who has seen the further shore of the ocean of merit has been beheld.
Baṭudāsadeva, who is skillful in pleasing all,
[is the work] of the poet-king Vyāsa.

This fifth stream, titled "The High and the Low," composed by Śrīdharadāsa in the *Saduktikarṇāmṛta*, may it spread manifold delight among connoisseurs (*rasika*). Thus ends the fifth stream, named "The High and the Low," in the *Saduktikarṇāmṛta* composed by the great provincial governor (mahāmāṇḍalika) Śrī Śrīdharadāsa. Verses: 76; Ślokas: 380. In this *Saduktikarṇāmṛta* composed by Śrīdharadāsa, there are five streams (*pravāha*) and four hundred and seventy-six verses (*vīci*). The total number of verses is two thousand three hundred and eighty. And the entire work consists of five thousand seven hundred and sixty. In this Śaka year [1027], during the twenty-first year of the reign of the illustrious King Lakṣmaṇasena—a time rich in aesthetic flavor—on the twentieth day of Phālguna, according to the course of the sun, Śrīdharadāsa composed this *Saduktikarṇāmṛta* out of curiosity for the sake of others. May the king be devoted to righteousness, and may this earth be supremely prosperous. May the pair of lotus feet of Keśava bestow happiness upon the world.
